docs.title: SRv6 for AI
docs.text:
SRv6 now runs inside some of the largest AI training networks in the world. OpenAI, Microsoft and Oracle use static SRv6 uSID source routing in their GPU fabrics through MRC, with no BGP in the backend. Meta and Alibaba use SRv6 traffic engineering to connect AI clusters across sites. The SRv6 for AI section covers who runs it, how it works, how to design a fabric, and the standards behind it.

docs.title: SRv6 (IPv6 Segment Routing) in a Nutshell
docs.text:
SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6) — also written Segment Routing v6, SR v6 or IPv6 Segment Routing — is the IPv6 data plane of the Segment Routing architecture (RFC 8402). It encodes forwarding instructions directly in IPv6 packet headers. Instead of relying on MPLS labels and signaling protocols like LDP or RSVP-TE, SRv6 uses native 128-bit IPv6 addresses as Segment Identifiers (SIDs) to program network paths and behaviors.

The source node builds an ordered list of segments that defines the packet's path and the processing at each hop. The active segment sits in the IPv6 destination address; when there is more than one, the rest travel in a Segment Routing Header (SRH) — and with uSID compression a whole path often fits in the destination address with no SRH at all. Transit routers simply forward on the destination address. This enables traffic engineering, VPN services, fast reroute and service function chaining on a plain IPv6 network.

Why choose SRv6 over traditional MPLS?

  • Simplified operations — No more MPLS label management, LDP, or RSVP
  • Native IPv6 — Uses the existing IPv6 data plane with no overlays
  • Network programmability — Define custom network behaviors with SRv6 functions (End, End.DT4, End.DX6, etc.)
  • Scalability — 128-bit SID space supports massive networks and micro-segmentation
  • Unified data plane — Single protocol stack for transport, VPN, and TE services

docs.title: SRv6 for AI: The Complete Guide
docs.text:
Leer en español · 日本語で読む

SRv6 has become a foundational protocol for AI networking. In GPU training fabrics, the sending NIC writes the exact path of every packet as a list of 16-bit uSIDs in the IPv6 destination address. Switches forward it with static tables and no routing protocol, and the transport sprays traffic across hundreds of explicit paths and abandons a failing path within microseconds. Between data centers, SRv6 traffic engineering steers AI traffic across the WAN. OpenAI, Microsoft and Oracle run SRv6 in their AI training fabrics, Meta on the backbone that interconnects its AI clusters, and Alibaba Cloud across its AI computing network.

Key facts (October 2026)

  • Production: MRC over static SRv6 trains frontier models in OpenAI's largest GB200 clusters, Microsoft's Fairwater supercomputers and Oracle's OCI clusters, including Abilene, Texas. Reported jobs reach 75,000 GPUs on fabrics designed for 131,072 GPUs in two tiers.
  • No BGP in the backend: switches keep small static uSID tables written once at install time. Failure handling moves to the NIC.
  • 40 bytes: with uSID, a full path fits in one IPv6 destination address, with no Segment Routing Header.
  • Scale-across: Meta (regional backbone, SRv6 TE in production since October 2026) and Alibaba (a dedicated "eCore for AI" with per-job SRv6 TE) use SRv6 between AI sites.
  • Standards: data plane in RFC 8986 and RFC 9800; AI usage in draft-filsfils-srv6ops-srv6-ai-backend (-05, authors from Cisco, OpenAI, Microsoft, Oracle, IBM, NVIDIA and Arrcus); transport in OCP MRC 1.0; switch software in SONiC since 202505.

docs.title: Why SRv6 fits AI networks
docs.text:
1. Deterministic paths, not hashing. AI training is a few huge, synchronized flows, which is the worst case for ECMP. With SRv6 the sender places every packet on a known path, so there are no hash collisions and path changes are exact. See SRv6 vs ECMP, Adaptive Routing and Ultra Ethernet.
  2. A static, simpler fabric. Static uSID routes replace BGP and its reconvergence. The MRC operators reboot spine switches without coordinating with training teams.
  3. Ground-truth visibility. A probe that uses the same uSID path as data tests exactly what the data experiences. OpenAI's Clustermapper probes every link every millisecond. See AI Fabric Telemetry.
  4. Minimal overhead. uSID (RFC 9800) packs up to six hops into one 128-bit address. The cost is a single 40-byte outer IPv6 header, handled at line rate by mainstream switch ASICs.
  5. One technology from GPU to WAN. The same SRv6 data plane serves the backend fabric, the data center frontend and the inter-DC backbone, with no MPLS gateways at the DC edge. See Scale-Across.
  6. Open and multi-vendor. NICs from NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom; switches from NVIDIA, Arista (on Broadcom) and Cisco Silicon One; open-source SONiC, SAI and FRR.

docs.title: What is SRv6 used for in AI networks?
docs.text: SRv6 is used in AI networks for two things. Inside a GPU training cluster, the NIC uses SRv6 uSIDs to choose the exact path of every packet through the backend fabric, which removes ECMP hash collisions, lets switches run without dynamic routing and makes every path testable. Between data centers, SRv6 traffic engineering steers AI traffic onto paths with the right latency and capacity.

docs.title: Does OpenAI use SRv6?
docs.text: Yes. OpenAI's largest GB200 training clusters use MRC (Multipath Reliable Connection) over static SRv6 uSID source routing, with dynamic routing disabled on the switches. OpenAI, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom and NVIDIA described the design in May 2026, and OpenAI presented its SRv6-based Clustermapper monitoring at the OCP Global Summit in October 2026.

docs.title: Why is SRv6 good for AI training?
docs.text: AI training sends a few very large, synchronized flows, so per-flow hashing creates collisions and the slowest path slows the whole job. SRv6 lets the sender place each packet on an explicit path, spray across hundreds of paths and abandon a failing path in microseconds. The switches stay static and simple, and uSID keeps the overhead to one 40-byte IPv6 header.

docs.title: What is the difference between SRv6 and Ultra Ethernet?
docs.text: Ultra Ethernet defines a transport that sprays packets using entropy values that switches hash, without changing the network layer. SRv6 is a network-layer source-routing technology that can map each entropy value to an explicit path. They are complementary: MRC combines Ultra Ethernet-derived transport features with SRv6 source routing.

docs.title: Which switches support SRv6 for AI fabrics?
docs.text: Published deployments use NVIDIA Spectrum-4 and Spectrum-5 (Cumulus or SONiC), Arista EOS on Broadcom Tomahawk 5, and Cisco Silicon One systems running SONiC. SONiC has supported static SRv6 uSID configuration since release 202505.

docs.title: Is SRv6 used for AI inference?
docs.text: Yes, in the WAN. Cisco's October 2026 AI inference blueprint for service providers and neoclouds uses SRv6 uSID as the transport, with a Flex-Algo plane per inference SLA and BGP color to steer each inference service onto its plane. See SRv6 for AI Inference WAN.

docs.title: Is SRv6 used between AI data centers?
docs.text: Yes. Meta uses SRv6 traffic engineering on the regional backbone that interconnects its data center campuses and AI clusters, and Alibaba Cloud runs a dedicated SRv6 network for multi-site AI training with per-job traffic engineering.

docs.title: SRv6 AI Fabric Design
docs.text:
This page turns the public designs behind MRC and the IETF draft SRv6 for Deterministic Path Placement in AI Backends into a practical blueprint for building an SRv6 uSID GPU backend fabric. The model is simple. The switches are static SRv6 transit nodes, the NIC writes the path of every packet into the IPv6 destination address, and an orchestrator tells the NICs which paths exist.

The design in five lines

  1. Two-tier Clos, split into parallel planes (4 or 8) so it reaches 100K+ GPUs without a third tier.
  2. One SRv6 block for the fabric and one 16-bit uN uSID per switch (plus uSIDs for last-hop ports).
  3. Static tables on every switch: its own uSID plus one /48 route per neighbor. No BGP or IGP is needed for the backend.
  4. The NIC encapsulates RoCEv2 in an outer IPv6 header whose destination address is the path: up to six uSIDs, no SRH, 40 bytes of overhead.
  5. The transport (MRC or similar) sprays across many paths and abandons failing ones; probes use the same encoding to test every link.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role Responsibility Changes at run time? Orchestrator Discovers topology and uSIDs at bring-up; gives each NIC its path templates Rarely (topology changes) Switch uN shift-and-forward on static /48 routes No NIC Builds the uSID path per packet, encapsulates and decapsulates, reacts to ECN, trims, loss Per packet Host agent Probes paths, maintains denylists, configures NIC path profiles Continuously

The IETF draft is explicit that this "is not switch adaptive routing": switches never change their decisions. Only the source does.

docs.title: Step 1: Topology
docs.text:
Use the multi-plane two-tier Clos described in the MRC paper:

  • Break each 800G NIC into 8 × 100G (or 4 × 200G) ports, one per plane.
  • In each plane, 51.2 Tb/s switches run as 512 × 100G. A T0 has 256 NIC-facing ports and 256 uplinks, and a T1 connects to 512 T0s.
  • Capacity: 512 T0 × 256 NICs = 131,072 GPUs in two tiers. Microsoft has shown variants of the design up to 524,288 GPUs.
  • Paths: T0-local (NIC → T0 → NIC) or cross-T1 (NIC → T0 → T1 → T0 → NIC). Every path stays inside one plane.

The draft's minimal example is the same idea at small scale: two spines, four leaves, and NICs dual-homed to two leaves.

docs.title: Step 2: Addressing plan
docs.text:
Pick one block for the backend: the IANA SRv6 block 5f00::/16 (RFC 9602) or a ULA such as fcbb:bb00::/32. The IETF draft uses 5f00:0::/32, and the MRC paper uses a 32-bit block followed by 16-bit uSIDs (the F3216 format of RFC 9800).

Each switch gets one 16-bit uN uSID. MRC's NICs copy the plane number into every uSID, so it pays to make the plane a field of the uSID. One possible plan for 8 planes:

16-bit uSID = | type (2) | plane (3) | index (11) |
  type 00 = T0 switch     index 0-511
  type 01 = T1 switch     index 0-255
  type 10 = last-hop port index 0-255 (the T0 downlink to a NIC)

Illustrative plan

This bit layout is an example built on the published constraints: 16-bit uN uSIDs, the plane copied into each uSID, and the last hop encoded as a port. The MRC paper does not publish its own numbering. Any scheme works if uSIDs are unique within a plane and a NIC can compute them from the plane and indices.

A cross-T1 path then looks like this:

DA = block | T0(src) | T1 | T0(dst) | PORT(dst) | 0000 | 0000

Four uSIDs fit with room to spare. Six uSIDs fit in the destination address without an SRH, which is enough to pin a five-hop path through a three-tier Clos (leaf, spine, super-spine, spine, leaf). An SRH is needed only beyond six instructions.

The IETF draft walks through the same encoding on its small example:

GPU1 → GPU3 via Leaf1, Spine5, Leaf3:   5f00:0:0100:0500:0300::
GPU2 → GPU3 via Leaf2, Spine6, Leaf4:   5f00:0:0200:0600:0400::
Avoid congested Spine5 (NIC rewrite):   5f00:0:0100:0600:0300::

docs.title: Step 3: Static switch tables
docs.text:
Each switch needs exactly:

Switch Entries Count (8-plane, 131K GPUs) T0 its own uN SID; a /48 route to each T1's uSID (uplink); a /48 route to each port uSID (downlink) 1 + 256 + 256 = 513 T1 its own uN SID; a /48 route to each T0's uSID (downlink) 1 + 512 = 513

The table size grows with the switch radix, not with the number of paths, flows or GPUs, and it is written once. The MRC paper describes these routes as configured at install time and generally never changed. Microsoft's NANOG 96 example uses the same pattern: static uN SIDs as /48s plus a static route to each neighbor's SID.

docs.title: SONiC
docs.text:
Since SONiC 202505, static SRv6 is configured in CONFIG_DB with two tables, which bgpcfgd compiles into FRR (the 202505 release notes rate the feature Alpha). This is the format from the SONiC static SRv6 design document:

{
  "SRV6_MY_LOCATORS": {
    "loc1": { "prefix": "FCBB:BB00:0103::", "block_len": "32", "node_len": "16", "func_len": "16", "arg_len": "0" }
  },
  "SRV6_MY_SIDS": {
    "loc1|FCBB:BB00:0103::/48": { "action": "uN", "decap_dscp_mode": "pipe" }
  }
}

bgpcfgd renders it as FRR static SIDs:

segment-routing
 srv6
  locators
   locator loc1
    prefix fcbb:bb00:103::/48 block-len 32 node-len 16 func-bits 16
    behavior usid
  static-sids
   sid fcbb:bb00:103::/48 locator loc1 behavior uN

The neighbor routes (fcbb:bb00:<neighbor uSID>::/48 pointing at the port that faces that neighbor) are ordinary static IPv6 routes.

SONiC release SRv6 static configuration via CONFIG_DB FRR 202505 uN, uDT46 10.3 202511 uN, uDT46 (FRR itself also supports static uA) 10.4.1 202605 uN, uDT46 10.5.4 master (Aug 2026 onward) adds uA with interface and optional adj fields 10.7.1

The SAI and orchagent layers already map uN, uA, uDT4/6/46 and uDX4/6 to the ASIC. See SONiC and SONiC & SAI.

docs.title: uN or uA?
docs.text:
• uN names a switch. The switch forwards the shifted address on its route to the next uSID, so a T0 that has several parallel links to the same T1 still hashes across them.
  • uA names a specific link (an adjacency). It is the tool for pinning one member of a bundle. OpenAI's Clustermapper team asked vendors at OCP 2026 for exactly this: a supported way to select individual links among parallel adjacencies.

The MRC deployment uses uN. Meta's SRv6 backbone uses uA (scale-across). The IETF draft allows either.

docs.title: Step 4: The NIC
docs.text:
• Encapsulation: H.Encaps.Red, which places the path in the outer destination address with no SRH when it fits. The inner IPv6 destination is the remote NIC's own address, which it uses to recognize and decapsulate the packet.
  • Path set: per connection, a set of paths (MRC: 128–256 entropy values) spread evenly across planes. The orchestrator provides a template per destination group, and the NIC fills in the plane and uplink fields.
  • Reaction: on ECN, the NIC deprioritizes a path for a while; on untrimmed loss, it retires the path at once and uses a backup; background probes restore paths that recover.
  • Hardware: AMD lists "NIC-based source routing (SR/SRv6)" for its Vulcano 800G AI NIC. ConnectX-8, Pollara and Thor Ultra run MRC over SRv6 in the published clusters.

For lab work, Linux can play the NIC role. With encap.red and a single uSID container, no SRH is added (see SRv6 on Linux):

# Path to the remote GPU host: src T0 0103 -> T1 0b07 -> dst T0 0141 -> port 0012
ip -6 route add 2001:db8:3::3/128 \
  encap seg6 mode encap.red segs fcbb:bb00:0103:0b07:0141:0012:: dev eth0

docs.title: Step 5: Telemetry and probing
docs.text: Give every host the ability to probe paths that loop back to itself through a T0 and through each T1, and run the probes continuously. This is what turns a static fabric into a well-observed one. See AI Fabric Telemetry.

docs.title: Hardware support (published)
docs.text:
Vendor Published SRv6 capability relevant to AI backends NVIDIA Spectrum-⅘ with Cumulus or SONiC forward SRv6 for MRC (MRC paper). Cumulus Linux 5.18 documents static uN and uA on Spectrum-4. Arista EOS on Broadcom Tomahawk 5 forwards SRv6 for MRC. EOS 4.36.2F documents uN (NEXT-CSID) in F3216 format. Broadcom Tomahawk 5 switches and Thor Ultra NICs in the MRC clusters. Cisco Silicon One G200 is marketed with native SRv6 uSID for GPU-to-GPU path steering. SRv6 on a SONiC system depends on the vendor's SAI implementation, so confirm uSID support for the specific Silicon One platform and SONiC image. AMD Vulcano NIC: NIC-based SR/SRv6 source routing; Pollara and Vulcano run MRC.

Check each vendor's current documentation for the exact behaviors and formats, because support differs. Arista's documentation lists F3216 only and H.Encaps.Red as unsupported on the switch, which matters if the switch rather than the NIC is the head-end.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
A host that can write any SRv6 path can steer traffic anywhere in the fabric. The IETF draft recommends:

  • limiting which workloads may originate SRv6 traffic;
  • constraining hosts to paths the orchestrator has authorized;
  • keeping the backend block unreachable from the frontend and the Internet, and filtering it at every boundary (SRv6 Security, SID block filtering).

For multi-tenant GPU clouds, adding a VPN service SID (for example uDT46 in a tenant VRF) at the end of the path separates tenants on the same fabric.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Planes, radix and tiers sized for the target GPU count
  • One block; uSIDs unique per plane; plane encoded in the uSID
  • Static uN SID plus neighbor /48 routes on every switch; no dynamic routing on the backend
  • Fabric MTU sized for the extra 40-byte outer IPv6 header
  • NICs (or a host stack) able to encapsulate H.Encaps.Red per packet
  • Orchestrator that publishes path templates and denylists to NICs
  • Continuous self-probing of every NIC–T0 and T0–T1 link
  • SRv6 origination restricted to authorized workloads; block filtered at the edge

docs.title: Do AI fabrics with SRv6 still need BGP?
docs.text: Not for the backend data path in the static model. The MRC deployments at OpenAI and Microsoft disable dynamic routing on backend switches and use static uSID routes configured at install time. BGP may still run elsewhere, for example on the frontend network or for management.

docs.title: How many uSIDs does an AI fabric path need?
docs.text: A path through a two-tier Clos needs three or four uSIDs: source leaf, spine, destination leaf and optionally the last-hop port. Six uSIDs fit in the IPv6 destination address without a Segment Routing Header, enough for a five-hop path through a three-tier Clos.

docs.title: Does SONiC support SRv6 for AI backends?
docs.text: Yes. SONiC 202505 added static SRv6 configuration through the SRV6_MY_LOCATORS and SRV6_MY_SIDS CONFIG_DB tables, with uN and uDT46 behaviors. Support for the uA behavior in CONFIG_DB was merged to the master branch in August 2026.

docs.title: What is the overhead of SRv6 in an AI fabric?
docs.text: When the whole path fits in one uSID container, the only overhead is the 40-byte outer IPv6 header. No Segment Routing Header is added.

docs.title: AI Fabric Telemetry with SRv6
docs.text: In an AI backend fabric, the expensive failures are not the clean ones. A link that goes down is noticed at once. The costly cases are gray failures: a switch whose control plane and links are up but that has stopped forwarding, or a link that drops a small share of packets. The training job slows down or stalls, and switch counters look healthy. SRv6 helps because it makes the exact path of every probe explicit, so the network can be tested the same way the GPUs use it.

docs.title: Why hash-based probing falls short
docs.text:
The classic data center approach is a pingmesh: every server pings a sample of other servers and the results are aggregated. On an ECMP fabric this has two built-in limits:

  • The probe's path is unknown. Each probe is hashed onto one of many equal-cost paths. When it is lost, you know that some path between two hosts is bad, not which link or switch.
  • The probe may not follow the data. A probe with a different 5-tuple from the training traffic can hash onto a different path, so a healthy probe says little about the flow that is actually slow.

Probing the switches directly with ICMP has its own limit: those packets go to the switch CPU, which rate-limits them, and they test the control plane rather than the forwarding ASIC.

docs.title: Source-routed probes
docs.text:
With SRv6 uSID, a host can send a probe along an explicit path that loops back to itself: out to its top-of-rack switch (T0), optionally up to a specific spine (T1), and back down to the same host. Because the path is in the destination address:

  • the probe crosses exactly the links and switches you name;
  • switches forward it as ordinary data-plane traffic at line rate, with no CPU involvement and no rate limiting;
  • a probe that uses the same path as a data packet, for example the same MRC entropy value, tests exactly what that packet would experience;
  • the sender is also the receiver, so the result needs no coordination with a remote host.
  • Host NIC → T0 switch (probe 1: T0 and back)
  • T0 switch → Host NIC
  • Host NIC → T0 switch (probe 2: up to a T1 and back)
  • T0 switch → T1 switch
  • T1 switch → T0 switch
  • T0 switch → Host NIC
graph LR
    H[Host NIC] -->|probe 1: T0 and back| T0[T0 switch]
    T0 --> H
    H -->|probe 2: up to a T1 and back| T0b[T0 switch]
    T0b --> T1[T1 switch]
    T1 --> T0b
    T0b --> H

docs.title: Localizing faults by tier
docs.text:
Comparing the two kinds of self-probe narrows a fault down quickly:

T0 self-probe T1 self-probe Most likely fault OK OK Healthy Fail Fail NIC–T0 link or the T0 switch OK Fail (one T1) That T0–T1 link or that T1 OK Fail (same T1 from many T0s) The T1 switch itself OK Fail (one T1, from one T0 only) The T0–T1 link between them

Aggregating results from many hosts is what turns "one path is bad" into "this specific link or switch is bad".

docs.title: Clustermapper: SRv6 probing in production
docs.text:
OpenAI's Clustermapper, described in the MRC paper and presented at the OCP Global Summit in October 2026, applies this method at the scale of 100K-GPU-class clusters:

  • An agent on every node probes each directly connected T0 (16 or 32 of them, one per NIC port across four NICs) with probes source-routed to the T0 and back, and probes a subset of T1s the same way.
  • Together, the agents probe every link in the network every millisecond. Probing runs continuously, even when no job is running, because the cost is negligible.
  • The resulting link-health map can feed denylists that tell MRC NICs which paths to avoid. In practice, pre-training has not needed denylists for spine-side (T0–T1) failures, because MRC maps those out by itself within microseconds.
  • In one production incident, a T1 switch stopped forwarding while it still appeared up. Automation detected it, and the switch was rebooted without coordination with the training team.

The OCP 2026 talk also set out what is still missing: switch and ASIC vendors (and SONiC) should qualify longer SRv6 paths that use an SRH, and provide a supported way to select one link when two switches have several parallel adjacencies. It also asked operators to make path testing part of fabric acceptance, including payload-integrity checks.

Why it matters

Routing-protocol telemetry tells you what the control plane believes. Source-routed probing tells you what the forwarding plane does, on the exact paths the GPUs use. In a fabric without dynamic routing, such as an MRC fabric, this is the main health signal.

docs.title: Complementary SRv6 telemetry
docs.text:
Source-routed self-probes sit alongside the standard SRv6 operations toolset:

Tool What it adds in an AI fabric Page SRv6 OAM (RFC 9259) Ping and traceroute to SIDs, and the O-flag for marking packets for telemetry OAM & Troubleshooting STAMP / SRPM Standard one-way and two-way delay and loss measurement along explicit SRv6 paths Performance Measurement IPFIX for SRv6 (RFC 9487) Flow records that include SRv6 fields such as the active SID and segment list RFC 9487 Path Tracing (IETF draft) Hop-by-hop timestamps and interface IDs recorded in a compact form in the packet, for ECMP-aware path discovery draft-filsfils-ippm-path-tracing Streaming telemetry Queue occupancy, ECN marks, drops and trimming counters from switches Telemetry

docs.title: Operational checklist
docs.text:
• Give every switch an SRv6 locator and uN uSID so that any host can build a self-probe through it
  • Probe every NIC–T0 and T0–T1 link continuously from the hosts, not only during incidents
  • Use the same path encoding for probes as for data, so a probe result maps one-to-one to a data path
  • Feed probe results into path denylists or load-balancing weights on the NICs
  • Track "up but not forwarding" as its own failure class and automate the reboot or drain
  • Add explicit-path testing, with payload-integrity checks, to fabric acceptance before handing it to training

docs.title: What is Clustermapper?
docs.text: Clustermapper is OpenAI's agent-based monitoring system for AI backend networks. An agent on every node sends SRv6 source-routed probes to its directly connected switches and to spine switches and back to itself, so that together the agents test every link every millisecond and pinpoint failed or lossy links and switches.

docs.title: Why use SRv6 for network probing instead of ping?
docs.text: A normal ping on an ECMP fabric follows a hashed path that you cannot see, and pings to a switch are handled and rate-limited by its CPU. An SRv6 probe carries its exact path in the destination address and is forwarded in hardware like data traffic, so a lost probe identifies the specific link or switch that failed.

docs.title: What is a gray failure in an AI fabric?
docs.text: A gray failure is a partial failure that normal monitoring misses, such as a switch that reports its links and control plane as up but no longer forwards packets, or a link with a low but steady loss rate. In synchronized AI training, a single gray failure can slow down the entire job.

docs.title: AI Networking Glossary
docs.text: AI training clusters bring two vocabularies together: the GPU/HPC world (collectives, RDMA, job completion time) and the routing world (Clos, ECMP, SIDs). This glossary defines the terms you need to read the rest of the SRv6 for AI section, with a note on where SRv6 fits for each.

docs.title: Workloads and collectives
docs.text: All-reduce A collective operation in which every GPU contributes a buffer and every GPU receives the element-wise sum (or other reduction) of all buffers. Data-parallel training runs an all-reduce of the gradients at every step, which makes it the dominant source of backend traffic. All-to-all A collective in which every GPU sends a distinct chunk to every other GPU. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models use it to route tokens to experts. It creates many simultaneous flows between all pairs of nodes, which is where hash-based load balancing suffers most. Collective communication library (NCCL, RCCL) The software that implements collectives on GPUs: NCCL for NVIDIA, RCCL for AMD. It decides the algorithm (ring, tree) and opens the network connections, so its traffic pattern is what the fabric actually sees. Job completion time (JCT) The wall-clock time of a training job, or of one training step. Collectives are synchronous, so a step finishes only when the slowest flow finishes: one congested link delays every GPU in the job. This is why AI fabrics are judged on tail latency rather than average throughput. Elephant flow A long-lived, high-bandwidth flow. AI training produces few, very large flows with low entropy (few distinct 5-tuples), the worst case for per-flow hashing. Checkpointing Periodically writing model state to storage so training can resume after a failure. Checkpoint traffic usually runs on the frontend or storage network, not the GPU backend.

docs.title: Cluster networks
docs.text: Backend (scale-out) network The dedicated network that connects GPU servers to each other for collective traffic, typically RoCEv2 or InfiniBand at 400G–800G per GPU NIC. SRv6 for AI is about this network. See SRv6 AI Fabric Design. Frontend network The conventional data center network for storage, management, user traffic and job scheduling. It is often a separate fabric from the backend. Scale-up network The very high-bandwidth domain inside a server or rack that lets GPUs share memory semantics (for example NVLink, or UALink). It is not IP-routed, so SRv6 does not apply inside it. Scale-across Connecting AI clusters in different buildings or data centers so that a single training job, or a group of jobs, can span them. This is where AI meets the WAN and backbone. See SRv6 for Multi-Datacenter AI. Rail-optimized topology A design in which GPU n of every server connects to the same leaf ("rail"), so most collective traffic between same-index GPUs stays one hop away. Multi-plane fabric A backend split into several independent parallel networks ("planes"). Each NIC port, or each lane group of a NIC port, attaches to a different plane. More planes give each switch more effective radix, so a large cluster fits in fewer tiers, and the loss of one link removes a smaller share of a node's bandwidth. MRC uses this design. Clos / fat-tree The leaf-spine (two-tier) or leaf-spine-superspine (three-tier) topology used by almost every AI backend. It provides many equal-cost paths between any two GPUs, and the question is how to use them evenly.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: RDMA Remote Direct Memory Access: a NIC writes directly into the memory of a remote host without involving its CPU. GPU collectives run over RDMA, usually GPUDirect RDMA straight to GPU memory. RoCEv2 RDMA over Converged Ethernet version 2: RDMA carried in UDP/IP (UDP port 4791), so it is routable and can be carried inside SRv6. Classic RoCEv2 expects in-order delivery and recovers poorly from loss, which is why it is usually paired with a lossless fabric (PFC) and per-flow ECMP. Queue pair (QP) The RDMA connection endpoint, a pair of send and receive queues. Traffic of one QP traditionally follows one network path, because the path is chosen by hashing its 5-tuple. PFC (Priority Flow Control) IEEE 802.1Qbb link-level pause per traffic class, used to make Ethernet lossless for RoCEv2. It prevents drops but can cause head-of-line blocking and congestion spreading. ECN / DCQCN Explicit Congestion Notification marks packets at congested queues; DCQCN is the congestion-control algorithm that RoCEv2 NICs commonly use to slow down in response. Multipath transport A transport that deliberately spreads one connection over many paths and tolerates out-of-order arrival. MRC and the Ultra Ethernet Transport are examples. Multipath transport is the natural partner of SRv6 source routing: the transport chooses among paths, and SRv6 makes each path explicit.

docs.title: Load balancing
docs.text: ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) The switch picks one of several equal-cost next hops by hashing packet header fields. It works well for many small flows and badly for a few elephant flows: two large flows that hash to the same link halve each other's throughput while other links stay idle. Hash collision / polarization Two or more flows landing on the same link because of the hash (collision), or every switch making correlated choices so that some paths are never used (polarization). Both lengthen JCT. Entropy / entropy value (EV) Header bits that vary per flow or per packet so that hashing spreads traffic. In MRC, an entropy value is a per-path identifier the NIC chooses; each EV maps to one explicit SRv6 path, so changing the EV changes the path deterministically rather than probabilistically. Packet spraying Sending consecutive packets of the same flow over different paths. It gives near-perfect load balance but delivers packets out of order, so it needs a transport that handles reordering. Flowlet switching Moving a flow to a new path only during a gap in its packets that is long enough for reordering not to occur. It is a middle ground between per-flow ECMP and per-packet spraying. Adaptive routing Switches choose the egress port per packet or per flowlet based on local queue occupancy. It is used in InfiniBand and in some Ethernet AI fabrics. It reacts to congestion but makes the path invisible and hard to reproduce. Deterministic path placement The sender (host, NIC or controller) chooses the exact path of each flow or packet and encodes it in the packet, for example as an SRv6 uSID list. The network then forwards without making any load-balancing decision. See SRv6 vs ECMP, Adaptive Routing and InfiniBand.

docs.title: SRv6 terms in AI fabrics
docs.text: uSID (micro-SID) A compressed SRv6 SID of 16 bits carried inside a 128-bit IPv6 destination address together with a shared block prefix, so that one address holds several hops. Standardized as the NEXT-C-SID flavor in RFC 9800. See uSID compression. uN The uSID "node" behavior: the switch recognizes its own uSID at the front of the active container, shifts the remaining uSIDs left and forwards on the new destination address. In AI fabrics, a path is simply the list of uN uSIDs of the switches it traverses. uA The uSID "adjacency" behavior: like uN but forwards out of one specific link, for when the path must name an exact link rather than a switch. Locator block The common prefix shared by all uSIDs in a domain, for example a 32-bit block. Every switch advertises or is configured with its uSIDs under this block. DA-only encapsulation When the whole path fits in one uSID container, the packet carries no Segment Routing Header at all: just an outer IPv6 header whose destination address is the path. This keeps AI traffic overhead at 40 bytes (the IPv6 header) and keeps processing on the fast path of every ASIC.

docs.title: SRv6 for AI Inference WAN
docs.text:
Training happens in a few giant GPU clusters. Inference happens everywhere. Prompts come from enterprise sites, homes and phones, and the models that answer them run in edge cabinets, metro sites, regional data centers and other clouds. The network between them decides the time to first token, whether regulated data stays in the country, and whether a voice agent feels instant or broken.

In October 2026 Cisco published an AI Inference White Paper: Architecture for Wide Area Networks, a high-level design for service providers and neoclouds. Its transport is SRv6 uSID, with a Flex-Algo plane per inference SLA and BGP color to put each inference service on its plane. This page explains that design in vendor-neutral terms and maps every building block to its standard.

In one paragraph

Every inference location, from a far-edge cabinet to a regional facility, is treated as a data center. One SRv6 uSID backbone connects them to each other (DCI) and to enterprise and consumer access. The IGP computes several planes with Flex-Algo: best effort plus one or more inference planes (low latency, sovereign, secure links). Each plane has its own locator block inside 5f00::/16. The router in front of an inference service advertises its prefix in BGP with a color that names the plane, and every access router then encapsulates traffic for that prefix with the matching SRv6 SID. No per-request path computation: the planes are computed before the first prompt arrives.

docs.title: Why inference is a WAN problem
docs.text:
Driver What it means for the network Latency Voice agents, robotics and industrial vision cannot absorb a cross-continent round trip, so inference moves toward users Sovereignty Prompts and responses carry regulated data that must stay in a country or facility, so paths must be constrained, not just short Economics Many smaller GPU sites pooled as one capacity reduce peak contention and token cost, which needs any-to-any connectivity between sites Data gravity Video and sensor data is cheaper to process where it is produced; only the result crosses the backbone

The blueprint places inference in four tiers, all reached through the same WAN:

Tier Where Typical role Far edge Access site or street cabinet Latency-critical, lightweight models; first-hop inference Metro edge Aggregation or metro site Mainstream interactive inference for a metro Central edge Regional data center or central office Large models, model hosting, capacity pooling, DCI anchor Peering Cloud or private peering Models the provider does not host

docs.title: The design, layer by layer
docs.text:
Layer Choice in the blueprint Standard Data plane SRv6 with uSID RFC 8986, RFC 9800 Addressing IANA SRv6 block, one /32 per plane RFC 9602, draft-ietf-srv6ops-srv6addressing IGP IS-IS, multiple domains, summarization at the borders RFC 9352 SLA planes Flex-Algo per plane RFC 9350, Flex-Algo Steering BGP color on service routes; SR-TE on demand for tactical cases; PCE between domains RFC 9256, RFC 9830, RFC 9603 Services L3VPN (VPNv4/VPNv6), EVPN, multicast VPN RFC 9252, BGP overlay Protection Fast reroute; with Flex-Algo, TI-LFA computes repairs per plane RFC 9855, TI-LFA Assurance SR Performance Measurement (TWAMP Light), PTP timing SRPM Transport security MACsec or IPsec, post-quantum ready Security

Nothing in this list is Cisco-specific. Every building block is an IETF standard that other SRv6 implementations also ship; see the support matrix.

docs.title: SLA planes with Flex-Algo
docs.text:
Each plane is a Flex-Algo topology with its own constraints: lowest delay, links with a given affinity (for example only encrypted links), links inside one jurisdiction, or disjointness from another plane. The IGP computes every plane on every router ahead of time, so a new inference session finds its path already programmed.

Each plane gets its own locator block. The blueprint's example uses 5f00:bb00::/32 for best effort (algorithm 0) and 5f00:bb01::/32 for the inference plane (Flex-Algo 128). Nodes keep the same low-order bits in every plane, so the border between metro and backbone can advertise one summary per plane instead of every node locator. That is what lets the design grow to many inference sites without a routing-table explosion.

  • Enterprise or subscriber → Access PE
  • Access PE → Metro P1 (Flex-Algo 128 · low delay)
  • Metro P1 → Core P1
  • Core P1 → DCI
  • Metro P1 → Core P3
  • Core P3 → DCI
  • Access PE → Metro P2 (Algo 0 · best effort)
  • Metro P2 → Core P2
  • Core P2 → DCI
  • DCI → AI front-end leaf
  • AI front-end leaf → AI gateway / LLM
graph TB
    U[Enterprise or subscriber] --> A[Access PE]
    A i1@-->|Flex-Algo 128 · low delay| M1[Metro P1]
    M1 i2@--> C1[Core P1]
    C1 i3@--> D[DCI]
    M1 r1@--> C3[Core P3]
    C3 r2@--> D
    A b1@-.->|Algo 0 · best effort| M2[Metro P2]
    M2 b2@-.-> C2[Core P2]
    C2 b3@-.-> D
    D --> L[AI front-end leaf] --> G[AI gateway / LLM]
    i1@{ animate: true }
    i2@{ animate: true }
    i3@{ animate: true }

Inference traffic rides the Flex-Algo 128 plane; everything else stays on best effort. If a link in the inference plane fails, TI-LFA computes the repair inside the same Flex-Algo topology, so inference traffic stays on a path that meets the plane's constraints instead of falling back to best effort.

docs.title: SLA signaling with BGP color
docs.text:
The router in front of an inference service, usually the DCI, advertises the service prefix in BGP VPNv4 or VPNv6 (or plain IPv4/IPv6 for the global table) with:

  • a color extended community whose value names the SLA plane, and
  • the SRv6 service SID for that VRF, allocated from the locator of that plane.

Every access router that imports the route encapsulates matching traffic with that SID, so packets toward the inference service follow the inference plane end to end. When a device in the AI front-end cannot set colors, it tags routes with a standard BGP community and the DCI translates it into a color. This is the same color-based steering defined for SR Policy (RFC 9256); with Flex-Algo, the color simply resolves to the plane's locator instead of to an explicit path.

docs.title: Connectivity models
docs.text:
The blueprint describes six ways to attach an inference component, and a real deployment mixes them along one application path (user to LLM router to model):

Model How it works Fits Local Both components hang off the same router; no transport needed Agent and gateway in one edge site Direct IP handoff Compute connects to a routed interface on the access or edge router, which advertises the prefix with its color Small front-ends at the edge AI front-end overlay The fabric uses EVPN over VXLAN; the DCI terminates VXLAN, looks up the VRF, and re-encapsulates in SRv6 toward the backbone (and the reverse) Large, multi-tenant regional data centers External peering The model sits in another network; the peering router colors the prefix (or translates a community) and removes SRv6 at the edge Cloud and third-party models Unified The front-end leaf joins the backbone IGP and does SRv6 encapsulation and plane steering itself Small and medium sites Shared IP endpoint One user address needs two SLAs: it is advertised from two VRFs with two colors and two SIDs, and each service imports the plane it needs Users reaching both web and inference services

docs.title: The DCI: where the data center meets the WAN
docs.text:
The DCI is the boundary between the AI front-end fabric (often EVPN-VXLAN on NX-OS or SONiC) and the SRv6 backbone. It does three jobs:

  1. Data-plane interworking. Terminate VXLAN (or front-end SRv6), do a Layer 3 lookup in the right VRF, re-encapsulate in SRv6 for the backbone.
  2. Control-plane interworking. Translate EVPN Route Type 5 routes from the fabric into VPNv4/VPNv6 routes for the backbone, keeping or adding the SLA color, and the reverse.
  3. Summarization. The fabric carries a host route per compute node; the DCI keeps those locally and advertises only aggregates to the backbone.

A lighter variant splits the job: a border leaf terminates VXLAN and hands plain IP to a PE that does the SRv6 side. The blueprint also notes that SRv6 uSID is an option inside the front-end fabric itself, which would remove the VXLAN-to-SRv6 translation entirely; that is the end-to-end model Nebius already runs.

docs.title: Inference WAN vs training fabric
docs.text:
SRv6 shows up at both ends of AI networking, but for opposite reasons:

Training back-end (MRC) Inference WAN (this page) Scope One data center, GPU to GPU Provider WAN, user to model and site to site Who picks the path The sending NIC, per packet The IGP (Flex-Algo planes) and BGP color, per service Control plane None in the switches: static uSID routes IS-IS with Flex-Algo, BGP services, optional PCE Goal Spray across 128–256 paths, bypass failed paths in tens of microseconds Meet a per-service SLA (delay, sovereignty, isolation) end to end Failure handling NIC retires the failed path TI-LFA within the plane, then IGP convergence Typical traffic Collective operations (all-reduce) Prompts and tokens, KV-cache and model transfers between sites

Between the two sits scale-across: SRv6 traffic engineering between AI data centers for training jobs that span sites.

docs.title: What to take from it
docs.text:
• SRv6 uSID moved from hyperscaler back-ends into a vendor's provider-WAN reference design. The inference blueprint makes SRv6 uSID the primary transport and lists SR-MPLS only as an alternative.
  • Flex-Algo is the SLA tool. Planes computed in advance avoid any per-request path computation, which is what an inference service with millions of sessions needs.
  • Address planning matters more than ever. One /32 per plane inside 5f00::/16, with consistent node bits, is what keeps summarization and filtering simple. See SID structure and the SRv6 White Paper 2026.
  • Measure the user experience, not just the link. The blueprint ties network telemetry to inference metrics such as time to first token and inter-token latency, so operators can tell whether a slow answer came from the network or from the model.

docs.title: How is SRv6 used for AI inference?
docs.text: SRv6 uSID carries inference traffic across the provider WAN between users, edge sites and inference data centers. Flex-Algo builds separate planes for different SLAs, such as low latency or in-country paths, and BGP color on each inference service's route puts its traffic on the right plane.

docs.title: What is an AI inference WAN?
docs.text: It is the wide area network that connects users and enterprises to distributed AI inference sites, and those sites to each other. It has to deliver per-service SLAs, data sovereignty and isolation, because prompts and responses carry sensitive data and interactive AI is latency-bound.

docs.title: Why use Flex-Algo for AI inference?
docs.text: Flex-Algo lets the IGP compute several topologies at once, each with its own constraint: lowest delay, specific link affinities, or a jurisdiction. Each becomes a plane with its own SRv6 locators, ready before any inference request arrives, and TI-LFA protects traffic inside each plane.

docs.title: Is AI inference networking different from AI training networking?
docs.text: Yes. Training back-ends use static SRv6 source routing chosen by the NIC per packet inside one data center, as in OpenAI's MRC. Inference WANs use routing protocols, Flex-Algo planes and BGP color to meet a per-service SLA across a provider network.

docs.title: MRC and SRv6: How OpenAI's AI Supercomputer Network Works
docs.text:
MRC (Multipath Reliable Connection) is an RDMA transport for AI training clusters that sprays every connection across hundreds of network paths. It pairs with static SRv6 source routing: each path is an explicit list of switch uSIDs written by the NIC into the IPv6 destination address, and the switches run no dynamic routing at all. MRC was released as an open OCP specification on 5 May 2026. It runs in production in OpenAI's and Microsoft's largest GPU training clusters, and it is the strongest production validation of SRv6 for AI to date.

MRC + SRv6 in 60 seconds

  • What: a multipath extension of the RoCEv2 Reliable Connection transport, specified by AMD, Broadcom, Intel, Microsoft, NVIDIA and OpenAI and published through the Open Compute Project (OCP MRC 1.0).
  • Where: OpenAI's largest NVIDIA GB200 training clusters, including the Oracle Cloud site in Abilene, Texas, and Microsoft's Fairwater AI supercomputers. It has trained frontier models used in ChatGPT and Codex.
  • SRv6 role: the NIC encodes the full path (one 16-bit uN uSID per switch hop after a 32-bit block) in the outer IPv6 destination address. Switches shift and forward using static routes that are configured at install time and never changed. No BGP, no IGP.
  • Topology: 800G NICs broken out into 8×100G (or 4×200G) parallel planes, so 131,072 GPUs fit in a two-tier Clos.
  • Transport: per-packet spraying across typically 128–256 paths, lossy Ethernet with no PFC, packet trimming, selective retransmission, and failed paths bypassed in tens of microseconds.
  • Results: ≈770 Gb/s (≈96% of peak) per 800G NIC, NCCL at 42,020 GPUs, and production jobs of 50K–75K GPUs riding through link flaps and switch reboots.

docs.title: Why MRC exists
docs.text:
Large training jobs synchronize thousands of GPUs at every step, so the slowest flow sets the pace for the whole job (see AI Networking Glossary). The conventional AI backend, RoCEv2 on a lossless fabric with per-flow ECMP and BGP, has three problems at 100K-GPU scale:

  1. ECMP collisions. Each RDMA queue pair (QP) follows one hashed path. A few elephant flows collide on the same links while others sit idle. In the MRC paper's comparison, a single RoCE QP reached about half the achievable all-reduce throughput because of collisions.
  2. Slow, opaque failure handling. With dynamic routing, a failed link or switch is repaired by protocol convergence, which takes seconds to tens of seconds. Meanwhile, the transport cannot tell which physical path each packet took. The paper notes that a 512-port T0 has ECMP groups of up to 256 next hops, and that convergence can take very many round-trip times.
  3. Two adaptive systems fighting. A multipath transport that reacts to loss and a routing protocol that reacts to the same failures are hard to reason about together.

The MRC authors' answer was to make the transport responsible for both load balancing and failure recovery, and to make the network as simple and static as possible. In the paper's own words, they "took the unusual position of disabling dynamic routing in the switches".

docs.title: The topology: multi-plane, two-tier Clos
docs.text:
A 51.2 Tb/s switch has 64 ports of 800G. A conventional three-tier 800G Clos built from it tops out at 65,536 NICs; going bigger needs a fourth tier, oversubscription or separate rails. MRC clusters instead break each 800G NIC out by lane into 8×100G ports and build 8 parallel 100G planes from the same switches, which now have 512 ports each:

Conventional 800G Clos MRC multi-plane (8×100G) Tiers for ~131K GPUs 3 or more 2 Switch radix 64 × 800G 512 × 100G Longest path 5 switches 3 switches GPUs one hop away 32 256 Optics / switches at full bisection baseline ≈⅔ of the optics, ≈⅗ of the switches Capacity lost per node when one T0–T1 link fails ≈3% ≈0.4%

Each T0 connects 256 NIC ports down and 256 T1s up, and each T1 connects 512 T0s: 512 T0s × 256 NICs = 131,072 NICs in two tiers. Losing a NIC-to-T0 link still costs a node 12% of its NIC bandwidth, but the job survives it. Production clusters use both 4-plane (4×200G) and 8-plane (8×100G) variants.

docs.title: The packet
docs.text:
MRC packets are IPv6-in-IPv6. The NIC does all SRv6 encapsulation and decapsulation; every switch is a plain SRv6 transit node.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Outer IPv6 header                                             │
│   DA = SRv6 path: 32-bit block | uSID | uSID | uSID | uSID |0│
│   Flow label = part of the 32-bit entropy value (EV)          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Inner IPv6 header                                             │
│   DA = destination NIC address (used to decapsulate)          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ UDP  (source port = rest of the EV)                           │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ RDMA transport headers + payload (MRC)                        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The deployment described in the paper never mentions a Segment Routing Header: a whole cross-fabric path fits in the outer destination address, so the overhead is a single 40-byte IPv6 header. This "DA-only" form of reduced encapsulation is what keeps SRv6 on the fast path of every switch ASIC.

docs.title: uSID format and forwarding
docs.text:
The destination address follows the uSID format of RFC 9800: a 32-bit locator block followed by 16-bit uSIDs, one per hop, using the uN behavior (each switch on the path is named explicitly). Every switch does the same three steps at line rate:

  1. Compare the first 48 bits of the destination address with its own block + uSID.
  2. On a match, shift the remaining uSIDs left by 16 bits (the uN shift).
  3. Look up the new destination address in a static /48 route that names the egress port.

For a path that crosses a T1 (source T0 → T1 → destination T0 → NIC), the address carries four uSIDs:

| 32-bit block | source T0 | T1 | destination T0 | last-hop port | 0000 | 0000 |

The last uSID is not a switch: it identifies the destination T0's downlink port to the receiving NIC. The two empty slots are End-of-Container zeros.

Illustrative example (values are made up)

DA = fcbb:bb00:0103:0b07:0141:0012::
     └─block─┘ └T0┘ └T1┘ └T0┘ └port┘
At source T0 (0103):      shift → fcbb:bb00:0b07:0141:0012::
At T1 (0b07):             shift → fcbb:bb00:0141:0012::
At destination T0 (0141): shift → fcbb:bb00:0012::  → static route to port 0x12
The paper defines the layout (32-bit block, 16-bit uN uSIDs, last-hop downlink as the final uSID) but does not publish its numbering plan. See SRv6 AI Fabric Design for how to build one.

docs.title: Entropy values map to explicit paths
docs.text:
This is the core idea that ties the transport to SRv6:

  • When a QP starts, the NIC generates an EV set, typically 128–256 entropy values, split equally across planes. Each EV corresponds to one explicit path on one plane.
  • From a per-node configuration file, the NIC gets an SRv6 address template for the destination's T0 group and fills in the last-hop downlink.
  • For every packet, the NIC picks the next EV and specializes the template from it: the plane number goes into every uSID and the T0 uplink number goes into the T1 uSID. The mapping is algorithmic, so the NIC does not need a table of 256 addresses per QP.
  • The EV is also written into the UDP source port and the IPv6 flow label. Switches do not hash it, because the path is already explicit. It is there so the receiver can echo it in acknowledgements, since the uSID shifts have consumed the destination address by the time the packet arrives.

Because the EV-to-path mapping is exact, "this EV saw loss" means "this physical path saw loss". That is something per-flow ECMP hashing can never tell a transport.

docs.title: A static control plane
docs.text: Switch forwarding tables are configured when the switch is installed and are not changed afterwards. There is no BGP, no IGP and no controller programming the switches. A per-node host agent configures only the NICs: their EV profiles and path denylists. The authors also rejected the middle ground of static ECMP with MRC on top, because it still gives no simple mapping from EV to physical path for failure reporting. Their motivation includes switch software itself: they cite a study in which 17% of switch failures were software bugs, and they observed switches whose control plane and links were up while they were not forwarding.

docs.title: How the transport uses the paths
docs.text:
Mechanism What MRC does Spraying A different EV for each packet, rotating through the EV set across all planes. Every packet carries its RDMA address, so the receiver writes it to GPU memory on arrival in any order. No PFC The fabric runs lossy, best-effort Ethernet. With hundreds of paths converging on the last hop, PFC would cause head-of-line blocking. ECN as a load-balancing signal Switches mark ECN (except on the last hop); the receiver echoes it per EV and the sender temporarily avoids that path. Packet trimming A congested switch trims the payload instead of dropping the packet and forwards the header with priority, so the receiver can NACK it. Trimmed loss means congestion; untrimmed loss means a failed path. Path failure An untrimmed loss retires the EV immediately and replaces it with a backup EV on the same plane. Failed paths are bypassed in a few tens of microseconds. Path recovery Background probes resurrect retired EVs once their paths work again. Congestion control UET's sender-based NSCC (ECN + delay), with optional receiver-side window penalties. NIC port failure Signalled to remote QPs with a port-state bitmap so they stop using that plane. This is the slow case: under a second in the testbed and a few seconds in production.

Replacing a retired EV with one from the same plane keeps every plane equally loaded. The trade-off: any single-path traffic sharing the backend, or heavy link loss in one plane, limits MRC to the most congested plane.

docs.title: The OCP specification is broader than the deployment
docs.text:
OCP MRC 1.0 defines three forwarding models: plain ECMP hashing, Structured EV (switches read per-hop fields from the flow label and UDP port) and SRv6. For SRv6 it allows:

  • uSID-only or uSID + one SRH, with any SRH in RFC 9800 compressed encoding;
  • both uN and uA behaviors (the latter selects a specific link);
  • F3216 and F1616 container formats, up to 6 uSIDs in the destination address;
  • an informative model in which source routing reaches an upper-tier switch and normal IP forwarding takes over from there. This differs from the paper's deployment, which source-routes the full path down to the last-hop port.

So the specification is a framework that SRv6 operators can adopt at different depths, from "pin the spine" to "pin every hop".

docs.title: Telemetry: Clustermapper
docs.text: Because every path is explicit, OpenAI's Clustermapper agents on every node send source-routed probes from the host to each directly connected T0 and to a subset of T1s, and back to themselves. Collectively they probe every link in the network every millisecond. Comparing T0 and T1 self-probes localizes a fault to a NIC–T0 link, a T0–T1 link or a switch. Switches forward the probes as ordinary data-plane traffic, unlike rate-limited ICMP to the switch CPU, and each probe takes exactly the path an MRC packet with the same EV would take. Details: AI Fabric Telemetry with SRv6.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Production (GB200 clusters):

Event Outcome Job start, 75K GPUs, no pre-populated denylist Losses fell well below 1 packet/s per NIC within a couple of minutes; fewer than 5 packets lost per QP in the first minute Constant T0–T1 link flaps (up to ~12/min) "Almost no impact"; flapping links are left in service T0 transceiver flap, 50K-GPU job ≈25% throughput dip for the minute of flaps, then full recovery; no QP failed and no node was evicted T1 switch silently stopped forwarding, 75K-GPU job Detected automatically and rebooted; throughput largely unaffected; four T1 reboots needed no coordination with the training team

Testbed (GB200 + ConnectX-8, 8×100G planes, NVIDIA Spectrum-5):

Test Result Point-to-point 32 KB writes ≈770 Gb/s ≈ 96% of the 800G peak, both T0-local and cross-T1 2-byte latency (one way) 5.09 µs T0-local, 6.54 µs cross-T1 20 T0–T1 links disabled one per second Minimal throughput impact T1 switch down No steady-state degradation T0 switch down Bandwidth drops ≈100 Gb/s, in proportion to lost capacity 20% loss injected on one path Path retired at once and line rate sustained NCCL sendrecv at 42,020 GPUs Up to 92 GB/s per NIC (≈92% of 800G)

MRC vs RoCEv2 on identical hardware (64 GPUs; RoCE on single-plane 400G with ECMP, PFC and DCQCN, versus MRC on 4×100G planes with SRv6 and no PFC):

  • One MRC QP spraying across 256 paths beat 16 RoCE QPs on ring all-reduce. MRC also won all-to-all at every message size.
  • With 1% injected loss, RoCE was "pretty much unusable" while MRC kept about a third of its throughput (the injected loss hit every plane, which is worse than real failures).
  • In a 7:1 incast test, a RoCE victim flow lost about 25% (one QP), while an MRC victim flow saw no impact.

docs.title: Hardware and software
docs.text:
Layer Implementations named by the authors NICs NVIDIA ConnectX-8 (800G), AMD Pollara (400G), AMD Vulcano (800G), Broadcom Thor Ultra (800G) Switches running SRv6 uN NVIDIA Spectrum-4 and Spectrum-5 with Cumulus or SONiC; Arista EOS on Broadcom Tomahawk 5 Software libMRC (OCP), Microsoft's open-source NCCL MRC plugin, ibverbs shim, MSCCL++ support, and SONiC SRv6 work

Testbed results were published for ConnectX-8, Pollara and Thor Ultra. Broadcom has also said that Tomahawk 6 supports SRv6 uSID and packet trimming.

docs.title: Limitations the authors acknowledge
docs.text:
• The NIC transceiver is a single point of failure. In the 4×200G design one 800G optic carries all four ports, so if it flaps, QPs fail.
  • NIC-side failures are slower to handle than fabric failures: remapping EVs across many QPs is not instantaneous on current NICs.
  • Sustained 1% loss still cuts MRC to about a third of its throughput: enough to ride out transients, not to keep training.
  • Reverse paths: simply reversing the SRv6 forward path does not always work, so receivers keep a separate, heuristic set of reverse EVs.
  • SRv6 gaps called out at OCP 2026: switch vendors still need to qualify longer paths that use an SRH, and to provide a supported way to pick one link among parallel adjacencies.
  • Large-scale MRC-vs-RoCE comparisons were not published; the head-to-head tests used small testbeds.

docs.title: What this means for network engineers
docs.text:
• SRv6 in the data center is no longer a lab idea. The largest AI training networks in production use it, specifically for its simplest property: an explicit path in the destination address.
  • The value is in the static network plus explicit paths. Fewer moving parts in the switches and exact path identity for every packet give the transport and the telemetry ground truth.
  • uSID is what makes it practical: a three-switch path plus the last-hop port fits in one IPv6 address, with no SRH and 40 bytes of overhead.
  • Day-2 operations change. Link flaps become background noise, switch reboots need no coordination, and monitoring shifts from routing state to path probing.

docs.title: What is MRC in AI networking?
docs.text: MRC (Multipath Reliable Connection) is an RDMA transport that extends RoCEv2 so that one connection sprays its packets across hundreds of network paths, tolerates out-of-order arrival and recovers from path failures in microseconds. It was specified by AMD, Broadcom, Intel, Microsoft, NVIDIA and OpenAI and released through the Open Compute Project in May 2026.

docs.title: Does MRC require SRv6?
docs.text: No. The OCP MRC specification also supports ECMP hashing and a "Structured EV" mode. The production deployment described by OpenAI and Microsoft uses static SRv6 uSID source routing, because it maps every entropy value to an exact physical path and lets the switches run without dynamic routing.

docs.title: How does MRC use SRv6?
docs.text: The NIC writes the whole path into the outer IPv6 destination address as a 32-bit block followed by one 16-bit uN uSID per switch and a final uSID for the last-hop port. Each switch matches its own uSID, shifts the address and forwards on a static route. Each entropy value the NIC uses maps algorithmically to one such path.

docs.title: Do MRC switches run BGP?
docs.text: No. In the deployment described in the MRC paper, dynamic routing is disabled. Switch forwarding tables are static routes configured at install time and never changed. Failure handling moves entirely to the MRC transport at the edge.

docs.title: How large are MRC clusters?
docs.text: The multi-plane design supports 131,072 GPUs in two switch tiers. The paper reports production jobs of 50,000 and 75,000 GPUs and an NCCL benchmark at 42,020 GPUs.

docs.title: Which hardware supports MRC with SRv6?
docs.text: The authors name NVIDIA ConnectX-8, AMD Pollara and Vulcano, and Broadcom Thor Ultra NICs, plus NVIDIA Spectrum-⅘ switches (Cumulus or SONiC) and Arista EOS on Broadcom Tomahawk 5 for SRv6 uN forwarding.

docs.title: SRv6 for Multi-Datacenter AI (Scale-Across)
docs.text:
AI training has outgrown the single building. Power and space limits push the largest jobs across several data centers, campuses or regions, and that brings the WAN into the training loop. This third dimension of AI networking, after scale-up inside a rack and scale-out inside a cluster, is usually called scale-across. This page covers where SRv6 is used to carry AI traffic between sites, what each deployment does, and which well-known scale-across products are not SRv6.

Summary (October 2026)

  • Meta runs SRv6 uSID traffic engineering on its regional backbone, which interconnects data center campuses and AI clusters. The first site with SRv6 TE went into production in October 2026, on FBOSS and Cisco Silicon One with 800G ZR+ spans of up to 650 km.
  • Alibaba Cloud runs a dedicated "eCore for AI (Scale Across)" built from SONiC + SRv6 routers, with per-training-job SRv6 traffic engineering, described as in production.
  • China Telecom has published an architecture, with live-network trials, that uses L3EVPN over SRv6 Policy plus tenant slices for cross-cluster training at 100–500 km.
  • The IETF AI-backend draft notes that the same NIC-driven SRv6 model can extend across data centers. That is a capability statement, not a reported deployment.
  • Several prominent scale-across efforts publish no SRv6 role: Cisco 8223/Silicon One P200, NVIDIA Spectrum-XGS and Microsoft's AI WAN.

docs.title: Why scale-across needs traffic engineering
docs.text:
Inside a cluster, the fabric is symmetric and over-provisioned, so spraying traffic evenly works. Between sites, the conditions change:

Inside a cluster (scale-out) Between sites (scale-across) Symmetric Clos, full bisection Asymmetric topology, a few fiber routes Capacity is plentiful Capacity is scarce and expensive Microsecond RTTs Milliseconds of RTT, which collectives feel One traffic class dominates AI traffic shares links with storage, replication and user traffic

Alibaba and Cisco summarize the consequence at OCP 2026 in two words: traffic engineering is a must for AI DCI. AI traffic needs to be kept on the paths with the right latency and capacity, kept away from queues it would congest, and moved off degrading optical paths before they fail. SRv6 fits because data center networks are IP-only (there is no MPLS in SONiC, nor on most DC switching silicon), and SRv6 provides explicit paths, SLA classes and VPNs on plain IPv6, end to end from one data center to another.

docs.title: Meta: SRv6 on the regional backbone
docs.text:
Meta is building regional backbone (RBB) rings that let data center campuses in a region share compute and storage within a latency envelope. They sit below the global Express Backbone and carry AI and non-AI traffic between sites.

  • Topology: rings with 1, 5 or 10 ms RTT and 64 parallel planes, full mesh between sites within a plane. Each RBB domain is routed and traffic-engineered as one.
  • Hardware: shallow-buffer, data-center-class platforms on 800G ZR+ spans of up to 650 km, running FBOSS over OCP SAI on Cisco Silicon One. ECN-based congestion control (Meta's GLIDE), not deep buffers, keeps queues short.
  • SRv6 data plane: uSID with the block fcbb:bb00 and up to six uSIDs in the outer destination address. The head-end uses H.Encaps.Red, transit hops uA (adjacency) uSIDs, and the egress End.DT46. When a path needs more than six uSIDs, an End.B6.Encaps.Red binding SID stitches two lists.
  • Control plane: one controller per plane programs every switch every 30 seconds through a TE agent. The SID table is installed once at bootstrap, with one entry per adjacency rather than one per path. Fast reroute sits below the controller.
  • Timeline: first IP-only RBB site in July 2026, first long-haul site in August 2026, first site with SRv6 TE in October 2026, with expansion planned.

Why SRv6 instead of MPLS

Meta already runs MPLS SR-TE at scale and still chose SRv6 for the RBB. The deciding factor was QoS: it needs six strict-priority classes, and its MPLS encoding (3-bit Traffic Class) supports four, while the 8-bit IPv6 Traffic Class carries all six.

Meta's separate backend aggregation (BAG) layer, which stitches training fabrics into one cluster across buildings and regions, uses eBGP, not SRv6.

docs.title: Alibaba Cloud: eCore for AI, with per-job TE
docs.text:
Alibaba's backbone, eCore, is the largest published SRv6 DCI/WAN. Cisco describes it as an SRv6 deployment across about 1,000 cities in China, running since 2023. At OCP 2025, Alibaba described eCore as SRv6-only (no MPLS), built from single-chip "pizza box" routers running its SONiC-based NOS, spanning 29 regions and 91 availability zones.

At the OCP Global Summit 2026, Alibaba presented a dedicated eCore for AI (Scale Across): a separate, single-tenant network with no overlay, built from SONiC + SRv6 routers with 64 × 800G ports and 400G/800G links, and engineered per training job:

  1. The job scheduler hands the job's identity and endpoints to the TE system.
  2. A controller computes an SR Policy for the job and advertises a Binding SID (BSID) for it via BGP.
  3. Traffic is steered onto the BSID. The primary path is a <uA, uN> list protected by echo BFD, and an anycast SID provides the backup path.
  4. Optical degradation signals withdraw a path from use before it fails.

Alibaba compared three places to steer AI traffic onto SRv6: classify at the aggregation router (no SRv6 on the host), have the host encode the full SID list, or have the host choose a BSID that the router expands. At IETF 125 (March 2026), Alibaba described host agents that set the IPv6 Flow Label per application, which the SRv6 head-end maps to a SID list such as a dedicated "RDMA path". The goal is to keep cross-region RDMA from competing with other traffic for backbone queues. Alibaba also stated that its AI computing is now fully based on IPv6/SRv6.

docs.title: China Telecom: cross-cluster training over SRv6 Policy
docs.text: China Telecom Research Institute's 2025 computing-power metro white paper, co-written with Huawei, specifies L3EVPN over SRv6 Policy between compute gateways to carry cross-cluster collaborative training. It adds tenant-level slicing for remote storage-compute training, and SRv6 Policy with a low-latency slice for inference. It reports live-network trials in Shanghai, Zhejiang and Guangdong with less than 3% degradation in compute efficiency and in inference latency metrics (vendor-reported figures). It targets 400G/800G links for training across 100–500 km with less than 5% efficiency loss.

docs.title: Other signals from China
docs.text:
• China Mobile says it has built the world's largest G-SRv6 network and is developing new layer-3 protocols based on G-SRv6 evolution for cross-data-center AI, where it warns that 2% packet loss drops RDMA throughput to zero. It has not tied a specific training run to G-SRv6.
  • China Unicom uses SRv6 network programming on its IP backbone. It has proposed an SRv6-based task scheduling scheme, piloted on a Shanghai–Ningxia "East Data, West Computing" transfer, and says SRv6 is applied on its 400G AI-compute network.
  • China's long-distance training records (500 km, 1,500 km, 2,000 km runs by China Telecom, China Unicom and national testbeds) were published without naming SRv6 as the transport. Treat them as proof that scale-across training works, not as SRv6 deployments.

docs.title: What is not SRv6 (as published)
docs.text: Effort What it is SRv6? Cisco 8223 / Silicon One P200 (Oct 2025) 51.2 Tb/s deep-buffer router for scale-across Not mentioned at launch. P200 is used for SRv6 by customers: Alibaba's per-job TE runs on P200-based systems. NVIDIA Spectrum-XGS (Aug 2025) Distance-aware congestion control and telemetry for Spectrum-X No routing or SRv6 component Microsoft AI WAN (Fairwater) Dedicated fiber between Fairwater sites No public SRv6 claim; Microsoft's published SRv6 use is inside the cluster (MRC) Meta BAG Super-spine joining training fabrics across sites eBGP Google multi-DC training Virgo / Jupiter across sites Google's only published SRv6 use is bare-metal source routing inside Virgo

docs.title: Design patterns
docs.text:
Two patterns emerge from these deployments:

  1. Controller-driven SR Policy at the DC edge (Meta, Alibaba, China Telecom). Hosts and cluster fabrics stay as they are. Border routers classify AI traffic by DSCP, Flow Label or VRF and steer it onto controller-computed uA/uN lists or BSIDs. This is classic SR Policy and traffic engineering applied to AI.
  2. End-to-end source routing from the NIC (the IETF AI-backend draft's cross-datacenter extension). The same uSID path a NIC writes inside the cluster is extended with DCI and WAN hops. No production deployment of this has been published yet.

What SRv6 does not solve on long haul

SRv6 picks the path; it does not make a 650 km link lossless. Meta relies on ECN-based congestion control, China Telecom on large buffers and flow-level congestion control, and the research community on transport changes. Explicit paths make those mechanisms predictable, because each job's traffic stays on known links.

docs.title: What is scale-across in AI networking?
docs.text: Scale-across means connecting AI clusters in different buildings, campuses or regions so that one training job, or a pool of jobs, can use them together. It complements scale-up (inside a server or rack) and scale-out (across a cluster's backend fabric) and brings data center interconnect and WAN design into AI infrastructure.

docs.title: Does Meta use SRv6?
docs.text: Yes. Meta has deployed SRv6 with FBOSS on its regional backbone, which interconnects data center campuses and AI clusters across geographies. It uses uSID with adjacency (uA) segments programmed by a central TE controller, on Cisco Silicon One platforms with 800G ZR+ links of up to 650 km. The first site with SRv6 traffic engineering went into production in October 2026.

docs.title: Is SRv6 used for multi-datacenter AI training?
docs.text: Yes. Alibaba Cloud runs a dedicated SRv6 network for scale-across AI with per-job traffic engineering, and China Telecom has trialed cross-cluster training over L3EVPN on SRv6 Policy. Other large multi-site training efforts, such as Microsoft's AI WAN, have not published an SRv6 role.

docs.title: Why use SRv6 instead of MPLS for AI data center interconnect?
docs.text: Data center switches and SONiC are IP-only, so SRv6 lets traffic engineering run end to end on IPv6 without MPLS gateways at the DC edge. Meta also cites QoS: the IPv6 Traffic Class field carries the six priority classes it needs, while its MPLS encoding supports four.
