docs.title: RFC 9960 - SR P2MP Policy
docs.text: Field Value Title Segment Routing Point-to-Multipoint Policy Authors R. Parekh (Ed.), D. Voyer (Ed.), C. Filsfils, H. Bidgoli, Z. Zhang Date April 2026 Status Proposed Standard Updates RFC 9524 Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9960

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9960 is the architecture behind Tree-SID. It defines the SR P2MP Policy: a construct, identified by <Root, Tree-ID>, that names a root node and a set of leaf nodes and carries one or more candidate paths (CPs) with constraints and optimization objectives, reusing the candidate-path model and selection rules of RFC 9256.

A controller (typically a PCE) computes a P2MP tree instance (PTI) for each candidate path and instantiates it by programming RFC 9524 Replication segments on the root, the intermediate replication nodes, and the leaves. The Replication-SID at the root is the Tree-SID; the RFC recommends reusing the same value at every node of the instance to simplify troubleshooting. For SRv6, the Replication-SID is the FUNCT part of the SID, so even with a common Tree-SID value the locator differs per node.

It works for both SR-MPLS and SRv6, and it updates RFC 9524 by giving the Replication-ID a precise structure: <Root, Tree-ID, Instance-ID>.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 2 SR P2MP Policy Identification, components, candidate paths and tree instances 3 Steering Local-policy steering at the root vs BSID/Tree-SID steering from upstream 4 P2MP Tree Instance Leaf Replication segments, shared Replication segments, forwarding 5 Controller Tree compute, SID management, instantiation order, protection App. A Illustration SR-MPLS and SRv6 examples with adjacent and non-adjacent replication

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
Identifier Size / Scope Purpose Tree-ID 32-bit, unique per root Identifies the SR P2MP Policy together with the root address Instance-ID 16-bit, unique per policy Identifies one PTI (e.g., old and new instance during make-before-break) Replication-ID <Root, Tree-ID, Instance-ID> Updated RFC 9524 identifier; full control-plane key adds Node-ID Tree-SID Replication-SID at the root Data-plane identifier of the PTI BSID Per policy Steers traffic into the policy when the root is not the domain ingress

Shared Replication segments (for example, one protecting the X→Y adjacency for many trees) use Root = ::/0.0.0.0 and Instance-ID = 0. The simple 32-bit Replication-ID of RFC 9524 maps to <::, Tree-ID, 0>.

docs.title: How a Tree Is Built
docs.text:
• Controller / PCE → Root (Replication segment)
  • Controller / PCE → Replication node (Replication segment)
  • Controller / PCE → Leaf 1 (Replication segment)
  • Controller / PCE → Leaf 2 (Replication segment)
  • Controller / PCE → Leaf 3 (Replication segment)
  • Root → Replication node (copy, DA = M Replication-SID)
  • Root → Leaf 1 (copy, DA = L1 Replication-SID)
  • Replication node → Leaf 2 (copy)
  • Replication node → Leaf 3 (copy)
graph TD
    PCE[Controller / PCE] -.->|Replication segment| R[Root]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| M[Replication node]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L1[Leaf 1]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L2[Leaf 2]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L3[Leaf 3]
    R r1@-->|copy, DA = M Replication-SID| M
    R r2@-->|copy, DA = L1 Replication-SID| L1
    M r3@-->|copy| L2
    M r4@-->|copy| L3
    r1@{ animate: true }
    r2@{ animate: true }
    r3@{ animate: true }
    r4@{ animate: true }
Step Controller action 1 Learn topology and node P2MP capability 2 Compute a loop-free tree for the active CP (constraints from RFC 9256 SR Policy) 3 Assign Replication-SIDs (from SRLB for SR-MPLS, or reserved blocks) and the BSID 4 Program leaves and intermediate nodes first, then the root, then activate the instance 5 On topology change, recompute — optionally via make-before-break with a new Instance-ID

docs.title: SRv6-Specific Rules
docs.text: Rule Why Leaf nodes must have a Replication segment No penultimate-hop popping: the Tree-SID is in the IPv6 DA Multiple services on one PTI need a service-context SID as the last SID in the SRH Leaves derive the VPN/EVPN context from it Non-adjacent downstream nodes are reached via the Replication-SID's locator, or an optional segment list Same mechanics as RFC 9524 Section 2.2

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
Type Mechanism Local Backup SR Policies per replication branch, or node-local LFA / TI-LFA plus micro-loop avoidance Path A backup CP whose PTIs are disjoint from the active CP's PTIs

Common Pitfalls

  • RFC 9960 defines the architecture, not the signaling. PCEP (draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy) and BGP (draft-ietf-idr-sr-p2mp-policy) encodings are still Internet-Drafts, so vendor implementations may differ.
  • Only one PTI of a CP may be active at a time; two active instances deliver duplicate traffic to leaves.
  • Allocating Replication-SIDs from the SRGB is not recommended — trees are local state and can exhaust the global block.
  • A statically provisioned tree does not adapt to topology changes.
  • If the root's Replication segment fails to install, the controller should tear the instance down rather than leave a partial tree.

docs.title: SRv6 SID Decoder and uSID Calculator
docs.text:
Paste any SRv6 SID — a classic SID or a uSID container — and the decoder splits it into its Locator-Block, node, function and argument bits, flags what the address tells you, and walks the container hop by hop the way an RFC 9800 NEXT-CSID router processes it. Every decode has its own URL, so you can link a colleague straight to it. It runs entirely in your browser: nothing you paste is sent anywhere.

SRv6 SID or IPv6 address SID format uSID F3216: 32-bit block, 16-bit uSIDs uSID F4816: 48-bit block, 16-bit uSIDs uSID F1616: 16-bit block, 16-bit uSIDs uSID with custom lengths Classic SID: Block, Node, Function, Argument uSID lengths in bits Locator-Block uSID (LNFL) Field lengths in bits (RFC 8986 Section 3.1) Block (B) Node (N) Function (F) Argument (A) Examples: F3216 uSID path 5f00::/16 SID RFC 9800 container Classic SID Malformed

The decoder needs JavaScript. The explanations below work without it.

docs.title: How to Read an SRv6 SID
docs.text:
An SRv6 SID is a 128-bit IPv6 address that the network treats as an instruction. RFC 8986 splits it into three parts, written LOC:FUNCT:ARG:

Part What it is Who reads it Locator (L bits) A routable prefix that leads to one node. It is itself split into the Block (B), the prefix shared by the whole SR domain, and the Node (N) part that picks one router Every router: it is an ordinary IPv6 route in IS-IS, OSPFv3 or BGP Function (F bits) Selects the behavior bound to the SID on that node: End, End.X, End.DT4, and so on Only the node that owns the locator Argument (A bits) Optional per-packet parameter for the behavior, such as the ESI filter of End.DT2M Only the owning node, and only for behaviors that take one

L + F + A can be at most 128, and when it is less, the remaining low bits must be zero (RFC 8986 Section 3.1). The lengths are a design choice of the operator, not something you can infer from the address, which is why the decoder asks for them. A common classic layout is a /48 locator (32-bit block + 16-bit node), a 16-bit function, and no argument: fc00:0:2:e004:: is function 0xe004 on the node with locator fc00:0:2::/48.

Transit routers never look past the locator: they do a longest-prefix match on the destination address like for any IPv6 packet. That is the whole trick that lets SRv6 run over routers with no SRv6 support. The full anatomy, including the IANA block, is in SID Structure.

docs.title: SRv6 SID Formats: Classic SIDs and uSIDs
docs.text:
A classic SID spends 128 bits on one instruction. A uSID (micro-SID, the NEXT-CSID flavor of RFC 9800) packs several short instructions into one 128-bit container: a Locator-Block followed by a list of compressed SIDs, each one the Node and Function of a SID with the shared block left out. The format name gives the two lengths: F3216 means a 32-bit Locator-Block and 16-bit uSIDs.

Format Locator-Block uSID length uSIDs per container Where you see it F3216 32 bits 16 bits 6 The format every NEXT-CSID implementation must support (RFC 9800 Section 4.1). Cisco IOS-XR and IOS-XE call it usid-f3216; Arista EOS and Juniper use it too F4816 48 bits 16 bits 5 The examples in RFC 9800, with blocks such as 2001:db8:b1::/48 F1616 16 bits 16 bits 7 Maximum packing, but the block takes a whole /16 Custom NEXT-CSID any any floor((128 − block) / uSID) RFC 9800 allows other lengths; leftover bits are padding Classic SID — — 1 RFC 8986 SIDs, one per SRH entry

The capacity formula is from RFC 9800: a container holds K = floor((128 − LBL) / LNFL) uSIDs, where LBL is the Locator-Block length and LNFL the uSID length. RFC 9800's other flavor, REPLACE-CSID (G-SRv6), uses 16- or 32-bit C-SIDs and an index in the argument instead of a shift, so it is not visualized here. See uSID Compression for the overhead comparison.

docs.title: Reading an F3216 uSID
docs.text:
fcbb:bb00:0100:0200:0300:e004:0000:0000
└─block──┘└uN1┘└uN2┘└uN3┘└uDT┘└EoC┘
  • fcbb:bb00 is the 32-bit Locator-Block, the same on every node of the domain.
  • 0100 is the active uSID. Node 1 advertises fcbb:bb00:0100::/48 in the IGP, so plain longest-prefix match delivers the packet there.
  • 0200, 0300 are the next nodes; e004 is a local service uSID (here uDT4 on node 3).
  • 0000 is the end-of-container marker. CSID value 0 is reserved for exactly this (RFC 9800 Section 5).

A common convention from the uSID draft splits the 16-bit space into a GIB (0x0000–0xDFFF, global uSIDs such as a node's uN) and a LIB (0xE000–0xFFFF, local uSIDs such as uA adjacencies and uDT/uDX services). RFC 9800 Section 9.2 leaves the split to the operator, so the decoder labels it as a hint, not a fact.

docs.title: How uSID Shift-and-Forward Works
docs.text:
When a router receives a packet whose destination matches one of its NEXT-CSID SIDs, it applies RFC 9800 Section 4.1.1, lines N01 to N09:

  1. If the Argument (every bit after the active uSID) is not zero, copy it into the bits right after the Locator-Block, overwriting the active uSID, and set the last uSID-length bits to zero. In F3216, that is "shift bits 48–127 left by 16".
  2. Decrement the Hop Limit and forward on the new destination address. Segments Left in the SRH is not touched, and in many deployments there is no SRH at all.
  3. If the Argument is zero, this uSID is the last one in the container: the node runs the ordinary RFC 8986 behavior, taking the next 128-bit entry from the SRH if Segments Left is above zero, or acting as the final destination (a uDT4, for example, decapsulates and looks up the inner packet).

Applied to the example above:

received       fcbb:bb00:0100:0200:0300:e004:0000:0000   node 1 (uN 0100) shifts
after node 1   fcbb:bb00:0200:0300:e004:0000:0000:0000   node 2 (uN 0200) shifts
after node 2   fcbb:bb00:0300:e004:0000:0000:0000:0000   node 3 (uN 0300) shifts
after node 3   fcbb:bb00:e004:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000   node 3 (uDT4 e004): Argument 0, decapsulate

Four instructions, sixteen bytes, no SRH. The decoder's step-through shows the same walk for whatever you paste.

docs.title: Worked Examples
docs.text:
Each link opens the decoder with the example loaded.

  1. F3216 uSID path with a VPN service. fcbb:bb00:100:200:300:e004:: carries three node uSIDs and a local uDT4 in one destination address, the case walked through above.
  2. A SID from the IANA block. 5f00:0:1:e001:: uses 5f00::/32 as its Locator-Block, carved from 5f00::/16, the block RFC 9602 reserves for SRv6 SIDs: node uSID 0001, then local service uSID e001. It is the layout of the Juniper example. Using 5f00::/16 is optional; operator GUA and ULA locators are just as valid.
  3. A full container from RFC 9800. 2001:db8:b1:10:20:30:40:50 has a 48-bit block and five uSIDs with no end-of-container marker, like the first container of RFC 9800 Figure 2. After the fifth uSID the Argument is zero and processing continues with the next SRH entry.
  4. A classic SID. fc00:0:2:e004:: with B=32, N=16, F=16, A=0 is function 0xe004 behind locator fc00:0:2::/48, the End.DT4 SID used in the L3VPN example.
  5. A malformed container. fcbb:bb00:100:0:300:: has a uSID after the end-of-container. Node 1 shifts 0000 into the active position, no node owns the resulting address, and the decoder says so.

docs.title: Function Bits vs Behavior Codepoints
docs.text:
The function bits in a SID are allocated locally by the router; 0xe004 means End.DT4 on one node and something else on the next. What is standardized is the behavior codepoint a router advertises next to each SID in IS-IS, OSPFv3, BGP and BGP-LS, from the IANA "SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors" registry. So you cannot tell a SID's behavior from its bits alone: look the SID up in the router's SID table, or take the codepoint from the routing protocol and look it up here.

Codepoint (decimal or 0x hex) or behavior name Try: 48 (uN) 57 (uA) End.DT* NEXT-CSID RFC 8986

The lookup needs JavaScript; see the table in Network Programming.

The registry above is the complete IANA list as of October 2026, including codepoints assigned to drafts. Vendors shorten the common NEXT-CSID behaviors as uN (End with NEXT-CSID, PSP & USD, codepoint 48) and uA (End.X with NEXT-CSID, PSP & USD, codepoint 57). Network Programming explains what each behavior does.

docs.title: What is an SRv6 SID?
docs.text: An SRv6 Segment Identifier (SID) is a 128-bit IPv6 address that encodes an instruction. Its locator routes the packet to a node, its function selects what that node does (forward, cross-connect, decapsulate into a VRF), and its optional argument parameterizes the function. Routers that do not own the locator forward it as normal IPv6.

docs.title: What does F3216 mean?
docs.text: F3216 is the most common SRv6 uSID format: a 32-bit Locator-Block followed by 16-bit uSIDs, so one 128-bit address holds up to six uSIDs. RFC 9800 requires every NEXT-CSID implementation to support it, and Cisco IOS-XR and IOS-XE configure it as usid-f3216.

docs.title: How many uSIDs fit in one container?
docs.text: floor((128 − Locator-Block length) / uSID length). That is 6 for F3216, 5 for a 48-bit block with 16-bit uSIDs, and 7 for F1616. When a path needs more, the source puts further containers in the SRH and the last uSID of each container moves processing to the next one.

docs.title: What is the end-of-container (0000) in a uSID?
docs.text: RFC 9800 reserves the CSID value 0 to mark the end of a container. When the bits after the active uSID are all zero, the node knows it holds the last uSID of the container and takes the next SID from the SRH, or is the final destination if there is none.

docs.title: Do SRv6 SIDs have to be in 5f00::/16?
docs.text: No. RFC 9602 reserves 5f00::/16 so SIDs are easy to recognize and filter, and marks it as not globally reachable, but operators can keep using their own global unicast or unique local prefixes as locators. Whatever the prefix, filter it at the SR domain edge.

docs.title: Can I tell the behavior of a SID from its bits?
docs.text: No. Function values are allocated locally by each router. The behavior is known from the router's SID table or from the IANA codepoint it advertises in the IGP or BGP, which you can look up in the behavior table on this page.

docs.title: BGP Overlay Services over SRv6
docs.text: SRv6 provides a clean, unified underlay for delivering L3VPN and L2VPN (EVPN) services using BGP — without MPLS, without LDP, without RSVP-TE. Just IPv6 + BGP.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
• PE1 BGP → PE2 BGP (MP-BGP with SRv6 SIDs)
  • PE1 → P Node (SRv6 Transport)
  • P Node → PE2 (SRv6 Transport)
  • CE1 - Customer → PE1
  • CE2 - Customer → PE2
  • Overlay - BGP Control Plane → CE1 - Customer
  • Overlay - BGP Control Plane → CE2 - Customer
graph TB
    subgraph overlay[Overlay - BGP Control Plane]
        BGP1[PE1 BGP] <-->|MP-BGP with SRv6 SIDs| BGP2[PE2 BGP]
    end

    subgraph underlay[Underlay - SRv6 Data Plane]
        PE1[PE1] -->|SRv6 Transport| P1[P Node]
        P1 -->|SRv6 Transport| PE2[PE2]
    end

    CE1[CE1 - Customer] --- PE1
    CE2[CE2 - Customer] --- PE2
    overlay ~~~ CE1
    overlay ~~~ CE2

Key principle: BGP carries service information (VPN prefixes, EVPN routes) with SRv6 SIDs instead of MPLS labels. The SRv6 SID tells the remote PE exactly what to do with the packet (decap to which VRF, cross-connect to which interface, etc.).

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. PE1 learns customer prefix 10.1.0.0/24 from CE1 in VRF CUSTOMER-A
  2. PE1 advertises via MP-BGP VPNv4/VPNv6 with an SRv6 SID instead of a VPN label:
    • Prefix: 10.1.0.0/24
    • Next-Hop: PE1 IPv6 address
    • SRv6 Service SID: fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4 (End.DT4 behavior)
  3. PE2 receives the BGP update, installs the route
  4. When PE2 receives traffic for 10.1.0.0/24, it encapsulates with:
    • IPv6 DA = fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4
    • Inner packet = original IPv4
  5. PE1 receives, matches End.DT4 SID, decapsulates, looks up in VRF CUSTOMER-A

docs.title: SRv6 SID Allocation Modes
docs.text:
Mode Description SID per... Per-VRF One SID shared by all prefixes in a VRF VRF Per-CE One SID per CE neighbor CE Per-Prefix Unique SID for each prefix Prefix

Per-VRF is most common

Per-VRF allocation (End.DT4 / End.DT6) is the default and most scalable option. The SID says "decap and lookup in this VRF table."

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! VRF definition
vrf CUSTOMER-A
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  import route-target 100:1
  export route-target 100:1
 !
!

!! BGP with SRv6
router bgp 65000
 address-family vpnv4 unicast
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
  !
 !
 vrf CUSTOMER-A
  rd 100:1
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
    alloc mode per-vrf
   !
  !
 !
!

set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A instance-type vrf
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A route-distinguisher 100:1
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A vrf-target target:100:1
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A protocols bgp source-packet-routing srv6 locator myloc

docs.title: EVPN over SRv6
docs.text: EVPN (Ethernet VPN) provides L2 services (E-Line, E-LAN, E-Tree) and integrated L2/L3 services over SRv6 transport.

docs.title: EVPN Route Types with SRv6
docs.text: Route Type Name SRv6 Behavior Type 2 MAC/IP Advertisement End.DX2 or End.DT2 Type 3 Inclusive Multicast BUM traffic handling Type 5 IP Prefix Route End.DT4 / End.DT6 (IP-VRF)

docs.title: EVPN-VPWS (E-Line) with SRv6
docs.text:
Point-to-point L2 service using End.DX2 behavior:

CE1 ──[L2 Frame]──► PE1 ──[IPv6(DA=PE2::DX2)][SRH][L2 Frame]──► PE2 ──[L2 Frame]──► CE2

The End.DX2 SID tells PE2: "decapsulate and cross-connect this L2 frame to the specified attachment circuit."

docs.text: Aspect EVPN-VXLAN EVPN-SRv6 Encapsulation VXLAN (UDP) SRv6 (IPv6 + SRH) Underlay IPv4 or IPv6 IPv6 native TE capability Limited Full SR Policy support Network programming None Rich (service chaining, slicing) MTU overhead 50 bytes 40 bytes (no SRH) to 56+ bytes (with SRH)

docs.title: BGP SRv6 Service TLV (RFC 9252)
docs.text:
RFC 9252 defines how SRv6 SID information is carried in BGP updates using the SRv6 Services TLVs within the BGP Prefix-SID attribute:

BGP Update Message:
  ├── NLRI: 10.1.0.0/24 (VPNv4)
  ├── Next-Hop: 2001:db8::1
  ├── Extended Community: RT 100:1
  └── BGP Prefix-SID Attribute:
      └── SRv6 L3 Service TLV:
          ├── SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4
          ├── SRv6 SID Behavior: End.DT4 (19)
          └── SRv6 SID Structure:
              ├── Locator Block Length: 32
              ├── Locator Node Length: 16
              ├── Function Length: 16
              └── Argument Length: 0

docs.title: SID Transposition
docs.text: To save space in BGP updates, the function part of the SID can be transposed into (encoded within) the VPN prefix itself, rather than carrying the full 128-bit SID. This is an optimization defined in RFC 9252.

docs.title: CLOS Fabrics & Load Balancing
docs.text: Modern data center networks use CLOS (Spine-Leaf) topologies with multiple equal-cost paths. SRv6 provides deterministic traffic placement across these paths, solving the fundamental limitations of traditional ECMP hashing.

docs.title: CLOS Topology Refresher
docs.text:
A CLOS fabric provides full bisectional bandwidth between any two leaf switches through multiple spine switches:

  • Spine 1 → Leaf 1
  • Spine 1 → Leaf 2
  • Spine 1 → Leaf 3
  • Spine 1 → Leaf 4
  • Spine 2 → Leaf 1
  • Spine 2 → Leaf 2
  • Spine 2 → Leaf 3
  • Spine 2 → Leaf 4
  • Spine 3 → Leaf 1
  • Spine 3 → Leaf 2
  • Spine 3 → Leaf 3
  • Spine 3 → Leaf 4
graph TB
    S1[Spine 1] --- L1[Leaf 1]
    S1 --- L2[Leaf 2]
    S1 --- L3[Leaf 3]
    S1 --- L4[Leaf 4]
    S2[Spine 2] --- L1
    S2 --- L2
    S2 --- L3
    S2 --- L4
    S3[Spine 3] --- L1
    S3 --- L2
    S3 --- L3
    S3 --- L4

docs.title: The ECMP Problem
docs.text:
Traditional ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) uses a hash of packet headers (5-tuple) to select a path. This works well for diverse traffic, but fails with:

  • Elephant flows — large, long-lived flows that saturate a single path
  • Synchronized workloads — AI/ML training where thousands of flows start and end simultaneously
  • Hash collisions — multiple flows hashing to the same spine, causing congestion while other spines are idle
  • Hash polarization — similar hash results at multiple layers of the fabric

docs.title: SRv6 Deterministic Path Placement
docs.text:
Instead of relying on hashing, SRv6 allows the source (host, NIC, or controller) to explicitly choose which spine each flow traverses:

Traditional ECMP:
  Packet → Hash(5-tuple) → Spine selection    (probabilistic)

SRv6 Path Placement:
  Packet → SRv6 SID(Spine-N) → Spine selection  (deterministic)

Each spine is assigned an SRv6 uSID. The source encapsulates the packet with the desired spine's SID, guaranteeing the path.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text: Aspect ECMP SRv6 Deterministic Path selection Hash-based (probabilistic) Explicit (deterministic) Elephant flow handling Poor (collisions) Optimal (controlled placement) Fabric utilization 60-80% typical Near 100% achievable Application awareness None Source can control path Flowlet support Limited Native via SID switching

docs.title: What are Flowlets?
docs.text:
A flowlet is a burst of packets within a flow, separated by idle gaps. Unlike flow-level load balancing (which pins an entire flow to one path), flowlet-based load balancing can reassign traffic to different paths between bursts without causing reordering.

Flow timeline:
  ████████──gap──████████──gap──████████──gap──████████
  Flowlet 1       Flowlet 2       Flowlet 3       Flowlet 4
  → Spine 1       → Spine 2       → Spine 3       → Spine 1

docs.title: GLB with SRv6
docs.text:
Global Load Balancing (GLB) uses SRv6 to steer flowlets across different spines:

  1. Monitor fabric link utilization or congestion signals
  2. Assign each new flowlet to the least-loaded spine via SRv6 SID
  3. Reroute between flowlet gaps — no packet reordering

This is especially powerful for AI training workloads where collective operations (AllReduce, AllGather) create predictable traffic bursts with natural gaps.

docs.title: BGP in CLOS + SRv6
docs.text: BGP is the standard routing protocol for CLOS fabrics (replacing OSPF/IS-IS in many DC deployments). With SRv6:

docs.title: eBGP Underlay
docs.text:
Each leaf-spine link runs an eBGP session (each switch has its own ASN or uses BGP unnumbered):

Leaf ASN 65001 ──eBGP── Spine ASN 65100
Leaf ASN 65002 ──eBGP── Spine ASN 65100

docs.title: SRv6 Locator Advertisement
docs.text: Each switch advertises its SRv6 locator via BGP, making SRv6 SIDs reachable across the fabric.

docs.title: Overlay Services
docs.text:
BGP EVPN over SRv6 provides:

  • L2 bridging across the fabric (VXLAN replacement)
  • L3 routing between VRFs
  • Distributed anycast gateway at every leaf

docs.title: SRv6 vs VXLAN in Data Centers

docs.title: EVPN Multihoming
docs.text:
EVPN multihoming (often shortened to EVPN-MH or EVPN multi-homing) lets a customer device — a switch, router, server or access node — attach to two or more PE routers over a single logical link, with the PEs coordinating through BGP instead of a proprietary MC-LAG control channel. It is defined in RFC 7432 (the EVPN base specification) and refined by RFC 8584 (DF election framework). RFC 9252 and RFC 9819 carry the same machinery over SRv6.

This page covers the generic mechanisms first — they are identical whether the core runs MPLS, VXLAN or SRv6 — and then the parts that change with an SRv6 data plane.

  • CE LAG with 2 member links → PE1 (ES 1)
  • CE LAG with 2 member links → PE2 (ES 1)
  • PE1 → MPLS / SRv6 core
  • PE2 → MPLS / SRv6 core
  • MPLS / SRv6 core → PE3 remote
  • PE3 remote → Remote CE
graph LR
    CE[CE<br/>LAG with 2 member links] ---|ES 1| PE1[PE1]
    CE ---|ES 1| PE2[PE2]
    PE1 <--> CORE((MPLS / SRv6 core))
    PE2 <--> CORE
    CORE <--> PE3[PE3 remote]
    PE3 --- RCE[Remote CE]

docs.title: Ethernet Segment and ESI
docs.text:
An Ethernet Segment (ES) is the set of links that connect one customer site to several PEs. From the CE's point of view it is usually a single LACP bundle; each PE sees one member link. Every PE attached to the segment configures the same Ethernet Segment Identifier (ESI).

The ESI is 10 octets: a 1-octet type followed by a 9-octet value (RFC 7432 §5). Two values are reserved: all zeros means "single-homed, no ES", and all FF (MAX-ESI) is reserved.

Type Value is built from Typical use 0 9 octets configured by the operator Most common; you pick a unique value per segment 1 CE LACP system MAC (6) + port key (2) + 0 Auto-derived from LACP when the CE runs LACP 2 IST root bridge MAC (6) + root bridge priority (2) + 0 CE is a bridged LAN running MSTP; the PE learns the values from BPDUs 3 System MAC (6) + local discriminator (3) Auto-generated by the PE from a MAC 4 Router ID (4) + local discriminator (4) + 0 Auto-generated from the PE/CE router ID 5 AS number (4) + local discriminator (4) + 0 Auto-generated from an ASN

Type 0 vs auto-derived ESIs

Type 0 is explicit and portable between vendors. Auto-derived types save configuration on large access networks, but check what your vendor actually derives from: RFC 7432 Type 1 uses the CE's LACP system MAC and port key, while Junos auto-derive lacp builds the ESI from the PE's own LACP system ID and admin key (which must then be identical on every PE). Either way, all PEs on an all-active LAG must present the same LACP system ID to the CE, or the CE will not bundle the links.

docs.title: EVPN Routes Used for Multihoming
docs.text: Route Name Multihoming role Type 4 Ethernet Segment Discovery of the other PEs on the same ES and DF election. Carries the ES-Import Route Target (auto-derived from the ESI value for types 1–3), so only PEs on that ES import it Type 1 Ethernet A-D per ES Advertises the redundancy mode (single-active flag in the ESI Label extended community) and the split-horizon label/argument; withdrawing it is the mass withdrawal signal Type 1 Ethernet A-D per EVI Advertised per service instance; lets remote PEs build aliasing (all-active) or backup paths (single-active) Type 2 MAC/IP Advertisement MAC and ARP/ND bindings; synced between PEs on the same ES Type 3 Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag BUM delivery; in SRv6 also carries the End.DT2M SID Type 5 IP Prefix (RFC 9136) Routed prefixes, used by EVPN L3 multihoming

docs.title: All-Active vs Single-Active
docs.text:
All-active Single-active Who forwards known unicast Every PE on the ES Only the DF for that VLAN/EVI CE side One LAG across the PEs Separate links or LAG with standby members; the non-DF blocks its port for that service Remote PE behavior ECMP to all PEs on the ES (aliasing) Primary path to the DF, pre-programmed backup path to the non-DF BUM toward the CE Only the DF sends Only the DF sends Loop prevention needed Split-horizon filtering (BUM received from the ES must not be sent back into it) Not for the CE (the non-DF does not forward) Typical use Data center leaf pairs, access aggregation, bandwidth Hand-offs to devices that cannot run a cross-chassis LAG, strict per-VLAN active/standby

A third mode, port-active (RFC 9786, June 2025), elects one PE per interface rather than per VLAN — a drop-in replacement for MC-LAG active/standby. The DF election for port-active can use any of the algorithms below.

docs.title: Designated Forwarder (DF) Election
docs.text:
When the CE floods a broadcast or unknown-unicast frame, every PE on the ES would deliver remote BUM copies back to it. The DF is the one PE per that sends BUM toward the CE; the others drop it.

PEs learn each other through Type 4 routes, wait for the DF election timer (3 seconds by default) so all routes arrive, then run the election.

Algorithm Defined in How it picks the DF Trade-off Modulo / service carving (default) RFC 7432 §8.5 Sort PE IPs ascending (index 0..N-1); DF for VLAN V is index V mod N Simple, but when a PE joins or leaves, almost every VLAN moves HRW (Highest Random Weight) RFC 8584 §3 Each PE computes a hash weight of (VLAN, ESI, PE address); highest wins, ties go to the lowest IP Only the VLANs of the failed/added PE move; even spread with sparse VLAN IDs Preference-based RFC 9785 (June 2025) Operator sets a 2-octet preference per PE per ES; highest (DF Alg 2) or lowest (DF Alg 3) wins; the D (Don't Preempt) bit makes it non-revertive Deterministic primary/backup per ES; the norm for single-active designs AC-influenced (AC-DF) RFC 8584 Any of the above, but a PE whose attachment circuit is down for that EVI is excluded Avoids electing a DF that cannot actually forward

RFC 8584 also introduced the DF Election extended community on the Type 4 route: a 5-bit algorithm field (0 = modulo, 1 = HRW, ⅔ = highest/lowest preference) and a capability bitmap (D, AC-DF, …). If the PEs on a segment disagree, they all fall back to modulo. Vendor support varies: Cisco IOS-XR and Junos expose modulo and preference-based election in configuration, so check the release notes before designing around HRW.

Modulo example: ES with PE1 (192.0.2.1) and PE2 (192.0.2.2), N = 2
  Ordered list: [PE1, PE2]
  VLAN 100 → 100 mod 2 = 0 → PE1 is DF
  VLAN 101 → 101 mod 2 = 1 → PE2 is DF
  If you only use even VLANs, PE1 is DF for everything — HRW avoids this.

docs.title: Aliasing and Backup Path
docs.text:
A MAC address behind a multihomed CE may only be learned (and advertised in a Type 2 route) by one of the PEs — the one whose LAG member the CE hashed that flow onto. Without help, remote PEs would send all traffic for that MAC to that single PE.

Aliasing fixes this: each PE advertises an Ethernet A-D per EVI route for the ES. A remote PE that sees a Type 2 route with a non-zero ESI looks up every PE that advertised A-D per EVI for that ESI and load-balances across all of them, even the ones that never learned the MAC.

In single-active mode the same routes provide a backup path: the remote PE installs the DF as primary and the other PE as a pre-programmed backup, ready for fast switchover.

docs.title: Mass Withdrawal
docs.text:
If PE1 loses its link to a CE with 10 000 MACs, withdrawing 10 000 Type 2 routes takes time. Instead, PE1 withdraws a single Ethernet A-D per ES route. Every remote PE immediately removes PE1 from the next-hop set of all MACs associated with that ESI — a prefix-independent convergence step — and the individual Type 2 withdrawals follow in the background.

PE3 (remote)PE2PE1CEPE3 (remote)PE2PE1CELink CE–PE1 failsAll flows now go to PE2 onlyWithdraw Ethernet A-D per ES (ESI 1)Remove PE1 from every MAC/IP with ESI 1(later) Withdraw individual Type 2 routes

docs.title: Split-Horizon Filtering
docs.text:
In all-active mode, a BUM frame from the CE arrives at PE1, which floods it to every PE in the EVI — including PE2, which is attached to the same ES. If PE2 is the DF, it would send the frame straight back to the CE, creating a loop or duplicate. Split-horizon stops this: the receiving PE must know which ES the frame came from and skip that ES.

How the "came from" information is carried depends on the data plane:

Data plane Mechanism Defined in MPLS ESI label: each PE advertises a label in its A-D per ES route; the ingress PE pushes the egress PE's ESI label beneath the EVPN label on BUM sent to it. The egress PE sees the label and does not forward onto that ES RFC 7432 §8.3 VXLAN / NVO Local bias: no label space for an ESI label, so the egress PE uses the outer source IP to recognize a peer on the same ES; the ingress PE always floods locally to its own ESs regardless of DF state RFC 8365 §8.3.1 SRv6 ESI-filtering argument (Arg.FE2) carried in the argument bits of the egress PE's End.DT2M SID — the SRv6 equivalent of the ESI label. Local bias is also allowed RFC 8986 §4.12, RFC 9252 §6.1.1/§6.3, RFC 9819

RFC 9746 (March 2025) lets PEs signal which method they use, with a Split-Horizon Type field in the ESI Label extended community: MPLS defaults to ESI-label filtering, VXLAN to local bias, and SRv6 defaults to ESI filtering but supports both. Local bias only works with all-active redundancy.

docs.title: EVPN Multihoming over SRv6
docs.text:
SRv6 has no label stack to push an ESI label onto, so the egress PE's local ES identifier travels as an argument inside the SID itself:

  1. Each PE allocates an End.DT2M SID per bridge domain for BUM traffic and advertises its LOC:FUNC part in the Type 3 (IMET) route.
  2. For each local ES it allocates an Arg.FE2 value and advertises it in the Type 1 A-D per ES route (SRv6 L2 Service TLV).
  3. When PE1 floods BUM that it received from ES 1 to PE2, it combines PE2's End.DT2M LOC:FUNC with PE2's Arg.FE2 for ES 1 into the destination address.
  4. PE2 executes End.DT2M: it decapsulates and floods into the bridge domain, excluding the interfaces of the ES identified by the argument.
PE2 Type 3 route:  End.DT2M LOC:FUNC = fc00:0:2:e002::   SID structure 32/16/16, AL 16
PE2 Type 1 route:  Arg.FE2 for ES 1  = 0x00a1             AL 16
PE1 → PE2, BUM received from ES 1:
    argument inserted at offset 32+16+16 = 64 bits
    DA = fc00:0:2:e002:a1::
PE2: End.DT2M with argument 0x00a1 → flood to every AC in the bridge domain except ES 1

Why RFC 9819 exists

RFC 9252 said the ingress PE SHOULD bitwise-OR the Type 3 SID and the Type 1 argument. That only works when both routes use the same SID structure; interop testing found implementations disagreeing. RFC 9819 (July 2025) replaces the OR with an explicit rule: insert the argument at offset LBL + LNL + FL taken from the Type 3 route's SID Structure, and stop forwarding BUM from that ES if the two routes announce different argument lengths. If you mix vendors on an SRv6 EVPN all-active segment, check RFC 9819 support first.

Known unicast does not need split-horizon. Remote PEs use End.DT2U (bridge-table lookup) or End.DX2 (cross-connect, for EVPN-VPWS) SIDs from the Type 1 per-EVI and Type 2 routes, and aliasing simply becomes ECMP across the SRv6 SIDs of all PEs on the ES. With uSID these service SIDs are typically uDT2U/uDT2M micro-SIDs on the PE's locator.

The underlay contributes too: TI-LFA protects the core paths between PEs, while mass withdrawal and aliasing protect the attachment circuit — the two mechanisms are complementary.

docs.title: EVPN L3 Multihoming (Routed CE)
docs.text:
When the CE is a router and the service is an L3VPN, the same ES concepts apply to a routed hand-off. draft-ietf-bess-evpn-l3mh-proto specifies EVPN L3 multihoming:

  1. CE connects to PE1 and PE2 via an Ethernet Segment (same ESI on both PEs)
  2. PEs discover each other via Type 4 routes and elect a DF
  3. ARP/ND entries learned by one PE are synced to the other with Type 2 routes, so either PE can route to the CE immediately
  4. Prefixes are advertised to remote PEs as Type 5 (or VPNv4/VPNv6) routes with SRv6 End.DT4/End.DT6/End.DT46 service SIDs
  5. Remote PEs ECMP across both PEs; on PE or link failure, the Type 1 per-ES withdrawal triggers fast reconvergence
Aspect L2 multihoming (EVPN) L3 multihoming (EVPN L3MH) Service type L2VPN / bridging L3VPN / routing CE attachment Bridge domain VRF / routed interface MAC learning Required Only for ARP/ND sync Split-horizon Per ES (ESI label / Arg.FE2) Not needed for routed traffic Prefix advertisement Type 2 (MAC/IP) Type 5 (IP Prefix) + Type 2 (ARP/ND sync) SRv6 service SIDs End.DT2U, End.DT2M, End.DX2 End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DT46

Interoperability

EVPN L3 multihoming has been demonstrated in multi-vendor interoperability tests (EANTC) with Cisco and Nokia using both SRv6 and SR-MPLS underlays.

docs.title: EVPN Multihoming vs MC-LAG
docs.text: EVPN multihoming MC-LAG / MLAG Control plane Standard BGP (RFC 7432) Vendor-specific (ICCP, peer-link) Number of PEs 2 or more Usually exactly 2 Peer link between PEs Not required Usually required Multivendor PE pair Possible No Works across a routed core (MPLS, VXLAN, SRv6) Yes Typically same site only

docs.title: Configuration Examples
docs.text:
Both PEs on the segment get the same ESI and redundancy mode. The examples use the type 0 ESI 00:11:22:33:44:55:66:77:88:99 with preference-based DF election (PE1 preferred).

Cisco IOS-XRJunos 
!! PE1 (use weight 50 on PE2)
interface Bundle-Ether10
 lacp system mac 0011.2233.4455
!
evpn
 interface Bundle-Ether10
  ethernet-segment
   identifier type 0 11.22.33.44.55.66.77.88.99
   !! all-active is the default; alternatives:
   !! load-balancing-mode single-active | port-active
   service-carving preference-based
    weight 100
  !
 !
 !! SRv6: EVPN services take SIDs from this locator
 segment-routing srv6
  locator MAIN
 !
!

# PE1 (use preference value 50 on PE2)
set interfaces ae0 esi 00:11:22:33:44:55:66:77:88:99
set interfaces ae0 esi all-active
set interfaces ae0 esi df-election-type preference value 100
# identical LACP system ID on every PE of the segment
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp active
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp system-id 00:11:22:33:44:55

ESI notation

IOS-XR takes the 9-octet value after type 0; Junos takes all 10 octets, and a manually configured Junos ESI must start with 00 (type 0). The two lines above describe the same segment. IOS-XR locator precedence for EVPN SRv6 SIDs is per-service, then per-EVI (evi N segment-routing srv6 → locator), then the global evpn segment-routing srv6 locator.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
• ESI mismatch: a typo in one PE's ESI silently turns an all-active segment into two single-homed sites — the CE sees duplicate BUM and MAC flaps.
  • LACP system ID: for an all-active LAG, every PE must present the same LACP system ID and key to the CE.
  • Mixed DF algorithms: PEs that advertise different DF algorithms fall back to modulo; check the DF Election extended community on the Type 4 routes.
  • Core isolation: if a PE loses all core connectivity but keeps its CE link up, the CE keeps hashing traffic into a black hole. Most implementations bring the access interface down on core isolation — enable it.
  • SRv6 argument length: on SRv6, the End.DT2M argument length must match between Type 1 and Type 3 routes (RFC 9819); mismatches stop BUM from that segment.

docs.title: Flex-Algorithm
docs.text: IGP Flexible Algorithm (Flex-Algo) allows operators to define custom path computation algorithms within the IGP (IS-IS or OSPFv3). Combined with SRv6, it enables network slicing — multiple logical topologies over a single physical infrastructure.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Traditional IGP computes a single shortest path based on link metric. But modern networks need different paths for different services:

  • Voice/Video: Lowest latency path
  • Bulk data: Highest bandwidth path
  • Critical services: Path avoiding certain nodes/links
  • Redundancy: Disjoint paths for protection

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
Flex-Algo lets you define multiple algorithms (algo 128-255), each with its own:

  • Metric type (IGP metric, latency, TE metric)
  • Constraints (include/exclude affinities, SRLGs)
  • Calculation type (SPF, strict SPF)

Each algorithm produces its own set of SRv6 SIDs, creating independent forwarding planes.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• PE1 → P1 (10ms, BW:100G)
  • PE1 → P2 (2ms, BW:10G)
  • P1 → PE2 (5ms, BW:100G)
  • P2 → PE2 (3ms, BW:10G)
graph LR
    A[PE1] -->|10ms, BW:100G| B[P1]
    A -->|2ms, BW:10G| C[P2]
    B -->|5ms, BW:100G| D[PE2]
    C -->|3ms, BW:10G| D
Algorithm Metric Best Path PE1→PE2 Use Case Algo 0 IGP metric (default) PE1→P2→PE2 Default routing Algo 128 Latency PE1→P2→PE2 (5ms) Low-latency services Algo 129 TE metric (bandwidth) PE1→P1→PE2 (100G) High-bandwidth services

docs.title: Per-Algorithm SRv6 Locators
docs.text:
Each Flex-Algo gets its own SRv6 locator, which means its own set of SIDs:

Node PE2 advertises:
  Algo 0:   fcbb:bb01:0002::/48  → Default IGP path
  Algo 128: fcbb:bb02:0002::/48  → Latency-optimized path
  Algo 129: fcbb:bb03:0002::/48  → Bandwidth-optimized path

To steer traffic on the low-latency path, simply use the Algo 128 SID as the destination. The IGP handles path computation automatically.

docs.title: Network Slicing with Flex-Algo
docs.text:
Flex-Algo is the foundation of SRv6 network slicing for 5G and enterprise services:

  • Router 1 → Router 2
  • Router 2 → Router 3
  • R1 → R2
  • R2 → R3
  • R1 → R2
  • R2 → R3
graph TB
    subgraph Physical Network
        direction LR
        R1[Router 1] --- R2[Router 2] --- R3[Router 3]
    end

    subgraph Slice 1 - Low Latency - Algo 128
        direction LR
        S1R1[R1] -.-> S1R2[R2] -.-> S1R3[R3]
    end

    subgraph Slice 2 - High BW - Algo 129
        direction LR
        S2R1[R1] -.-> S2R2[R2] -.-> S2R3[R3]
    end

    style S1R1 fill:#1565c026,stroke:#1565c0
    style S1R2 fill:#1565c026,stroke:#1565c0
    style S1R3 fill:#1565c026,stroke:#1565c0
    style S2R1 fill:#2e7d3226,stroke:#2e7d32
    style S2R2 fill:#2e7d3226,stroke:#2e7d32
    style S2R3 fill:#2e7d3226,stroke:#2e7d32

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! Define Flex-Algo 128 (low latency)
router isis CORE
 flex-algo 128
  metric-type delay
  advertise-definition
 !
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  segment-routing srv6
   locator LATENCY algo 128
  !
 !
!

!! Define SRv6 locator for Algo 128
segment-routing
 srv6
  locators
   locator LATENCY
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fcbb:bb02::/48
    algorithm 128
   !
  !
 !
!

set protocols isis source-packet-routing flex-algorithm 128
set protocols isis source-packet-routing flex-algorithm 128 metric-type delay
set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator latency fcbb:bb02::/48 algorithm 128

docs.title: Flex-Algo Properties
docs.text: Property Options Description Algorithm ID 128-255 User-defined algorithm number Metric Type IGP, delay, TE Which metric to optimize Calculation Type SPF, Strict SPF How to compute the path Include-any Admin groups Links MUST have at least one of these affinities Include-all Admin groups Links MUST have ALL of these affinities Exclude-any Admin groups Links MUST NOT have any of these affinities Exclude SRLG SRLG values Avoid links sharing a risk group

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
show isis flex-algo 128
show segment-routing srv6 locator LATENCY
show isis route ipv6 fcbb:bb02:0002::/48 detail

show isis flex-algorithm 128
show spring-traffic-engineering srv6-sid

Production validated

According to a joint announcement by Cisco and SoftBank, SRv6 Flex-Algo was deployed on a commercial 5G network in April 2022.

  3. Cisco IOS-XR: Enabling Segment Routing Flexible Algorithm - Cisco IOS-XR configuration guide for Flex-Algo on NCS 5500 routers
  4. Cisco CVD: Quantum-Safe SRv6 Fabric for Mission-Critical Networks - Validated Flex-Algo 128/129 slicing design (secure + low-latency) with dedicated locator blocks per algorithm on IOS-XE

docs.title: SRv6 Glossary
docs.text:
This glossary defines the terms used in SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6) and throughout srv6.md. Each entry gives a short definition you can quote as-is, the RFC section that defines the term, and a link to the page that explains it in depth. Definitions follow the RFC text; when a term is a vendor name or comes from an Internet-Draft rather than an RFC, the entry says so.

AI networking terms

Looking for GPU-fabric vocabulary such as RoCEv2, NCCL, all-reduce or packet spraying? See the AI Networking Glossary.

0–9ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ

docs.title: 5f00::/16
docs.text:
5f00::/16 is the IPv6 block IANA allocated in 2024 for SRv6 SIDs. It is marked not globally reachable, which makes SRv6 traffic easy to recognize and filter at SR domain edges.

Defined in: RFC 9602 §6 · Learn more: SID Structure

docs.title: Active segment
docs.text:
The active segment is the segment the receiving node must process now. In SRv6 it is the IPv6 destination address; in SR-MPLS it is the top label.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §2 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: Adjacency SID (Adj-SID)
docs.text:
An Adj-SID identifies an IGP adjacency and makes the advertising node send the packet over that specific link, whatever the shortest path. In SRv6 an Adj-SID is an End.X (or uA) SID.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §3.4, RFC 9352 §8 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: Anycast-SID
docs.text:
An Anycast-SID is a Prefix-SID for a prefix advertised by several nodes, so each packet goes to the nearest of them. It is used for redundancy and load sharing, for example across a pair of border routers.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §3.3, RFC 9352 §6 · Learn more: Inter-Domain SRv6

docs.title: Argument
docs.text:
The argument is an optional field in the low-order bits of an SRv6 SID that gives the behavior per-packet or per-flow input, such as the remaining uSIDs of a NEXT-CSID container or the EVPN split-horizon value of End.DT2M.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §3.1 · Learn more: SID Structure

docs.title: Automated Steering (AS)
docs.text:
Automated Steering installs a BGP route on the SR Policy whose color and endpoint match the route's Color Extended Community and next hop, so service traffic follows the policy without per-route configuration.

Defined in: RFC 9256 §8.4 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: BGP-LS
docs.text:
BGP-LS (BGP Link-State) exports IGP topology to controllers and PCEs. RFC 9514 extends it to carry SRv6 locators, SIDs and their behaviors.

Defined in: RFC 9552, RFC 9514 · Learn more: RFC 9514 summary

docs.title: BGP Prefix-SID attribute
docs.text:
The BGP Prefix-SID attribute (path attribute 40) carries segment routing information with a BGP route. RFC 9252 uses it to carry SRv6 Service TLVs for VPN and EVPN routes.

Defined in: RFC 8669, RFC 9252 §2 · Learn more: BGP Overlay

docs.title: BGP SR Policy
docs.text:
BGP SR Policy is the BGP extension (SAFI 73) a controller uses to push SR Policy candidate paths, with their segment lists, color and endpoint, to headends.

Defined in: RFC 9830 · Learn more: RFC 9830 summary

docs.title: Binding SID (BSID)
docs.text:
A Binding SID is a SID bound to an SR Policy: a packet whose active segment is the BSID is steered into that policy. It hides the policy's path from upstream nodes and keeps their SID lists short; in SRv6 it is an End.B6.Encaps or End.B6.Encaps.Red SID.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §5, RFC 9256 §6 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: Candidate path
docs.text:
A candidate path is one way to realize an SR Policy: explicit (given segment lists), dynamic (computed from an objective and constraints) or composite. The valid candidate path with the highest preference is the active one.

Defined in: RFC 9256 §2.2, RFC 9256 §2.9 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: Color
docs.text:
Color is a non-zero 32-bit value that ties an SR Policy to an intent such as low latency. BGP routes carry it in the Color Extended Community so the headend can steer them onto the matching policy.

Defined in: RFC 9256 §2.1, RFC 9012 §4.3 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: Compressed SID (CSID)
docs.text:
A CSID is a compressed encoding of an SRv6 SID that keeps only its Locator-Node and Function bits; the Locator-Block shared by a group of SIDs is written once. RFC 9800 defines it.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §2 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: CSID container (uSID carrier)
docs.text:
A CSID container is a 128-bit IPv6 address that holds one or more CSIDs and the argument of the last one. The uSID drafts call it the uSID container, and earlier versions the uSID carrier.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §2 · Learn more: SID Decoder

docs.title: End
docs.text:
End is the basic SRv6 endpoint behavior and the SRv6 form of a node segment: the node decrements Segments Left, copies the next SID into the destination address and forwards the packet.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.1 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: End.B6.Encaps
docs.text:
End.B6.Encaps is the SRv6 Binding SID behavior: the node finishes the current segment, then pushes a new outer IPv6 header and SRH carrying the SID list of a local SR Policy.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.13 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: End.B6.Encaps.Red
docs.text:
End.B6.Encaps.Red is End.B6.Encaps with a reduced SRH: the first SID of the new SR Policy goes only into the outer destination address and is left out of the pushed SRH.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.14 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: End.BM
docs.text:
End.BM binds an SRv6 SID to an SR-MPLS policy: the node pushes the policy's MPLS label stack onto the packet. It joins SRv6 and SR-MPLS domains.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.15 · Learn more: Migration

docs.title: End.DT2M
docs.text:
End.DT2M removes the outer IPv6 header, learns the inner source MAC and floods the frame to the L2 table's interfaces, minus any excluded by its argument for split horizon. It carries EVPN broadcast, unknown-unicast and multicast (BUM) traffic.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.12 · Learn more: EVPN Multihoming

docs.title: End.DT2U
docs.text:
End.DT2U removes the outer IPv6 header, learns the inner source MAC and looks up the destination MAC in a specific L2 table (bridge domain). It carries known-unicast EVPN bridged traffic.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.11 · Learn more: VPN Services

docs.title: End.DT4
docs.text:
End.DT4 removes the outer IPv6 header and looks up the inner IPv4 packet in a specific IPv4 table, typically a VRF. It is the per-VRF SID of an IPv4 L3VPN over SRv6.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.7 · Learn more: BGP Overlay

docs.title: End.DT46
docs.text:
End.DT46 removes the outer IPv6 header and looks up the inner packet, IPv4 or IPv6, in a specific VRF. One End.DT46 SID serves a dual-stack VRF.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.8 · Learn more: BGP Overlay

docs.title: End.DT6
docs.text:
End.DT6 removes the outer IPv6 header and looks up the inner IPv6 packet in a specific IPv6 table, typically a VRF. It is the per-VRF SID of an IPv6 L3VPN.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.6 · Learn more: BGP Overlay

docs.title: End.DTMC4, End.DTMC6, End.DTMC46
docs.text:
End.DTMC4 works like End.DT4 except that the inner packet is looked up in the VRF's IPv4 multicast table; End.DTMC6 and End.DTMC46 do the same for IPv6 and for both families. They are carried as the SRv6 Multicast Service SID in MVPN routes over SRv6.

Defined in: RFC 10018 §3.1 · Learn more: Multicast

docs.title: End.DX2
docs.text:
End.DX2 removes the outer IPv6 header and sends the inner Ethernet frame out of a specific Layer-2 interface. It is the SID of EVPN VPWS (point-to-point E-Line) service.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.9 · Learn more: VPN Services

docs.title: End.DX2V
docs.text:
End.DX2V removes the outer IPv6 header and looks up the inner frame's VLAN in a specific L2 table to pick the outgoing interface. It serves EVPN flexible cross-connect.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.10 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: End.DX4
docs.text:
End.DX4 removes the outer IPv6 header and forwards the inner IPv4 packet to a specific Layer-3 adjacency. It is the per-CE SID of an IPv4 L3VPN.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.5 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: End.DX6
docs.text:
End.DX6 removes the outer IPv6 header and forwards the inner IPv6 packet to a specific Layer-3 adjacency. It is the per-CE SID of an IPv6 L3VPN.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.4 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: End.LBS and End.XLBS
docs.text:
End.LBS (Locator-Block Swap) and End.XLBS let a compressed SID list cross into a domain that uses a different Locator-Block: the node rewrites the block in the destination address to the next domain's block (End.XLBS also cross-connects to a neighbor).

Defined in: RFC 9800 §7 · Learn more: Inter-Domain SRv6

docs.title: End.MAP
docs.text:
End.MAP replaces the destination address with a new mapped SID and forwards the packet without touching the SRH. Intermediate user plane functions (UPFs) use it in the SRv6 mobile user plane.

Defined in: RFC 9433 §6.2 · Learn more: 5G Transport

docs.title: End.M.GTP4.E
docs.text:
End.M.GTP4.E builds an IPv4 GTP-U packet toward a legacy gNB from an SRv6 packet. It is the downlink half of IPv4 GTP-U interworking.

Defined in: RFC 9433 §6.6 · Learn more: 5G Transport

docs.title: End.M.GTP6.D
docs.text:
End.M.GTP6.D terminates an IPv6 GTP-U tunnel from a legacy gNB and sends the payload into an SRv6 policy. It is the uplink half of GTP-U to SRv6 interworking.

Defined in: RFC 9433 §6.3 · Learn more: 5G Transport

docs.title: End.M.GTP6.D.Di
docs.text:
End.M.GTP6.D.Di is the drop-in variant of End.M.GTP6.D: it keeps the GTP-U packet's original destination address as the last SID, so a second SR gateway can rebuild the GTP-U tunnel and both mobile endpoints keep using GTP-U.

Defined in: RFC 9433 §6.4, RFC 9433 §5.4 · Learn more: 5G Transport

docs.title: End.M.GTP6.E
docs.text:
End.M.GTP6.E builds an IPv6 GTP-U packet toward a legacy gNB from an SRv6 packet, taking the session identifiers from the SID's argument (Args.Mob.Session). It is the downlink half of IPv6 GTP-U interworking.

Defined in: RFC 9433 §6.5 · Learn more: 5G Transport

docs.title: End-of-Container (End-of-Carrier)
docs.text:
End-of-Container is the reserved all-zero uSID value that fills unused positions of a uSID container. When nothing but End-of-Container follows the active uSID, the node moves on to the next SID in the SRH, or treats itself as the final destination if none is left.

Defined in: uSID draft §3, RFC 9800 §4.1.1 · Learn more: SID Decoder

docs.title: Endpoint behavior
docs.text:
An SRv6 endpoint behavior is the packet-processing program bound to a local SID and run when a packet's destination address matches it. RFC 8986 defines the base set (End, End.X, End.DT4 and others) and IANA keeps the codepoint registry.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4, RFC 8986 §10.2 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: End.Replicate
docs.text:
End.Replicate is the SRv6 behavior of a Replication segment: the node sends a copy of the packet to each downstream node, with that node's Replication-SID as the destination, and on a leaf or bud node also decapsulates it locally.

Defined in: RFC 9524 §2.2.1 · Learn more: Multicast

docs.title: End.T
docs.text:
End.T does what End does and then looks up the new destination address in a specific IPv6 table instead of the default one.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.3 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: End.X
docs.text:
End.X (Layer-3 cross-connect) does what End does and then sends the packet over a specific Layer-3 adjacency instead of looking up the new destination. It is the SRv6 Adjacency SID.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.2 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: EVPN over SRv6
docs.text:
EVPN over SRv6 carries SRv6 L2 service SIDs (End.DX2, End.DX2V, End.DT2U, End.DT2M) in EVPN routes to deliver E-Line, E-LAN and multihomed services over an IPv6 core.

Defined in: RFC 9252 §6 · Learn more: BGP Overlay, EVPN Multihoming

docs.title: F1616
docs.text:
F1616 is a uSID format with a 16-bit Locator-Block and 16-bit uSIDs, giving seven uSIDs per container at the cost of a whole /16 for the block.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §4.1 · Learn more: SID Decoder

docs.title: F3216
docs.text:
F3216 is the uSID format with a 32-bit Locator-Block and 16-bit uSIDs, giving six uSIDs per container. RFC 9800 requires every NEXT-CSID implementation to support this combination.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §4.1 · Learn more: SID Decoder, uSID Compression

docs.title: Flavor
docs.text:
A flavor is a variant of an endpoint behavior that adds or changes steps, such as PSP, USP and USD (RFC 8986) or NEXT-CSID and REPLACE-CSID (RFC 9800). Each behavior and flavor combination has its own IANA codepoint.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.16, RFC 9800 §4 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: Flex-Algo (Flexible Algorithm)
docs.text:
Flex-Algo lets an operator define extra IGP path computations, numbered 128 to 255, each with its own metric and constraints, so one network computes several constrained shortest-path topologies at once. In SRv6 each Flex-Algo gets its own locator.

Defined in: RFC 9350 §4, RFC 9352 §7.1 · Learn more: Flex-Algorithm

docs.title: Flexible Algorithm Definition (FAD)
docs.text:
The FAD is the IGP advertisement that defines a Flex-Algo: its metric type (IGP, minimum delay or TE), calculation type and constraints such as admin groups to include or exclude and SRLGs to avoid.

Defined in: RFC 9350 §5 · Learn more: Flex-Algorithm

docs.title: FRRouting (FRR)
docs.text:
FRRouting is an open-source routing suite (BGP, IS-IS, OSPF and more) for Linux. It configures SRv6 locators and SIDs, IS-IS SRv6 and BGP L3VPN over SRv6, programming the kernel's seg6 and seg6local routes.

Defined in: FRRouting · Learn more: FRRouting

docs.title: Function
docs.text:
The function is the part of an SRv6 SID after the locator: an opaque local value that selects which behavior the node runs, for example End.X toward one neighbor or End.DT4 for one VRF.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §3.1 · Learn more: SID Structure

docs.title: GIB and LIB
docs.text:
The GIB (Global Identifiers Block) is the range of CSID values allocated domain-wide, such as node uSIDs; the LIB (Local Identifiers Block) is the range each node allocates for local SIDs such as uA and uDT.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §5 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: G-SRv6
docs.text:
G-SRv6 (Generalized SRv6) is a SID compression scheme that packs 32-bit compressed SIDs (G-SIDs) into SRH entries. The IETF standardized it as the REPLACE-CSID flavor of RFC 9800.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §4.2 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: H.Encaps
docs.text:
H.Encaps is the SR headend behavior that wraps the received packet in a new outer IPv6 header with an SRH holding the SR Policy's SID list, with the first SID as the destination address.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §5.1 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: H.Encaps.L2
docs.text:
H.Encaps.L2 applies H.Encaps to a received Ethernet frame: the whole frame becomes the payload of the new IPv6 packet, identified by Next Header 143 (Ethernet).

Defined in: RFC 8986 §5.3, RFC 8986 §10.1 · Learn more: VPN Services

docs.title: H.Encaps.L2.Red
docs.text:
H.Encaps.L2.Red is H.Encaps.L2 with a reduced SRH, leaving the first SID out of the SRH (or omitting the SRH for a single-SID policy).

Defined in: RFC 8986 §5.4 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: H.Encaps.Red
docs.text:
H.Encaps.Red is H.Encaps with a reduced SRH: the first SID goes only in the destination address and is left out of the SRH. If the policy has a single SID and needs no flags, tag or TLVs, the SRH is omitted entirely.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §5.2 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: HMAC TLV
docs.text:
The HMAC TLV (SRH TLV type 5) carries a keyed hash over the source address, Last Entry, Flags, HMAC Key ID and full Segment List, so an SR domain edge can verify that an SRH was built by a trusted source. It authenticates the SRH but gives no confidentiality and no replay protection.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §2.1.2 · Learn more: Security

docs.title: H.M.GTP4.D
docs.text:
H.M.GTP4.D is a headend behavior on an SR gateway that terminates an IPv4 GTP-U tunnel and steers the payload into an SRv6 policy. It is the uplink half of IPv4 GTP-U interworking.

Defined in: RFC 9433 §6.7 · Learn more: 5G Transport

docs.title: Infrastructure ACL (iACL)
docs.text:
An infrastructure ACL on every external interface of the SR domain drops incoming packets whose destination is in the domain's SID block. RFC 8754 requires this filtering, or an equivalent, to keep the SR domain closed to outside sources.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §5.1 · Learn more: Security

docs.title: IOAM (In-situ OAM)
docs.text:
IOAM records operational data such as node IDs, timestamps and queue depth inside live data packets as they cross a domain. In IPv6 it is carried in Hop-by-Hop or Destination Options headers.

Defined in: RFC 9197, RFC 9486 · Learn more: OAM

docs.title: IPFIX for SRv6
docs.text:
IPFIX for SRv6 adds information elements, such as the active segment, Segments Left, the SRH segment list and the endpoint behavior, so flow exporters can report how traffic uses SRv6 paths.

Defined in: RFC 9487 · Learn more: Telemetry

docs.title: L3VPN over SRv6
docs.text:
L3VPN over SRv6 is BGP IP VPN service in which VPN routes carry an SRv6 service SID (End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DT46, End.DX4 or End.DX6) instead of a VPN label, so PE-to-PE traffic is plain IPv6 with no MPLS in the core.

Defined in: RFC 9252 §5 · Learn more: VPN Services

docs.title: Last Entry
docs.text:
Last Entry is the SRH field holding the zero-based index of the last element of the Segment List. Because the list is stored in reverse, that element is the first segment of the path, or the second with a reduced SRH.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §2, RFC 8754 §4.1.1 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: Locator
docs.text:
The locator is the leading part of an SRv6 SID: a routable IPv6 prefix that leads to the node instantiating the SID. It is written B:N, the SID block B followed by the node identifier N.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §3.1 · Learn more: SID Structure

docs.title: Locator-Node
docs.text:
The Locator-Node is the part of a locator after the SID block that identifies one node (the N in B:N). In compressed SRv6, the Locator-Node plus the function form the compressed SID.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §2 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: Loop-Free Alternate (LFA)
docs.text:
An LFA is a neighbor that can forward to the destination without looping back through the failed resource. Plain and remote LFA leave gaps that depend on topology; TI-LFA closes them with segment lists.

Defined in: RFC 5286, RFC 7490 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: Maximum SID Depth (MSD)
docs.text:
MSD advertisements tell headends and PCEs how many SIDs a node can process, pop or push, such as Maximum Segments Left and Maximum H.Encaps, so they never build a SID list the hardware cannot handle.

Defined in: RFC 9352 §4 · Learn more: Performance

docs.title: Microloop
docs.text:
A microloop is a short-lived forwarding loop during IGP convergence, caused by routers updating their FIBs at different times. Segment routing can avoid it by holding traffic on a loop-free segment list until every router has converged.

Defined in: RFC 5715 · Learn more: Micro-Loop Avoidance

docs.title: Network Programming
docs.text:
SRv6 Network Programming is the model in which a packet's SID list works as a program: each SID names an instruction on a specific node, and the source chains them into an end-to-end service.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §1 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: NEXT-CSID (NEXT-C-SID)
docs.text:
NEXT-CSID is the RFC 9800 flavor in which one 128-bit container holds the Locator-Block followed by several CSIDs; each node consumes its CSID by shifting the rest left and forwards on the new destination address. It is the standardized form of uSID.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §4.1 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: Node-SID
docs.text:
A Node-SID is a Prefix-SID whose prefix identifies one specific router, typically its loopback. In SRv6 the uN or End SID of a node plays this role.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §3.2 · Learn more: SID Structure

docs.title: O-flag
docs.text:
The O-flag is the OAM bit in the SRH Flags field. A segment endpoint that supports it makes a timestamped copy of the marked packet for its local telemetry process, and forwards the original unchanged.

Defined in: RFC 9259 §2.1 · Learn more: OAM

docs.title: On-Demand Next-hop (ODN)
docs.text:
ODN (On-Demand Next-hop) is a headend feature that creates an SR Policy from a template when a BGP route arrives with a matching color, so policies exist only for endpoints in use. It is a vendor feature built on RFC 9256 steering, not a protocol of its own.

Defined in: RFC 9256 §8.4 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: Path Computation Element (PCE)
docs.text:
A PCE is an entity, often a controller, that computes paths for network nodes using a topology database usually learned through BGP-LS. For SR it returns segment lists for SR Policies.

Defined in: RFC 4655, RFC 9256 §5.2 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: Path Tracing
docs.text:
Path Tracing is an SRv6 OAM method in which every hop writes a few bytes (outgoing interface ID, load and a truncated timestamp) into a Hop-by-Hop option, so one probe reveals the exact ECMP path and per-hop delay. It is an IETF draft, not yet an RFC.

Defined in: draft-filsfils-ippm-path-tracing · Learn more: OAM

docs.title: PCEP
docs.text:
PCEP (PCE Communication Protocol) runs between a PCE and its clients to request, delegate and initiate paths. RFC 8664 adds SR-MPLS segment lists and RFC 9603 adds SRv6.

Defined in: RFC 5440, RFC 8664, RFC 9603 · Learn more: RFC 9603 summary

docs.title: Per-flow steering
docs.text:
Per-flow steering sends flows to the same endpoint over different SR Policies according to a per-packet forwarding class (set from DSCP or other fields), rather than by destination prefix. Vendors sell it as Per-Flow Policy (PFP).

Defined in: RFC 9256 §8.6 · Learn more: QoS

docs.title: Point of Local Repair (PLR)
docs.text:
The PLR is the router that detects the failure of a directly attached link or node and redirects traffic onto its pre-computed backup path.

Defined in: RFC 9855 §2.1 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: Post-convergence path
docs.text:
The post-convergence path is the path traffic will follow once the IGP has converged after a failure. TI-LFA sends repaired traffic along it, avoiding a second path change when convergence completes.

Defined in: RFC 9855 §3 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: PQ-node
docs.text:
A PQ-node is a node in both the (extended) P-space and the Q-space for a failure. The PLR needs only one segment to reach it, and normal forwarding from there delivers the packet without crossing the failure.

Defined in: RFC 9855 §5.2, RFC 7490 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: Prefix-SID
docs.text:
A Prefix-SID is the SID of an IGP prefix segment: it sends the packet along the IGP shortest path, for the advertised algorithm, to the node that owns the prefix. In SRv6 a Prefix-SID is an IPv6 address, normally an End SID within the node's locator.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §3.1, RFC 8402 §3.1.3 · Learn more: SID Structure

docs.title: P-space
docs.text:
The P-space of a router for a protected resource is the set of nodes it can reach on pre-failure shortest paths that never cross that resource. The extended P-space adds the nodes its neighbors can reach that way.

Defined in: RFC 9855 §2.1, RFC 7490 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: PSP (Penultimate Segment Pop)
docs.text:
PSP (Penultimate Segment Pop) is a flavor of End, End.X and End.T in which the penultimate segment endpoint removes the SRH after writing the last SID into the destination address, so the final node receives a packet without an SRH.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.16.1 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: Q-space
docs.text:
The Q-space of a destination for a protected resource is the set of nodes from which that destination is reached on shortest paths that never cross the resource.

Defined in: RFC 9855 §2.1, RFC 7490 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: Repair list
docs.text:
The repair list is the segment list the PLR adds to protected traffic to force it along the post-convergence path, for example a node SID to a P node followed by an adjacency SID to a Q node.

Defined in: RFC 9855 §5 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: REPLACE-CSID (REPLACE-C-SID)
docs.text:
REPLACE-CSID is the RFC 9800 flavor in which later CSIDs are packed into SRH entries and each node replaces the CSID in the destination address with the next one, tracked by an index in the argument. It is the standardized form of G-SRv6 compression.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §4.2 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: Replication segment
docs.text:
A Replication segment makes a node replicate a packet to a set of downstream nodes, each reached directly or through a segment list. Replication segments are stitched together to form SR point-to-multipoint trees.

Defined in: RFC 9524 §2 · Learn more: Multicast

docs.title: Routing Header type 4 (RH4)
docs.text:
Routing Header type 4 is the IPv6 Routing Type value assigned to the Segment Routing Header. Only the node whose SID is in the destination address processes it; transit routers forward on the destination address alone.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §2, RFC 8200 §4.4 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface)
docs.text:
SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface) is the vendor-neutral C API that SONiC and other network operating systems use to program switch ASICs. Its SRv6 objects, such as SID lists and My SID entries, let one software stack drive different chips.

Defined in: OCP SAI · Learn more: SONiC & SAI

docs.title: seg6 and seg6local
docs.text:
seg6 and seg6local are the Linux kernel's SRv6 route types: seg6 encapsulates traffic matching a route into an SRv6 SID list (headend), and seg6local binds a local SID to an endpoint behavior such as End, End.X or End.DT4.

Defined in: ip-route(8) · Learn more: Linux Kernel

docs.title: Segment
docs.text:
A segment is an instruction a node executes on a packet, such as "forward along the shortest path to node X", "send out this link" or "deliver into this VPN". Segment Routing steers a packet by attaching an ordered list of segments to it.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §2 · Learn more: What is SRv6?

docs.title: Segment endpoint node
docs.text:
An SR segment endpoint node is a node that receives a packet whose destination address is one of its local SIDs and executes the behavior bound to that SID.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §3.3 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: Segment Identifier (SID)
docs.text:
A SID (Segment Identifier) identifies a segment. In SRv6 a SID is a 128-bit IPv6 address that routes the packet to the node that owns it and selects the behavior that node runs.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §2, RFC 8986 §3 · Learn more: SID Structure, SID Decoder

docs.title: Segment List
docs.text:
The Segment List is the SRH array of 128-bit SIDs, stored in reverse order: Segment List[0] is the last segment of the path and the highest index is the first.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §2 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: Segment Routing Header (SRH)
docs.text:
The SRH is the IPv6 Routing Header (type 4) that carries an ordered list of SRv6 SIDs, the Segments Left pointer, flags, a tag and optional TLVs. It can be left out when the whole path fits in the destination address, as with a single SID or one uSID container.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §2 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: Segments Left (SL)
docs.text:
Segments Left is the SRH field that counts how many segments remain to be visited. Each segment endpoint decrements it and copies Segment List[Segments Left] into the destination address.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §2, RFC 8986 §4.1 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: Service SID
docs.text:
A service SID is an SRv6 SID that an egress PE advertises in BGP to identify a VPN, VRF or EVPN instance, such as End.DT4 or End.DX2. It does the job the VPN label does in MPLS.

Defined in: RFC 9252 §2 · Learn more: BGP Overlay

docs.title: Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG)
docs.text:
An SRLG is a set of links that share a resource, such as a fiber duct or line card, and can fail together. TI-LFA and Flex-Algo can avoid a whole SRLG so a backup path does not share the primary's risk.

Defined in: RFC 9855 §4, RFC 9350 §6.5 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: SID block
docs.text:
The SRv6 SID block is the IPv6 prefix an operator reserves for the SRv6 SIDs of a domain (the B in B:N); every locator is carved from it. RFC 9800 calls it the Locator-Block.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §3.1, RFC 9800 §2 · Learn more: SID Structure

docs.title: SONiC
docs.text:
SONiC (Software for Open Networking in the Cloud) is an open-source, Linux-based network operating system for white-box switches, hosted by the Linux Foundation. It programs the ASIC through SAI and uses FRRouting as its routing stack, including for SRv6.

Defined in: SONiC project · Learn more: SONiC & SAI, SONiC

docs.title: SR domain
docs.text:
An SR domain is the set of nodes that take part in the segment routing model, normally under one administrative entity. SRv6 SIDs are meant for use inside this trusted domain and are filtered at its edges.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §2, RFC 8754 §5.1 · Learn more: Security

docs.title: SRH insertion (H.Insert)
docs.text:
SRH insertion (H.Insert) adds an SRH to the existing IPv6 packet instead of adding a new outer IPv6 header. It is not part of RFC 8986 and is specified only in an individual Internet-Draft.

Defined in: draft-filsfils-spring-srv6-net-pgm-insertion · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: SR-MPLS
docs.text:
SR-MPLS is Segment Routing on the MPLS data plane: each segment is an MPLS label and the segment list is a label stack.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §2, RFC 8660 · Learn more: SRv6 vs SR-MPLS

docs.title: SR P2MP Policy (Tree-SID)
docs.text:
An SR P2MP Policy carries traffic from a root to a set of leaves over a tree built from Replication segments, usually computed by a controller. Tree-SID is the common vendor name for this approach.

Defined in: RFC 9960 §2 · Learn more: Multicast

docs.title: SR Policy
docs.text:
An SR Policy is an ordered list of segments that a headend uses to steer traffic, identified by the tuple headend, color and endpoint, and realized by one or more candidate paths.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §2, RFC 9256 §2.1 · Learn more: SR Policy

docs.title: SR source node (headend)
docs.text:
The headend, or SR source node, is the node that builds the SRv6 packet or outer encapsulation and writes the SID list, typically to steer traffic into an SR Policy.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §3.1, RFC 8986 §5 · Learn more: Network Programming

docs.title: SRv6
docs.text:
SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6) is Segment Routing on the IPv6 data plane: each segment is an IPv6 address (a SID), and a path of several segments is listed in a Segment Routing Header.

Defined in: RFC 8402 §2, RFC 8754, RFC 8986 · Learn more: What is SRv6?

docs.title: SRv6 Locator TLV
docs.text:
The IS-IS SRv6 Locator TLV (type 27) advertises a node's locator with its algorithm and metric, plus the End SIDs instantiated in it. OSPFv3 carries the same information in the SRv6 Locator LSA.

Defined in: RFC 9352 §7.1, RFC 9513 §7 · Learn more: RFC 9352 summary

docs.title: SRv6 MUP (Mobile User Plane)
docs.text:
SRv6 MUP replaces GTP-U tunnels in mobile networks with SRv6 segments. RFC 9433 defines the SRv6 mobility behaviors, and the BGP MUP SAFI (an IETF draft, not yet an RFC) distributes the session routes.

Defined in: RFC 9433, draft-ietf-bess-mup-safi · Learn more: 5G Transport

docs.title: SRv6 ping and traceroute
docs.text:
SRv6 ping and traceroute are ordinary ICMPv6 and UDP probes sent to a SID, with or without an SRH, to check that the SID is reachable and programmed and to locate faults hop by hop. No new protocol is needed.

Defined in: RFC 9259 §2.2 · Learn more: OAM

docs.title: SRv6 Service TLV
docs.text:
The SRv6 L3 Service TLV (type 5) and SRv6 L2 Service TLV (type 6) of the BGP Prefix-SID attribute carry a route's service SID, its endpoint behavior and its SID structure.

Defined in: RFC 9252 §2 · Learn more: BGP Overlay

docs.title: STAMP
docs.text:
STAMP (Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol) sends UDP test packets to measure one-way and round-trip delay, delay variation and packet loss. SR performance measurement uses it to measure links and SR Policies.

Defined in: RFC 8762, draft-ietf-spring-stamp-srpm · Learn more: SRPM

docs.title: TI-LFA
docs.text:
TI-LFA (Topology-Independent Loop-Free Alternate) is segment routing fast reroute: each router pre-computes a repair segment list that follows the post-convergence path around a failed link, node or SRLG, and switches to it as soon as it detects the failure. It provides protection in any topology.

Defined in: RFC 9855 · Learn more: TI-LFA

docs.title: Transit node
docs.text:
A transit node forwards an SRv6 packet like any other IPv6 packet, using only the destination address. It needs no SRv6 support and does not inspect the SRH.

Defined in: RFC 8754 §3.2 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: Transposition
docs.text:
Transposition is the RFC 9252 scheme that moves part of a service SID, typically the function, into the label field of the BGP NLRI so routes with different SIDs can share one attribute and pack into fewer updates. The SID Structure Sub-Sub-TLV records which bits moved.

Defined in: RFC 9252 §4 · Learn more: BGP Overlay

docs.title: uA
docs.text:
uA is the uSID name for End.X with the NEXT-CSID, PSP and USD flavors: the adjacency uSID. It consumes its uSID and sends the packet over a specific link.

Defined in: uSID draft §4.1.2, RFC 9800 §4.1.2 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: uDT (uDT4, uDT6, uDT46)
docs.text:
uDT is the uSID form of the End.DT decapsulation behaviors: a service uSID that removes the outer header and looks the inner packet up in a VRF (uDT4, uDT6, uDT46) or bridge table (uDT2U, uDT2M).

Defined in: uSID draft §4.2.1, RFC 9800 §4 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: uN
docs.text:
uN is the uSID name for End with the NEXT-CSID, PSP and USD flavors: the node uSID. On a match the node shifts the next uSID into place and forwards, or, when no uSID is left, acts as a regular End SID.

Defined in: uSID draft §4.1.1, RFC 9800 §4.1.1 · Learn more: uSID Compression

docs.title: USD (Ultimate Segment Decapsulation)
docs.text:
USD (Ultimate Segment Decapsulation) is a flavor of End, End.X and End.T in which the last segment endpoint removes the outer IPv6 header with all its extension headers and forwards the inner IPv4 or IPv6 packet.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.16.3 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk

docs.title: uSID (micro-SID)
docs.text:
A uSID (micro-SID) is a short compressed SRv6 SID, usually 16 bits; with a 32-bit block, six fit in one IPv6 address, so a multi-hop path often needs no SRH at all. uSID is the industry name for SIDs with the RFC 9800 NEXT-CSID flavor.

Defined in: RFC 9800 §4.1, uSID draft · Learn more: uSID Compression, SID Decoder

docs.title: USP (Ultimate Segment Pop)
docs.text:
USP (Ultimate Segment Pop) is a flavor of End, End.X and End.T in which the last segment endpoint, where Segments Left is 0, removes the SRH before processing the rest of the packet.

Defined in: RFC 8986 §4.16.2 · Learn more: SRH & Packet Walk
