docs.title: Cloud-Native SRv6 Backbone
docs.text:
Running SRv6 natively inside a public cloud eliminates the tunnel complexity of traditional SR-MPLS deployments. Instead of layering MPLS over GRE over the hyperscaler underlay, operators can build a single SRv6 domain that spans on-prem, cloud regions, availability zones, and even multiple clouds — using nothing but IPv6.

Reference deployment

Boost Mobile operates the first cloud-native 5G network in the United States, built entirely on Open RAN and hosted in AWS. Their transport backbone migrated from SR-MPLS with over 100,000 GRE tunnels to a unified SRv6 domain. The patterns described here are drawn from their production architecture.

docs.title: The Problem: SR-MPLS over GRE in the Cloud
docs.text:
A typical cloud-hosted mobile core uses a multi-tier topology:

  • Edge DCs (per market) — user data functions
  • Regional DCs — voice and regional services
  • National DCs — IMS/VoLTE, messaging, SBC interconnects
  • Edge DC Market A → Regional DC (GRE Tunnels)
  • Edge DC Market B → Regional DC (GRE Tunnels)
  • Regional DC → National DC (GRE Tunnels)
  • On-Prem PE → Edge DC Market A (DX + GRE Inter-AS Opt A)
  • On-Prem PE → Edge DC Market B (DX + GRE Inter-AS Opt A)
graph LR
    EDGE_A[Edge DC<br/>Market A] -->|GRE Tunnels| REG[Regional DC]
    EDGE_B[Edge DC<br/>Market B] -->|GRE Tunnels| REG
    REG -->|GRE Tunnels| NAT[National DC]
    ONPREM[On-Prem PE] -->|DX + GRE<br/>Inter-AS Opt A| EDGE_A
    ONPREM -->|DX + GRE<br/>Inter-AS Opt A| EDGE_B

In this model, vRouters interconnect via GRE tunnels carrying SR-MPLS, and on-prem connections use per-VRF BGP (Inter-AS Option A) over GRE across Direct Connect.

docs.title: Scaling limitations
docs.text: Challenge Impact Per-flow bandwidth cap Each GRE tunnel supports ~1.25 Gbps (single flow in AWS) Tunnel explosion Up to 8 GRE tunnels per VRF to reach ~10 Gbps; 100,000+ tunnels total Per-VRF Inter-AS complexity Every new VRF requires updates on all interconnects Policy fragmentation Community-based policies break across SR-MPLS domain boundaries

docs.title: The Solution: Native SRv6
docs.text:
Replacing the SR-MPLS/GRE stack with a single SRv6 domain eliminates these constraints:

  • vRouter Edge DC A → vRouter Edge DC B (Native IPv6)
  • vRouter Edge DC A → vRouter Regional DC (Native IPv6)
  • vRouter Edge DC B → vRouter Regional DC (Native IPv6)
  • vRouter Regional DC → vRouter National DC (Native IPv6)
  • On-Prem → vRouter Edge DC A (SRv6 over DX)
  • On-Prem → vRouter Edge DC B (SRv6 over DX)
graph LR
    VR1[vRouter<br/>Edge DC A] <-->|Native IPv6| VR2[vRouter<br/>Edge DC B]
    VR1 <-->|Native IPv6| VR3[vRouter<br/>Regional DC]
    VR2 <-->|Native IPv6| VR3
    VR3 <-->|Native IPv6| VR4[vRouter<br/>National DC]
    ONPREM[On-Prem] <-->|SRv6 over DX| VR1
    ONPREM <-->|SRv6 over DX| VR2

    subgraph Single SRv6 Domain
        VR1
        VR2
        VR3
        VR4
    end

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• Single SRv6 domain — on-prem and cloud routers communicate natively using IPv6
  • No GRE or IGP in cloud — only IPv6 locator reachability is required
  • Direct vRouter-to-vRouter — no transit vRouters needed, only cloud-native IPv6 routing
  • Full path control — SRv6 steers services independent of the underlying infrastructure
  • Multi-cloud ready — add vRouters across AZs, regions, or clouds with minimal configuration

docs.title: Hierarchical SRv6 addressing
docs.text:
A well-designed addressing plan enables summarization and scales horizontally:

Level Prefix Purpose Global Block /24 Entire SRv6 address space Slice Blocks /32 Flex-Algo segmentation Domain Supersets /36 Regional boundaries (~4,000 routers per block); summarization between cloud and on-prem DC Sets /44 Per-DC addressing (256 sets per domain, 16 locators per set) Node Locators /48 One or more per vRouter

uSID alignment on 32-bit boundaries ensures single-SRH traversal.

docs.title: Underlay: summarization-driven reachability
docs.text:
• Superset aggregates (/36) are exchanged between cloud transit gateways and on-prem for end-to-end reachability
  • DC-specific prefixes (/44) are advertised through local interconnects for shortest-path routing
  • Once aggregate prefixes are configured, no further BGP reconfiguration is needed as the network grows

docs.title: Dynamic locator routing
docs.text:
vRouters advertise SRv6 locators via BGP, and a cloud-native route reflector programs the cloud route tables in real time:

  • SRv6 locators are advertised and withdrawn instantly — no static routes or overlay signaling
  • vRouter-to-vRouter communication works across AZs, regions, clouds, and on-prem
  • New slices or vRouters announce their locators automatically
  • ENI changes on redeployment are updated without manual intervention

docs.title: Solving ECMP Entropy in the Cloud
docs.text: One challenge in public cloud is that the underlay may ignore the IPv6 Flow Label for ECMP hashing — the standard SRv6 approach for entropy does not work.

docs.title: The solution: entropy in the source address
docs.text:
By copying the flow label into the least-significant bits of the SRv6 source address, each flow gets a unique source that the cloud underlay can hash on:

Standard SRv6:
  Source Address: [Locator]
  Flow Label:    [Hash]     ← Ignored by cloud ECMP

Cloud-optimized:
  Source Address: [Locator]:[Flow Label bits]  ← Cloud ECMP sees unique source per flow
  • Each flow gets a unique source address, enabling balanced ECMP across the cloud underlay
  • All generated source addresses remain within the SRv6 locator block — URPF and anti-spoofing validation passes
  • No hyperscaler changes needed

docs.title: Stack simplification
docs.text: Layer SR-MPLS (Before) SRv6 (After) Tunnel overlay GRE tunnels (100,000+) None — native IPv6 Service transport SR-MPLS over GRE SRv6 IGP in cloud Required Not required Inter-domain Per-VRF Inter-AS Opt A Single SRv6 domain Scaling model Add GRE tunnels per VRF Add vRouters with locator advertisement

docs.title: Mission-Critical & Defense Networks
docs.text:
Mission-critical WANs — defense, public safety, critical infrastructure — have historically run on layered patchworks of MPLS/RSVP-TE overlays and controller-driven SD-WAN. In 2026 Cisco published a Validated Design (CVD) that replaces this stack with a quantum-safe SRv6 uSID fabric, targeting exactly these environments. This page summarizes the architecture and its design rules.

Primary source

This page is based on the Cisco CVD Quantum-Safe SRv6 Fabric for Mission-Critical Networks (August 2026), validated on Cisco 8000 Series Secure Routers running IOS-XE 26.1 — a reminder that Cisco SRv6 is not only an IOS-XR story: IOS-XE has supported SRv6 uSID since 17.12.1a on the ASR 1000 and Catalyst 8000 edge routers. See Cisco IOS-XE for the platform details.

docs.title: Why SRv6 for Mission-Critical?
docs.text: Two requirements dominate this space, and both map directly onto SRv6 properties:

docs.title: 1. Survivability in DDIL environments
docs.text:
Tactical edges operate under DDIL conditions — Disconnected, Disrupted, Intermittent, Low-bandwidth. Links are cut, jammed, or fade with satellite handoffs, and reachability to a central controller cannot be assumed.

DDIL requirement SRv6 answer No controller dependency Path computation (CSPF) runs locally on the ingress head-end against the IGP link-state database — a cut-off site keeps steering traffic autonomously Narrow links can't afford signaling Source routing eliminates RSVP-TE refresh storms; the path travels in the packet header, so low-bandwidth SATCOM links carry payload, not protocol chatter Any available transport SRv6 runs over MACsec-secured private lines, GRE/IPsec over commercial internet, LTE/5G, or LEO satellite — the fabric is transport-agnostic Sub-50 ms failover without convergence TI-LFA pre-computes repair paths at each Point of Local Repair; failover happens locally, in hardware. The CVD reports sub-50 ms, but the IOS-XE configuration guide notes that IGP TI-LFA "cannot guarantee 50ms FRR failover" on these platforms, so measure it in your own design Detect degraded (not just dead) links Active performance measurement probes track per-link delay and steer around congestion or satellite fade before sessions drop

docs.title: 2. The quantum threat: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later
docs.text:
Adversaries intercept and archive encrypted traffic today, intending to decrypt it once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer can break the classical key exchange (RSA/DH/ECDH) with Shor's algorithm. For data with a 10+ year sensitivity horizon, classical IPsec is already insufficient — this is the HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) threat, and it drives mandates like NSA CNSA 2.0 (full PQC compliance by 2030).

SRv6 itself provides no encryption (it never did) — the CVD's answer is to run the fabric over post-quantum-ready transport:

  • Private links: WAN MACsec (802.1AE) at line rate, with EAP-TLS authentication using ML-KEM (FIPS 203, formerly Kyber) key exchange over TLS 1.3
  • Untrusted transits: GRE over IPsec with IKEv2 hybrid key exchange (RFC 9370) combining classical ECDH with ML-KEM-1024 — the SA only establishes if both exchanges succeed
  • Transitional/multi-vendor: Post-Quantum Pre-Shared Keys (RFC 8784) mixed into IKEv2 key derivation
  • Management plane: ML-KEM key-exchange algorithms enforced in SSH

PQC keys are big — enable IKEv2 fragmentation

An ML-KEM-1024 public key is 1,568 bytes, so IKEv2 handshake messages exceed the 1500-byte MTU. Since most firewalls drop IP fragments, PQC IPsec deployments must enable application-layer IKEv2 fragmentation (RFC 7383) or tunnels silently fail to establish.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The design is a single IS-IS Level-2 domain carrying uSID (F3216) locators, with all services delivered as BGP overlays — no LDP, RSVP-TE, or BGP-LU anywhere:

  • Field Site tactical edge → DC Hub 1 (MACsec E-Line)
  • Field Site tactical edge → DC Hub 2 (PQC GRE/IPsec over internet)
  • Processing Center dual routers → DC Hub 1 (MACsec)
  • Processing Center dual routers → DC Hub 2 (PQC IPsec)
  • DC Hub 1 → Route Reflector
  • DC Hub 2 → Route Reflector
graph LR
    FS[Field Site<br/>tactical edge] -->|MACsec E-Line| HUB1[DC Hub 1]
    FS -->|PQC GRE/IPsec<br/>over internet| HUB2[DC Hub 2]
    SPC[Processing Center<br/>dual routers] -->|MACsec| HUB1
    SPC -->|PQC IPsec| HUB2
    HUB1 --- RR[Route Reflector]
    HUB2 --- RR

Key building blocks, each covered in depth elsewhere on this site:

Layer Mechanism Notes Underlay IS-IS L2, multi-topology, wide metrics All Ethernet WAN links must be point-to-point — broadcast mode silently breaks adjacency-SID and SR-TE path computation Transport uSID F3216 (<32-bit block><16-bit node><16-bit function>) Stateless core; P routers do plain IPv6 longest-prefix-match on /48 locators Services BGP L3VPN over SRv6 with uDT4/uDT6 IOS-XE supports per-VRF SID allocation only — one Service SID per VRF, not per prefix Enclave isolation Red/black separation via VRFs bound to dedicated locators Classified (red) traffic never leaves trusted edge enclaves unencrypted; only ciphertext crosses the black transport Slicing Flex-Algo 128 (secure) + 129 (low-latency) Separate locator block per algorithm — see below Steering ODN + Automated Steering via BGP color; Per-Flow Policies ePBR/NBAR classification maps applications to forwarding classes, dispatched to per-color child policies Resiliency TI-LFA with node/SRLG/linecard-disjoint tiebreakers BFD-triggered, sub-50 ms, Flex-Algo-constraint-aware Telemetry Performance measurement probes at 3-second intervals Delay flooded into IS-IS; delay-metric policies re-optimize around congestion with zero packet loss Multicast BGP MVPN + ingress replication, End.DTMC4 Anycast RP + MSDP at the hubs; core stays multicast-stateless

docs.title: Design Rules Worth Stealing
docs.text:
The CVD codifies several rules that generalize beyond defense networks:

One locator block per Flex-Algo slice. Slice isolation is enforced through locator reachability, not a BGP attribute — BGP never signals "this route is Algo 128". Each slice gets its own 32-bit uSID block (e.g. FCBB:DEAA::/32 base, FCBB:DEAF::/32 secure, FCBB:DEAB::/32 low-latency), each VRF binds to the locator of its slice, and the IGP's per-algorithm SPF does the rest. A classified VRF bound to the Algo-128 locator cannot traverse an unencrypted link, because that link doesn't exist in the Algo-128 topology — even during TI-LFA failover, since the repair path is computed within the same algorithm's constraints.

Affinity-tag your cryptographic planes. Interfaces are tagged SECURED (MACsec/PQC-IPsec) or UNSECURED (plain internet) via IS-IS affinity maps. Both Flex-Algo definitions and SR-TE policies reference these affinities, so encryption becomes a routable constraint rather than an operational convention.

next-hop-unchanged at inter-domain boundaries. Default eBGP next-hop rewriting forces the ASBR to decapsulate, VRF-lookup, and re-encapsulate every packet — reintroducing state at the border and truncating end-to-end SR-TE (ODN policies would terminate at the ASBR instead of the real egress PE). Preserving the next-hop keeps ASBRs as pure control-plane reflectors and the data plane stateless end to end. See Inter-Domain SRv6.

Slicing vs. flow steering are different tools. Flex-Algo isolates entire prefixes/VRFs at the IGP level with no packet inspection; Per-Flow Policies differentiate applications to the same destination via edge classification. The order of operations: SR-TE policy match first, Flex-Algo routing-table fallback second.

Budget MTU for the full encapsulation stack. A tactical packet can carry Type-1 inline encryption (+~60 B), SRv6 encapsulation (+40 B), GRE (+24–44 B), IPsec (+~56–70 B), and MACsec (+32 B). The validated numbers: tunnel MTU 1400 (1300 over MACsec E-Lines, including clns mtu and IS-IS lsp-mtu), TCP MSS clamped to 1220/1200 at the LAN edge, and tunnel PMTUD enabled.

docs.title: Validated Case Study
docs.text: The CVD closes with "VeriVault", a fictional defense contractor migrating from an MPLS-TE + SD-WAN patchwork to the SRv6 fabric using three standardized site profiles (compact tactical field sites, dual-router processing centers, and redundant DC hubs with a dedicated route reflector). Migration is a phased parallel build: stand up the SRv6 fabric alongside the legacy WAN, cut over the DC hubs, bridge legacy and new domains via an NNI at the aggregation layer, then migrate spokes site by site. See Interworking & Migration for the general patterns.

  4. RFC 7383 - IKEv2 Message Fragmentation - Required for ML-KEM's large key payloads to survive fragment-dropping firewalls
  5. NIST FIPS 203 - Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) - The standardized post-quantum KEM (formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber)
  6. NIST FIPS 204 - Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) - Post-quantum signatures used for secure boot and device identity
  7. NSA Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0 - The compliance mandate driving PQC timelines in national security networks

docs.title: Network Slicing with SRv6
docs.text: Network slicing creates isolated logical networks over a shared physical infrastructure, each with its own topology, SIDs, QoS guarantees, and service-level objectives. SRv6 enables slicing natively through the combination of Flex-Algorithm, QoS policies, and SR Policy color steering — no additional overlay protocols required.

docs.title: What Is Network Slicing?
docs.text:
A network slice is an end-to-end logical partition that provides:

  • Topology isolation — each slice uses a different set of paths through the network
  • Resource guarantees — dedicated bandwidth, latency, or jitter targets per slice
  • Independent policies — each slice can have its own TE, protection, and routing constraints

docs.title: Slicing vs VPN vs Traffic Engineering
docs.text:
Concept Layer Isolation Type Mechanism VPN (VRF) L3 Routing table isolation Separate FIBs per customer Traffic Engineering Path Path selection SR Policy / RSVP-TE Network Slice Topology + Resources Topology + bandwidth + QoS Flex-Algo + QoS + Color

VPNs ride on slices

Network slicing and VPNs are complementary. A customer VPN can be mapped onto a specific slice (e.g., "Gold slice") to get both routing isolation and transport-level SLA guarantees.

docs.title: SRv6 Slicing Building Blocks
docs.text:
SRv6 network slicing combines three mechanisms:

  • Flex-Algorithm Topology Slicing → Network Slice
  • QoS Policy Resource Slicing → Network Slice
  • SR Policy + Color Service Steering → Network Slice
  • Network Slice → Slice 1: Low Latency
  • Network Slice → Slice 2: High Bandwidth
  • Network Slice → Slice 3: Best Effort
graph TB
    subgraph Slice Architecture
        FA[Flex-Algorithm<br/>Topology Slicing] --> SLICE[Network Slice]
        QOS[QoS Policy<br/>Resource Slicing] --> SLICE
        COLOR[SR Policy + Color<br/>Service Steering] --> SLICE
    end
    SLICE --> S1[Slice 1: Low Latency]
    SLICE --> S2[Slice 2: High Bandwidth]
    SLICE --> S3[Slice 3: Best Effort]

docs.title: 1. Flex-Algorithm (Topology Slicing)
docs.text:
Each slice maps to a Flex-Algorithm (128-255), which computes an independent topology based on constraints like latency, affinity, or TE metric. Every node in the slice advertises a per-algorithm locator and SID.

Slice Flex-Algo Constraint Effect Low Latency 128 Minimize delay metric Uses only low-latency links High Bandwidth 129 Minimize TE metric + affinity Avoids congested links Best Effort 0 (default) Minimize IGP metric Uses all links

For full details, see Flex-Algorithm.

docs.title: 2. QoS (Resource Slicing)
docs.text:
Flex-Algorithm provides topology isolation, but bandwidth guarantees require QoS policies:

  • DSCP marking per slice — each slice gets a distinct DSCP value
  • Per-slice scheduling — strict priority, weighted fair queuing, or bandwidth reservation
  • Policers — rate limiting per slice to enforce SLA boundaries

For full details, see QoS.

docs.title: 3. SR Policy + Color (Service Steering)
docs.text:
BGP color extended communities map services into the correct slice:

  1. Service route is advertised with a color community (e.g., color 128 = low-latency slice)
  2. Headend PE matches the color to an SR Policy or Flex-Algo SID
  3. Traffic is steered into the slice automatically

For full details, see SR Policy.

docs.title: Use Case 1: 5G Network Slicing
docs.text:
3GPP defines standardized slice types that map directly to SRv6 Flex-Algorithm slices:

3GPP Slice Type SST Description SRv6 Mapping eMBB 1 Enhanced Mobile Broadband Flex-Algo 129 (bandwidth-optimized) URLLC 2 Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Flex-Algo 128 (latency-optimized) mMTC 3 Massive Machine-Type Comm. Flex-Algo 0 (best effort)

docs.title: End-to-End 5G Slice
docs.text:
• RAN / gNB → Transport PE (URLLC: Algo 128)
  • RAN / gNB → Transport PE (eMBB: Algo 129)
  • Transport PE → SRv6 Core (Slice-specific path)
  • SRv6 Core → UPF / Core PE
graph LR
    RAN[RAN / gNB] -->|URLLC: Algo 128| TR1[Transport PE]
    RAN -->|eMBB: Algo 129| TR1
    TR1 -->|Slice-specific path| CORE((SRv6 Core))
    CORE --> UPF[UPF / Core PE]

The SRv6 MUP (Mobile User Plane) behaviors from RFC 9433 integrate with Flex-Algo slicing to provide end-to-end slice awareness from RAN to core.

For the full 5G transport architecture, see 5G Transport.

docs.title: Use Case 2: Enterprise Network Slicing
docs.text:
Enterprise operators use slicing to offer tiered services with guaranteed SLAs:

Tier Flex-Algo DSCP QoS Policy SLA Target Gold 128 EF (46) Strict priority, 30% BW guarantee <10ms latency, 99.999% Silver 129 AF31 (26) Weighted fair queue, 50% BW <50ms latency, 99.99% Bronze 0 BE (0) Best effort, remaining BW Best effort

docs.title: Configuration Example
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! Flex-Algorithm definitions
router isis CORE
 flex-algo 128
  metric-type delay
  advertise-definition
 !
 flex-algo 129
  affinity exclude-any CONGESTED
  advertise-definition
 !
!

!! Per-slice locators
segment-routing
 srv6
  locators
   locator GOLD
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fc00:128:1::/48
    algorithm 128
   !
   locator SILVER
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fc00:129:1::/48
    algorithm 129
   !
   locator BEST-EFFORT
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fc00:0:1::/48
   !
  !
 !
!

!! Color steering for VPN → slice mapping
route-policy SET-GOLD-COLOR
 set extcommunity color 128
end-policy

router bgp 65000
 vrf GOLD-CUSTOMER
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   route-policy SET-GOLD-COLOR out
  !
 !
!

# Flex-Algo definition
set protocols isis flex-algorithm 128 metric-type min-delay
set protocols isis flex-algorithm 129 affinity exclude CONGESTED

# Per-slice locators
set routing-options segment-routing-v6 locator GOLD fc00:128:1::/48 algorithm 128
set routing-options segment-routing-v6 locator SILVER fc00:129:1::/48 algorithm 129
set routing-options segment-routing-v6 locator BEST-EFFORT fc00:0:1::/48

# Color steering
set policy-options community GOLD-COLOR color 128
set policy-options policy-statement GOLD-EXPORT term 1 then community add GOLD-COLOR

docs.title: Use Case 3: Data Center Slicing
docs.text:
In CLOS fabrics, Flex-Algorithm slicing isolates different traffic types:

Slice Purpose Constraint GPU Fabric AI/ML training traffic Low-latency links, RDMA-capable paths Storage NVMe-oF, iSCSI High-bandwidth, redundant paths Management SSH, SNMP, telemetry Best-effort, any path

Each slice gets its own Flex-Algo and locator, ensuring that GPU traffic never contends with storage replication on the same path.

For CLOS fabric design, see CLOS & Load Balancing. For AI/ML-specific networking, see AI/ML Networks.

docs.title: SID Allocation per Slice
docs.text:
Each slice requires a dedicated locator block. Plan allocations carefully:

Slice Algorithm Locator Block Nodes Best Effort 0 fc00:0::/32 All Low Latency 128 fc00:128::/32 All High Bandwidth 129 fc00:129::/32 All Custom 130 fc00:130::/32 Subset

docs.title: Monitoring and SLA Assurance
docs.text:
Per-slice monitoring is essential for SLA compliance:

  • SRPM (SR Performance Measurement) — per-slice delay/loss probes using slice-specific SIDs. See SRPM.
  • Telemetry — per-slice counters on interfaces and forwarding entries. See Telemetry.
  • IPFIX — per-slice flow records using RFC 9487 SRv6 Information Elements.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
Factor Limit Notes Flex-Algorithms 128 (128-255) Practical limit: 4-8 slices per network Locators per node Platform-dependent Typically 8-16 concurrent locators FIB impact N x nodes Each algorithm multiplies the IPv6 FIB by the number of participating nodes

FIB scaling

Each additional Flex-Algorithm adds a full set of locator routes to the FIB. With 1000 nodes and 4 algorithms, expect ~4000 locator entries. Plan hardware FIB capacity accordingly.

docs.title: Comparison: SRv6 Slicing vs Alternatives
docs.text: Aspect VRF-Only MPLS TE Tunnels FlexE SRv6 Flex-Algo Isolation Routing only Path only Physical (TDM) Topology + path Complexity Low High (RSVP state) Medium (hardware) Low-medium Scalability High Limited (~10K tunnels) Low (port-based) High SLA granularity Coarse (per VRF) Fine (per tunnel) Exact (hard isolation) Fine (per algorithm) Automation Limited Manual Manual Color steering + ODN Hardware Any Any FlexE-capable Any SRv6-capable

docs.title: Satellite Connectivity with SRv6
docs.text: As LEO (Low Earth Orbit) satellite constellations become viable for enterprise and telecom transport, SRv6 is emerging as the natural overlay technology for delivering carrier-grade services over satellite links.

docs.title: The Opportunity
docs.text: LEO satellites offer low-latency broadband to locations where fiber is impractical — remote sites, maritime, disaster recovery, temporary deployments. The challenge is delivering carrier-grade L2/L3 services reliably over this transport.

docs.title: Why SRv6 for Satellite?
docs.text: Challenge SRv6 Solution IPv6-native transport LEO constellations like Starlink use IPv6 natively — SRv6 fits without protocol translation Variable latency and jitter SR Policies can steer traffic across satellite + terrestrial paths based on real-time conditions Service delivery EVPN and L3VPN over SRv6 enable MEF-compliant Ethernet services end-to-end Resiliency Multiple segment lists provide fast failover between satellite and terrestrial backup paths Simplified operations No MPLS signaling needed over the satellite link Edge compute SRv6 service chaining enables MEC (Multi-access Edge Computing) at remote sites

docs.title: Architecture Concept
docs.text:
A typical SRv6-over-satellite architecture uses SRv6/EVPN as the overlay, with the satellite link as one of potentially multiple underlay transport options:

  • Remote Site 1 → Head Office / Hub (LEO Satellite)
  • Remote Site 2 → Head Office / Hub (LEO Satellite)
  • Remote Site 1 → Head Office / Hub (Terrestrial Backup)
graph LR
    RS1[Remote Site 1] -->|LEO Satellite| HQ[Head Office / Hub]
    RS2[Remote Site 2] -->|LEO Satellite| HQ
    RS1 -.->|Terrestrial Backup| HQ

    subgraph SRv6/EVPN Overlay
        RS1
        RS2
        HQ
    end

docs.title: Key Design Elements
docs.text:
• Dual transport: Satellite as primary, terrestrial (4G/LTE, MPLS, internet) as backup
  • MEF L2 EVCs: Ethernet Virtual Connections with primary and backup paths for resiliency
  • SRv6/EVPN overlay: Unified service delivery regardless of underlay transport type
  • Performance monitoring: Assurance sensors at each site for SLA validation
  • Compact CPE: Low-power routers at remote sites suited for space-constrained deployments

docs.title: Applicable SRv6 Behaviors
docs.text: Behavior Use in Satellite Scenario End.DT4 / End.DT6 VRF termination at hub site End.DX2 Point-to-point L2 service (E-Line) across satellite End.DT2 Multipoint L2 service (E-LAN) for branch connectivity H.Encaps.Red Reduced encapsulation to minimize overhead on bandwidth-constrained satellite links

docs.title: Industry Validation
docs.text:
Multiple vendors and operators have demonstrated or deployed SRv6 over satellite transport, including validated architectures combining compact router platforms with LEO satellite connectivity for enterprise and telecom use cases. These are typically showcased at industry events such as Cisco Live and Mobile World Congress.

In 2026, Rivada Space Networks and Cisco published a joint whitepaper, "Creating a Blueprint for Advanced Data Networking from Space", outlining a secure, resilient space-based enterprise network built on a LEO constellation with Cisco routing technology — a transport profile where the overlay design principles on this page apply directly.

Overhead matters over satellite

Satellite bandwidth is expensive. SRv6 uSID compression (RFC 9800) is especially valuable here — it reduces SRv6 overhead by up to 83% compared to classic SRv6, making it practical even on bandwidth-constrained satellite links.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:

  • Traffic Engineering - SR Policies for path optimization
  • uSID / SRv6 Compression - Reducing overhead for constrained links
  • RFC 9252 - BGP Overlay Services (EVPN with SRv6)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. RFC 9252 - BGP Overlay Services Based on SRv6 - Defines EVPN and L3VPN signaling over SRv6 transport
  2. RFC 9800 - Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding - SRv6 uSID compression, critical for bandwidth-constrained links
  3. ETSI ISG IPE: IPv6 Enhanced Innovation - ETSI work on IPv6/SRv6 for diverse transport including non-terrestrial networks
  4. Rivada & Cisco: Creating a Blueprint for Advanced Data Networking from Space - Joint whitepaper on a secure, resilient space-based enterprise network over a LEO constellation

docs.title: SD-WAN & SRv6
docs.text: Traditional SD-WAN solutions build encrypted overlays (IPsec/GRE) on top of the WAN to steer traffic between branch sites. SRv6 introduces a fundamentally different model: the underlay itself becomes programmable, reducing or eliminating the need for tunnel overlays and enabling end-to-end traffic engineering from branch to data center to cloud.

docs.title: Traditional SD-WAN Architecture
docs.text:
In a conventional SD-WAN deployment, an orchestrator pushes policies to edge devices (CPEs) that build overlay tunnels across one or more WAN transports:

  • Branch 1 → Internet (IPsec Tunnel)
  • Branch 1 → MPLS WAN (IPsec Tunnel)
  • Branch 2 → Internet (IPsec Tunnel)
  • Branch 2 → MPLS WAN (IPsec Tunnel)
  • Internet → Hub / DC
  • MPLS WAN → Hub / DC
  • Orchestrator → Branch 1 (Policies)
  • Orchestrator → Branch 2 (Policies)
graph LR
    B1[Branch 1] -->|IPsec Tunnel| INET((Internet))
    B1 -->|IPsec Tunnel| MPLS((MPLS WAN))
    B2[Branch 2] -->|IPsec Tunnel| INET
    B2 -->|IPsec Tunnel| MPLS
    INET --> HUB[Hub / DC]
    MPLS --> HUB
    ORCH[Orchestrator] -.->|Policies| B1
    ORCH -.->|Policies| B2

    style INET fill:#5c6bc026,stroke:#5c6bc0
    style MPLS fill:#5c6bc026,stroke:#5c6bc0

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: Challenge Impact Overlay complexity Every site-to-site path requires tunnel establishment and maintenance No underlay visibility SD-WAN controller cannot influence how traffic traverses the SP network Double encapsulation IPsec + GRE + SP MPLS = significant overhead and MTU issues Limited SLA enforcement Application SLAs depend on best-effort underlay performance Scalability Full mesh of tunnels grows as O(n²) with number of sites

docs.title: SRv6-Enhanced SD-WAN
docs.text:
With SRv6, the service provider's network becomes an active participant in SD-WAN policy enforcement:

  • Branch 1 CPE → PE1 (SRv6 Policy)
  • Branch 2 CPE → PE2 (SRv6 Policy)
  • PE1 → SRv6 Core (SRv6 TE)
  • PE2 → SRv6 Core (SRv6 TE)
  • SRv6 Core → Data Center (SRv6)
  • SRv6 Core → Cloud (SRv6)
  • SD-WAN Controller → PE1 (SR Policies)
  • SD-WAN Controller → PE2 (SR Policies)
graph LR
    B1[Branch 1<br/>CPE] -->|SRv6 Policy| PE1[PE1]
    B2[Branch 2<br/>CPE] -->|SRv6 Policy| PE2[PE2]
    PE1 <-->|SRv6 TE| CORE((SRv6 Core))
    PE2 <-->|SRv6 TE| CORE
    CORE <-->|SRv6| DC[Data Center]
    CORE <-->|SRv6| CLOUD[Cloud]
    CTRL[SD-WAN Controller] -.->|SR Policies| PE1
    CTRL -.->|SR Policies| PE2

docs.title: Key benefits
docs.text: Benefit Description No tunnel overlays SRv6 provides native path steering — no IPsec/GRE tunnels needed for routing Underlay-aware steering SD-WAN controller programs SR Policies directly on PEs for end-to-end path control Single encapsulation One SRv6 header replaces IPsec + GRE + MPLS stack SLA guarantees Flex-Algo provides latency/bandwidth-constrained paths in the underlay Linear scaling No full mesh — traffic is source-routed via segment lists

docs.title: Model 1: SP-Managed SD-WAN with SRv6 Underlay
docs.text:
The service provider offers SD-WAN as a managed service with SRv6 as the transport:

  • CPE connects to the nearest PE via a simple L3 handoff
  • PE applies SR Policies based on application classification
  • SD-WAN controller translates application intent into SR Policies
  • End-to-end SLA is enforced by the SRv6 underlay (Flex-Algo)

This is the tightest integration — the SD-WAN controller speaks directly to the SR-PCE.

docs.title: Model 2: Enterprise SD-WAN over SRv6 VPN
docs.text:
The enterprise runs its own SD-WAN solution, and the SP provides SRv6-based VPN connectivity:

  • CPE builds standard SD-WAN overlays (IPsec)
  • SP network provides L3VPN over SRv6 with per-VPN SLA via Flex-Algo slices
  • Enterprise gets guaranteed performance without managing the underlay

The SD-WAN overlays ride on top of SRv6 VPN slices, each with different QoS characteristics.

docs.title: Model 3: SRv6-Native CPE
docs.text:
The CPE itself is SRv6-aware and can push segment lists:

  • CPE classifies traffic and encapsulates with SRv6 headers
  • No overlay tunnels — the CPE speaks SRv6 natively
  • Path selection is done at the branch based on application policy
  • Works with Linux-based or whitebox CPEs running FRRouting or SONiC

docs.title: Application-Aware Routing
docs.text:
SRv6 SD-WAN can classify traffic by application and steer each class to a different path:

Application Flex-Algo Path Characteristic Example Voice/Video (UCaaS) 128 Minimum latency Zoom, Teams Business Critical (ERP) 129 High reliability SAP, Oracle Bulk Transfer 130 Maximum bandwidth Backups, replication Internet/SaaS 0 (default) Best effort Web browsing

Each application class maps to a different SR Policy with a specific Flex-Algo constraint, ensuring traffic follows the optimal path without tunnel manipulation.

docs.title: Comparison: Traditional SD-WAN vs SRv6 SD-WAN
docs.text:
Aspect Traditional SD-WAN SRv6 SD-WAN Transport IPsec/GRE overlays Native SRv6 (no tunnels) Path control Overlay-level only End-to-end underlay + overlay Encapsulation overhead IPsec + GRE + MPLS (~60-80 bytes) SRv6 (~40 bytes) SLA enforcement Application-level probes Network-level (Flex-Algo constraints) Scalability O(n²) tunnel mesh Source-routed (stateless core) Multi-cloud Per-cloud tunnel config Unified SRv6 domain Encryption Always (IPsec) Optional (IPsec over SRv6 when needed) Underlay visibility None Full (telemetry, IOAM)

Encryption

SRv6 provides path control but not encryption. For confidentiality, IPsec can still be applied selectively — only on paths that traverse untrusted networks (e.g., internet), while private WAN segments use SRv6 natively without encryption overhead.

docs.title: Network Slicing for SD-WAN
docs.text:
SRv6 network slicing creates dedicated virtual networks per customer or application tier:

  • Branch CPE → Slice 1: Real-Time Algo 128 - Low Latency
  • Branch CPE → Slice 2: Business Algo 129 - High Reliability
  • Branch CPE → Slice 3: Best Effort Algo 0 - Default
  • Slice 1: Real-Time Algo 128 - Low Latency → Data Center
  • Slice 2: Business Algo 129 - High Reliability → Data Center
  • Slice 3: Best Effort Algo 0 - Default → Data Center
graph TB
    subgraph SD-WAN Slices
        S1[Slice 1: Real-Time<br/>Algo 128 - Low Latency]
        S2[Slice 2: Business<br/>Algo 129 - High Reliability]
        S3[Slice 3: Best Effort<br/>Algo 0 - Default]
    end

    CPE[Branch CPE] --> S1
    CPE --> S2
    CPE --> S3

    S1 --> DC[Data Center]
    S2 --> DC
    S3 --> DC

    style S1 fill:#66bb6a26,stroke:#66bb6a
    style S2 fill:#5c6bc026,stroke:#5c6bc0
    style S3 fill:#ff980026,stroke:#ff9800

Each slice provides hard isolation — traffic in one slice cannot impact another, and each has its own topology computed by the IGP.

docs.title: Service Chaining with SRv6
docs.text: Service Function Chaining (SFC) is the ability to steer traffic through an ordered set of network functions — firewalls, IDS/IPS, load balancers, DPI engines, NAT, WAN optimizers, etc. SRv6 provides one of the most elegant solutions for SFC by encoding the entire service chain as a segment list.

docs.title: The Problem with Traditional SFC
docs.text:
Without SRv6, service chaining typically relies on:

  • Manual VLAN/VRF stitching — each service function connected via dedicated VLANs, brittle and hard to change
  • Policy-Based Routing (PBR) — complex ACLs at every hop, doesn't scale
  • NSH (Network Service Header) — RFC 8300 overlay, requires all functions to support NSH
  • Traffic steering appliances — dedicated boxes that redirect traffic, adding cost and latency

These approaches share common pain points:

Problem Impact Topology dependent Service functions must be physically or logically adjacent Static chains Changing the order requires reconfiguring multiple devices State overhead Per-flow state at every classifier and service function Scalability Each new service in the chain multiplies complexity

docs.title: How SRv6 Solves Service Chaining
docs.text: With SRv6, the entire service chain is expressed as a segment list in the packet header. The ingress node encapsulates the packet once, and the network steers it through each function automatically.

docs.title: Key Principle
docs.text:
Each service function (or the node hosting it) is assigned an SRv6 SID. The segment list defines the chain:

Segment List: [FW::1, IDS::1, LB::1, Egress::DT4]
                 ↓        ↓        ↓         ↓
              Firewall → IDS → Load Balancer → Decap & deliver

The packet traverses the chain by following the SRv6 forwarding mechanics (decrement Segments Left, update DA, forward).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Client → Ingress PE
  • Ingress PE → Firewall (DA=FW::1 SL=3)
  • Firewall → IDS/IPS (DA=IDS::1 SL=2)
  • IDS/IPS → Load Balancer (DA=LB::1 SL=1)
  • Load Balancer → Egress PE (DA=Egress::DT4 SL=0)
  • Egress PE → Server
graph LR
    C[Client] --> I[Ingress PE]
    I -->|"DA=FW::1<br/>SL=3"| FW[Firewall]
    FW -->|"DA=IDS::1<br/>SL=2"| IDS[IDS/IPS]
    IDS -->|"DA=LB::1<br/>SL=1"| LB[Load Balancer]
    LB -->|"DA=Egress::DT4<br/>SL=0"| E[Egress PE]
    E --> S[Server]

docs.title: Packet Walk: Service Chain
docs.text: Let's trace a packet through a chain: Client → Firewall → IDS → Server

docs.title: Step 1: Ingress Classification
docs.text:
The ingress PE matches the traffic (e.g., by source IP, DSCP, VRF) and encapsulates with an SRv6 header containing the service chain:

Original:
  [IPv4: Client → Server][Payload]

After encapsulation:
  [IPv6: Ingress → FW::1]
  [SRH: SL=2, List=[Egress::DT4, IDS::1, FW::1]]
  [IPv4: Client → Server]
  [Payload]

docs.title: Step 2: Firewall (SRv6 Proxy)
docs.text:
The packet arrives at the firewall node. The SRv6 behavior depends on whether the firewall is SRv6-aware or not:

SRv6-Aware FunctionSRv6-Unaware Function (Proxy)

The firewall natively understands SRv6. It processes the packet, inspects the inner payload, applies its policy, and forwards with Segments Left decremented:

FW receives:  DA=FW::1, SL=2
FW processes:  Inspect payload, apply firewall policy
FW forwards:   DA=IDS::1, SL=1

Most existing network functions don't understand SRv6. SRv6 proxy behaviors solve this by stripping the SRv6 header before the function and re-adding it after:

Proxy receives:  [IPv6+SRH][IPv4][Payload]
Proxy strips:    [IPv4][Payload]  ← Sent to firewall
Firewall processes: Normal IPv4 inspection
Proxy re-adds:   [IPv6+SRH][IPv4][Payload]  ← SRH restored
Proxy forwards:  DA=IDS::1, SL=1

docs.title: Step 3: IDS
docs.text: Same process — the IDS inspects the packet (directly or via proxy), then the packet continues to the next SID.

docs.title: Step 4: Egress Decapsulation
docs.text: The egress PE matches Egress::DT4 (End.DT4 behavior), removes the SRv6 encapsulation, and delivers the original IPv4 packet to the server.

docs.title: SRv6 Proxy Behaviors
docs.text:
The key innovation for service chaining is the set of proxy behaviors defined in the IETF SR Service Programming draft. These allow SRv6-unaware functions to participate in an SRv6 service chain:

Behavior Name How It Works End.AS Static Proxy Caches the SRH, strips it before the function, restores it after. Static: one cached SRH per SID. End.AD Dynamic Proxy Like End.AS but dynamically caches the SRH per-packet. Supports functions that modify the inner packet. End.AM Masquerading Proxy Modifies the outer IPv6 DA to the function's address while caching the SRH. The function sees a normal IPv6 packet and routes it back.

docs.title: End.AD (Dynamic Proxy) — Most Common
docs.text:
Service FunctionSRv6 Proxy NodeNetworkService FunctionSRv6 Proxy NodeNetworkIPv6+SRH+Inner packetCache SRH, strip outer headerInner packet only (IPv4/IPv6)Process (firewall, IDS, etc.)Processed inner packetRestore SRH, update SLIPv6+SRH+Inner packet (next SID)

This is critical because it means any existing network function (physical or virtual) can be inserted into an SRv6 service chain without modification.

docs.title: Dynamic Chain Modification
docs.text:
One of SRv6's most powerful advantages for SFC: changing the chain requires only updating the segment list at the ingress. No reconfiguration of intermediate nodes or service functions.

Operation What Changes Add a service Insert a new SID in the segment list Remove a service Remove the SID from the segment list Reorder services Change the order of SIDs Bypass a service Skip its SID (e.g., during maintenance) A/B test Different segment lists for different traffic classes

All of this happens at the ingress only — the rest of the network and the service functions themselves are unchanged.

docs.title: Advantages over Traditional SFC
docs.text: Aspect Traditional SFC SRv6 Service Chaining Topology dependency Functions must be adjacent Functions can be anywhere Chain modification Reconfigure every hop Update segment list at ingress only Per-flow state in network Required at every classifier None (stateless forwarding) Legacy function support Often requires function modification Proxy behaviors (End.AS/AD/AM) Metadata transport NSH or custom headers SRH TLVs TE integration Separate mechanism Native (SR Policies) Scalability O(functions × classifiers) O(1) — just a segment list

docs.title: SFC + Traffic Engineering
docs.text:
SRv6 uniquely combines service chaining with traffic engineering in a single segment list:

Segment List: [LowLatencySpine::1, FW::1, IDS::1, Egress::DT4]
               └── TE segment ──┘  └── Service chain ──────────┘

The same packet can be steered through a specific network path and a specific service chain, all encoded in one SRH.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Network Programming - SRv6 behaviors including End.AD, End.AS
  • SRH Mechanics & Packet Walk - How SRH forwarding works
  • Traffic Engineering - Combining TE with service chains
  • Host-Based SRv6 - VPP and eBPF for service functions

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. RFC 8986 - SRv6 Network Programming - Defines base SRv6 endpoint behaviors used in service chains
  2. RFC 7665 - Service Function Chaining (SFC) Architecture - IETF architecture for creating and maintaining Service Function Chains
  3. draft-ietf-spring-sr-service-programming - Defines SR proxy behaviors (End.AS, End.AD, End.AM) for SRv6-unaware service functions
  4. RFC 8300 - Network Service Header (NSH) - Alternative SFC approach for comparison with SRv6-based service chaining

docs.title: Traffic Engineering with SRv6
docs.text: SRv6 Traffic Engineering (TE) enables operators to steer traffic along explicit paths through the network, optimizing for latency, bandwidth, or other constraints.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Instead of relying on shortest-path routing alone, SRv6 TE defines SR Policies that specify explicit segment lists (paths) for traffic.

  • Ingress PE → P1 (Low Latency Path)
  • P1 → P2
  • P2 → Egress PE
  • Ingress PE → P3 (High BW Path)
  • P3 → P4
  • P4 → Egress PE
graph LR
    A[Ingress PE] -->|Low Latency Path| B[P1]
    B --> C[P2]
    C --> D[Egress PE]
    A -->|High BW Path| E[P3]
    E --> F[P4]
    F --> D

docs.title: SR Policy Components
docs.text: Component Description Headend The node where the policy is applied Color Identifies the intent (e.g., low-latency) Endpoint Destination of the policy Candidate Path One or more segment lists for the policy Segment List Ordered list of SIDs defining the path

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Low-latency routing for real-time applications
  • Bandwidth reservation for critical flows
  • Disjoint paths for redundancy
  • WAN optimization across multiple domains

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• VPN Services
  • SR Policy - Deep dive into ODN, PCE, BSID, and color steering
  • RFC 9256 - SR Policy Architecture

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. RFC 9256 - Segment Routing Policy Architecture - IETF standard defining SR Policy headend, color, endpoint, candidate paths, and segment lists
  2. RFC 9252 - BGP Overlay Services Based on SRv6 - BGP signaling procedures for SRv6-based L3VPN, EVPN, and internet services
  3. Configure SR-TE Policies - Cisco 8000 Series, IOS XR - Cisco IOS XR configuration guide for SR-TE policies on Cisco 8000 series routers

docs.title: VPN Services with SRv6
docs.text: SRv6 provides a native mechanism to deliver L3VPN and L2VPN services without MPLS, using SRv6 SIDs as service identifiers. The BGP control plane (RFC 9252) signals SRv6 SIDs instead of MPLS labels — same MP-BGP, same address families, fundamentally different data plane.

docs.title: SRv6-based L3VPN
docs.text: SRv6 L3VPN uses End.DT4 / End.DT6 behaviors to decapsulate traffic and perform a lookup in the appropriate VRF table.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. PE router receives customer IPv4/IPv6 traffic
  2. Encapsulates with outer IPv6 header + SRH
  3. Sets destination to the remote PE's VPN SID (End.DT4)
  4. Remote PE decapsulates and forwards to the correct VRF

BGP VPNv4 with SRv6

BGP Update:
  Prefix: 10.0.0.0/24
  Next-Hop: 2001:db8::2
  SRv6 SID: fc00:0:2::DT4  (End.DT4 behavior)
  VRF: CUSTOMER-A

docs.title: L3VPN Configuration
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! VRF definition with SRv6
vrf CUSTOMER-A
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  import route-target 65000:100
  export route-target 65000:100
 !
!

!! BGP VPNv4 with SRv6
router bgp 65000
 vrf CUSTOMER-A
  rd 65000:100
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
    alloc mode per-vrf
   !
  !
 !
!

set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A instance-type vrf
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A route-distinguisher 65000:100
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A vrf-target target:65000:100
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A protocols bgp group PE-MESH family inet segment-routing-v6

docs.title: L3VPN Verification
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XR 
show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf CUSTOMER-A
show cef vrf CUSTOMER-A ipv4 10.0.0.0/24 detail
show segment-routing srv6 sid

docs.title: L3VPN: MPLS vs SRv6
docs.text: Aspect MPLS L3VPN SRv6 L3VPN Label signaling MP-BGP + LDP/RSVP MP-BGP only Service identifier VPN label SRv6 SID (End.DT4/DT6) Transport MPLS LSP IPv6 native Complexity Higher (multiple protocols) Lower (IPv6 + BGP)

docs.title: SRv6-based L2VPN
docs.text: SRv6 L2VPN uses EVPN signaling (RFC 7432) with SRv6 endpoint behaviors to deliver Layer 2 services. This replaces VPLS and MPLS-based pseudowires with a native IPv6 data plane.

docs.title: L2VPN SID Behaviors
docs.text:
Behavior Service Type Description End.DX2 E-Line (VPWS) Decapsulate and cross-connect to a single L2 attachment circuit End.DX2V E-Line with VLAN Same as End.DX2 but with VLAN-aware cross-connect End.DT2U E-LAN (unicast) Decapsulate and perform MAC lookup in a bridge table (known unicast) End.DT2M E-LAN (BUM) Decapsulate and flood to all attachment circuits in the bridge domain

Defined in RFC 8986

L2VPN behaviors are defined in RFC 8986 - SRv6 Network Programming alongside the L3VPN behaviors (End.DT4, End.DT6).

docs.title: EVPN Route Types for L2VPN
docs.text:
EVPN uses five route types to signal L2 reachability. In an SRv6 context, the SRv6 SID replaces the MPLS label in each route:

Type Name Purpose in L2VPN 1 Ethernet Auto-Discovery Per-EVI/ESI route for fast convergence and aliasing 2 MAC/IP Advertisement Advertises learned MAC (and optionally IP) with SRv6 SID 3 Inclusive Multicast Signals BUM replication membership per bridge domain 4 Ethernet Segment DF election for multihomed CEs (see EVPN Multihoming) 5 IP Prefix Advertises IP routes for integrated routing and bridging (IRB)

docs.title: EVPN-VPWS (E-Line) with SRv6
docs.text:
EVPN-VPWS provides point-to-point L2 connectivity — the SRv6 equivalent of a traditional pseudowire. Each direction uses an End.DX2 SID for cross-connection.

  • CE1 → PE1 (Eth Frame)
  • PE1 → SRv6 Core (SRv6 DA=PE2::DX2)
  • SRv6 Core → PE2
  • PE2 → CE2 (Eth Frame)
graph LR
    CE1[CE1] -->|Eth Frame| PE1[PE1]
    PE1 -->|SRv6 DA=PE2::DX2| CORE((SRv6 Core))
    CORE --> PE2[PE2]
    PE2 -->|Eth Frame| CE2[CE2]

docs.title: VPWS Configuration
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! EVPN-VPWS with SRv6
l2vpn
 xconnect group VPWS-SRV6
  p2p CUSTOMER-A-VPWS
   interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
   neighbor evpn evi 100 target 1 source 1
    segment-routing srv6
     locator MAIN
    !
   !
  !
 !
!

!! EVPN signaling
evpn
 evi 100
  bgp
   route-target import 65000:100
   route-target export 65000:100
  !
  advertise-mac
 !
!

set routing-instances VPWS-A instance-type evpn-vpws
set routing-instances VPWS-A protocols evpn interface ge-0/0/1 vpws-service-id local 1
set routing-instances VPWS-A protocols evpn interface ge-0/0/1 vpws-service-id remote 1
set routing-instances VPWS-A route-distinguisher 65000:100
set routing-instances VPWS-A vrf-target target:65000:100
set routing-instances VPWS-A protocols evpn srv6 locator SRV6-LOC

docs.title: VPWS Verification
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XR 
show l2vpn xconnect group VPWS-SRV6 detail
show evpn evi 100 detail
show evpn evi 100 mac
show segment-routing srv6 sid | include DX2

docs.title: EVPN-ELAN (E-LAN) with SRv6
docs.text:
EVPN-ELAN provides multipoint L2 connectivity — a virtual switch spanning multiple sites. MAC addresses are learned via EVPN Type-2 routes in the control plane, and BUM traffic is handled via ingress replication.

  • CE1 → PE1
  • CE2 → PE2
  • CE3 → PE3
  • PE1 → PE2 (SRv6 End.DT2U)
  • PE2 → PE3 (SRv6 End.DT2U)
  • PE1 → PE3 (SRv6 End.DT2U)
graph TB
    CE1[CE1] --- PE1[PE1]
    CE2[CE2] --- PE2[PE2]
    CE3[CE3] --- PE3[PE3]
    PE1 <-->|SRv6 End.DT2U| PE2
    PE2 <-->|SRv6 End.DT2U| PE3
    PE1 <-->|SRv6 End.DT2U| PE3

docs.title: MAC Learning
docs.text:
Unlike traditional bridging, EVPN learns MACs in the control plane:

  1. PE learns a local MAC on an attachment circuit
  2. PE advertises the MAC via EVPN Type-2 route with an SRv6 SID (End.DT2U)
  3. Remote PEs install the MAC in their bridge table pointing to the SRv6 SID
  4. Known unicast traffic is sent directly to the owning PE — no flooding

docs.title: BUM Traffic Handling
docs.text:
Broadcast, Unknown unicast, and Multicast traffic uses:

  • EVPN Type-3 (Inclusive Multicast) routes to signal which PEs participate in the bridge domain
  • Ingress replication — the source PE sends a unicast SRv6 copy (with End.DT2M SID) to each remote PE
  • ARP/ND suppression — PEs proxy ARP/ND locally using EVPN Type-2 MAC/IP bindings, reducing broadcast floods

For large-scale BUM

When ingress replication doesn't scale, consider Tree-SID or BIER for bandwidth-efficient BUM delivery.

docs.title: ELAN Configuration
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! Bridge domain with EVPN + SRv6
l2vpn
 bridge group ELAN-SRV6
  bridge-domain BD-100
   interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/2
   !
   evi 200
   !
  !
 !
!

evpn
 evi 200
  bgp
   route-target import 65000:200
   route-target export 65000:200
  !
  advertise-mac
  !
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
  !
 !
!

set routing-instances ELAN-A instance-type mac-vrf
set routing-instances ELAN-A protocols evpn srv6 locator SRV6-LOC
set routing-instances ELAN-A bridge-domains BD-100 interface ge-0/0/2
set routing-instances ELAN-A route-distinguisher 65000:200
set routing-instances ELAN-A vrf-target target:65000:200
set routing-instances ELAN-A service-type vlan-aware

docs.title: E-Tree with SRv6
docs.text:
E-Tree provides hub-and-spoke L2 connectivity where leaf sites can communicate with root sites but not with other leaves.

Role Can Reach Cannot Reach Root All roots + all leaves — Leaf All roots only Other leaves

E-Tree is implemented using EVPN with leaf indication in the EVPN routes. PEs filter traffic based on the root/leaf role of the source and destination attachment circuits.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Hub-and-spoke VPN — branch offices communicate only through the data center
  • Multicast distribution — content pushed from root to leaves, no leaf-to-leaf

docs.title: EVPN-SRv6 vs EVPN-VXLAN vs EVPN-MPLS
docs.text: Aspect EVPN-SRv6 EVPN-VXLAN EVPN-MPLS Encapsulation IPv6 + SRH UDP + VXLAN MPLS labels Underlay IPv6 native IPv4 or IPv6 MPLS LSP (LDP/RSVP) Traffic engineering SR Policy / Flex-Algo Limited (ECMP only) RSVP-TE Service chaining SRv6 SID list Requires overlay Complex Network programming Native (SRv6 behaviors) None None MTU overhead 40B (IPv6) + 24B (SRH) 50B (UDP+VXLAN) 4-16B (labels) MAC learning Control plane (BGP EVPN) Control plane (BGP EVPN) Control plane (BGP EVPN) Typical deployment SP / large enterprise Data center Service provider

docs.title: SRv6 White Papers
docs.text:
Every public white paper and in-depth technical paper on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6), in one place. Each entry links to the original publisher and has a short summary written by the SRv6.md community, so you can pick the right paper before downloading 250 pages. Last checked: 22 October 2026.

Start here: the SRv6.md white paper

SRv6 White Paper 2026: Architecture, Design and Deployment is a vendor-neutral paper for architects: why operators adopt SRv6, uSID addressing, control plane choices, MTU, security, migration from MPLS and AI fabrics. Free, MIT licensed, available as PDF.

docs.title: Vendor white papers
docs.text: Paper Publisher Year Format What it covers Building Quantum-Resilient Mission-Critical Networks with SRv6 Cisco (Validated Design) 2026 HTML An SRv6 uSID (F3216) core on Cisco 8000 Secure Routers with IOS-XE, replacing MPLS/RSVP-TE, with TE, Flex-Algo slicing, TI-LFA, multicast VPN and post-quantum MACsec, IPsec and SSH. Includes complete site configurations. Our summary: Mission-Critical Networks. Cisco AI Inference White Paper: Architecture for Wide Area Networks Cisco 2026 HTML A provider and neocloud design for distributed AI inference: SRv6 uSID transport, one Flex-Algo plane per inference SLA with its own 5f00::/16 locator block, BGP color steering, and six ways to attach inference sites through the DCI. Our summary: SRv6 for AI Inference WAN. XR Multicast VPN with SRv6 — Dual Stack White Paper Cisco 2024 HTML, PDF How to keep unicast VPNs on an SRv6 core while multicast VPN runs over a separate IPv4 PIM core on IOS XR, with the BGP session split, configuration and limitations. Segment Routing IPv6 (SRv6) on Nokia routing platforms Nokia (application note) 2024 PDF The SRv6 data plane, SID structure and uSID, and the SR OS feature set (VPN services, TE, protection, OAM, SR-MPLS interworking), applied to mobile backhaul and multi-domain IPv6 backbones. Day One: Introduction to SRv6 Juniper Networks Books 2022 PDF, 253 pp A hands-on Junos book: migration preparation, SRv6 transport and services, TI-LFA, SRv6–MPLS interworking, Flex-Algo, micro-loop avoidance, SRv6-TE, EVPN-VPWS, multi-domain and cRPD. SRv6 Technology White Paper New H3C Technologies 2024 HTML, PDF Protocol reference for the SRH, SID structure and flavors, IS-IS SRv6 TLVs, G-SRv6 (32-bit G-SID) compression, BGP-EPE and BGP-LS for SRv6. Research and Deployment of SRv6 Header Compression Technology ZTE 2022 HTML Why full 128-bit SIDs cost bandwidth and chip resources, how G-SRv6 compresses them, how it compares with uSID, and China Mobile trials in Henan and Fujian. Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) xFlow Research 2023 PDF, 28 pp A tutorial paper on SR architecture, the SRH and its TLVs, SID format and behaviors, with the Bell Canada uSID deployment and open-source data planes (Linux, VPP).

docs.title: Operator and industry papers
docs.text: Paper Publisher Year Format What it covers Compressed SRv6 Deployment and Operations White Paper China Mobile, Bell Canada, Swisscom, Deutsche Telekom, Alibaba, MTN, Telefonica (IETF srv6ops) 2025 PDF, 33 pp Written by operators: both compression flavors of RFC 9800 (uSID and G-SRv6), interop history, SID planning, inter-AS design, visibility, and case studies from China Mobile and an African operator. The most practical operations paper available. EANTC Transport & Cloud Networks Interop Test Report 2026 EANTC 2026 PDF, 16 pp Independent multi-vendor interop results: SRv6 L3VPN, EVPN and IRB, BGP PIC with summarized locators, S-BFD, Flex-Algo, uSID SR Policies via PCEP and SRv6–SR-MPLS interworking. Static Configuration of SRv6 in SONiC (HLD) SONiC project 2024 HTML Design for configuring SRv6 locators and uSID SIDs statically in SONiC without BGP, for controller-driven fabrics. See SONiC & SAI. SRv6: A new approach for the evolution of IP networks IHS Markit 2019 PDF, 4 pp A short analyst brief on SRv6 for 5G transport: fewer protocols, network programming and SDN path computation. Useful for the business case.

docs.text:

The RFCs themselves are summarized in the RFCs & Standards section, starting with RFC 8754 (SRH), RFC 8986 (network programming) and RFC 9800 (compression).

docs.title: AI networking
docs.text: Paper Publisher Year Format What it covers Resilient AI Supercomputer Networking using MRC and SRv6 OpenAI, Microsoft, AMD, NVIDIA, Broadcom 2026 PDF, 18 pp Production GPU training clusters built from the MRC multipath transport, multi-plane two-tier Clos fabrics and static SRv6 uSID source routing, with failed paths bypassed in tens of microseconds. Also on arXiv. Our explainer: MRC and SRv6. Mostly about the transport; SRv6 appears as the path encoding.

docs.text: Paper Authors Year Format What it covers Segment Routing: a Comprehensive Survey of Research Activities, Standardization Efforts and Implementation Results Ventre, Salsano, Polverini, Cianfrani, Abdelsalam, Filsfils, Camarillo, Clad 2019 HTML, PDF The reference survey of SR and SRv6: standards, research, open-source and hardware implementations. See uSID Compression. Implementing IPv6 Segment Routing in the Linux Kernel Lebrun, Bonaventure (ANRW 2017) 2017 PDF The first open-source SRv6 implementation, merged in Linux 4.10, with measurements of encapsulation and HMAC cost. See Linux Kernel. SRPerf: a Performance Evaluation Framework for IPv6 Segment Routing Abdelsalam, Ventre, Scarpitta, Mayer, Salsano, Camarillo, Clad, Filsfils 2020 HTML, PDF An open benchmarking framework for SRv6 throughput and latency on Linux and VPP, which also found behaviors that were missing or wrong. docs.title: SRv6 White Paper 2026: Architecture, Design and Deployment
docs.text:
A vendor-neutral white paper on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) for network architects and engineering leaders. It explains why operators adopt SRv6, how to design an SRv6 network, and what to plan for when migrating from MPLS. Edition of October 2026. Written by Daniel Navas and the SRv6.md community, MIT licensed.

Download the PDF All SRv6 white papers

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
• SRv6 is source routing on plain IPv6. The ingress node writes the path into the packet as a list of IPv6 addresses called segment identifiers (SIDs). Every other router either forwards on the destination address like any IPv6 packet, or executes the instruction that the SID encodes.
  • It collapses the transport stack. One IPv6 data plane replaces MPLS, LDP, RSVP-TE and most of the tunnelling protocols that sit on top of them. VPNs, traffic engineering, fast reroute and network slicing all use the same encapsulation.
  • It is standardized and shipping. 23 RFCs are explicitly about SRv6, and 8 of the 11 implementations tracked in the support matrix support the compressed uSID encoding.
  • It is in production at large scale. 19 organizations have documented SRv6 in their own networks, from SoftBank, Rakuten Mobile and Reliance Jio to Microsoft, Meta, Alibaba Cloud and OpenAI.
  • uSID solved the overhead objection. Compressed SIDs carry up to six hops in a single 128-bit address, so most paths need no extension header at all.
  • AI changed the conversation in 2025–2026. Hyperscalers now use static SRv6 source routing inside GPU training fabrics to spread traffic across many network planes and to steer around failed paths in tens of microseconds.

docs.title: The problem with today's transport
docs.text: A typical service provider or large enterprise backbone runs IS-IS or OSPF, plus LDP or RSVP-TE for MPLS labels, plus BGP for services, plus VXLAN or GRE wherever MPLS does not reach (data centers, public clouds, hosts). Every boundary between these domains needs stitching, and every protocol needs its own operations, troubleshooting and scaling plan.

docs.title: What SRv6 changes
docs.text:
Area MPLS / RSVP-TE / LDP SRv6 Data plane MPLS labels, one more header format Native IPv6 Label distribution LDP or RSVP-TE None: SIDs are advertised by the IGP Traffic engineering Per-path state in every transit router State only at the headend Fast reroute RSVP-TE FRR or LFA with coverage gaps TI-LFA with full topology coverage Reach into DC, cloud and hosts Needs gateways or VXLAN stitching Any IPv6 node can be an endpoint Services L3VPN, EVPN over MPLS Same services, signalled by BGP with SRv6 SIDs

The operational gain comes from removing protocols, not from adding features. The SRv6 vs SR-MPLS comparison covers the trade-offs in detail, including when SR-MPLS is still the right call.

docs.title: Business drivers seen in public deployments
docs.text:
• 5G transport and mobile user plane. SoftBank built its 5G transport on SRv6 with Flex-Algo and later deployed the SRv6 Mobile User Plane on a commercial network. Rakuten Mobile migrated its IP transport to SRv6 uSID. See 5G transport.
  • One fabric from data center to WAN. Nebius runs SRv6 uSID L3VPN from the data center front end to the WAN and peering, replacing VXLAN-EVPN and SR-MPLS stitching, and Alibaba Cloud runs full-stack SRv6 on SONiC routers. See deployments and cloud-native backbones.
  • AI training networks. Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle use SRv6 inside GPU fabrics. Meta and Alibaba use it for traffic engineering between AI sites. See SRv6 for AI.
  • Public sector and mission-critical networks. Rijkswaterstaat migrated its national infrastructure backbone from MPLS to SRv6 uSID. Cisco has published a validated design for quantum-safe SRv6 fabrics. See mission-critical networks.

docs.title: SIDs are instructions
docs.text:
An SRv6 SID is a 128-bit IPv6 address with three parts: a locator that routes the packet to the node, a function that tells the node what to do, and optional arguments (SID structure). RFC 8986 defines the standard behaviors:

Behavior What the endpoint does Typical use End (uN) Move to the next segment Node waypoint for traffic engineering End.X (uA) Move to the next segment, send out a specific link Adjacency steering, TI-LFA repair paths End.DT4 / End.DT6 / End.DT46 Decapsulate and look up in a VRF L3VPN End.DX4 / End.DX6 Decapsulate and send to a fixed next hop Per-CE VPN End.DT2U / End.DT2M Decapsulate into a bridge domain EVPN End.B6.Encaps Apply a new SR Policy (binding SID) Inter-domain, scaling

docs.title: The packet
docs.text: The headend encapsulates the customer packet in an outer IPv6 header. The active segment is always the destination address, so transit routers that know nothing about SRv6 forward the packet on a normal IPv6 lookup. When a path needs more SIDs than the destination address can carry, the headend adds a Segment Routing Header (RFC 8754) with the list. The SRH packet walk shows each hop.

docs.title: uSID: the compressed form
docs.text:
RFC 9800 standardizes compressed SIDs. With the common F3216 format, a 32-bit block is followed by 16-bit micro-SIDs, so one 128-bit address carries up to six instructions. Each endpoint shifts its own uSID out of the address and forwards on the next one. In practice:

  • A VPN path with a few traffic engineering waypoints fits in the destination address alone: 40 bytes of overhead, the same as plain IPv6-in-IPv6, and no SRH.
  • Hardware only looks at the first 128 bits for most forwarding decisions, which keeps line rate on merchant silicon.

The uSID page and the SID decoder let you step through the shift operation on real addresses.

docs.title: Addressing plan
docs.text:
1. Pick the SID block. Either use a prefix from the IANA block reserved for SRv6 SIDs, 5f00::/16 (RFC 9602), or carve a block out of your own global prefix. 5f00::/16 makes edge filtering trivial because nothing outside the SR domain should ever use it.
  2. Choose the uSID format. F3216 (32-bit block, 16-bit uSID) is the default on most platforms and gives 65,536 uSID values per block, enough for node and local IDs in all but the largest single domains.
  3. Give every node a locator, typically a /48 inside the block. Keep loopbacks outside the SID block so management traffic and SRv6 traffic can be filtered separately.
  4. Reserve one locator per Flex-Algo if you plan to slice the network. Each algorithm gets its own locator per node, which is what makes the path selection automatic.

docs.title: Control plane
docs.text:
Function Recommended choice Reference Underlay and locator advertisement IS-IS (or OSPFv3) with SRv6 extensions RFC 9352, RFC 9513 Intent-based paths (low latency, disjoint planes) Flexible Algorithm RFC 9350, Flex-Algo Fast reroute TI-LFA RFC 9855, TI-LFA VPN and EVPN services BGP with SRv6 service SIDs RFC 9252, BGP overlay Explicit traffic engineering SR Policy from a PCE or BGP RFC 9256, RFC 9603, RFC 9830 Topology export to controllers BGP-LS RFC 9514

A sound default is IS-IS + Flex-Algo for the transport, BGP for services, SR Policy only where Flex-Algo cannot express the intent. Most networks need far fewer explicit policies than they had RSVP-TE tunnels, because Flex-Algo and TI-LFA cover the common cases with no per-path state.

Large data center fabrics often run BGP as the only routing protocol. SRv6 works there too: locators are advertised as ordinary IPv6 prefixes in BGP. The trade-off is that Flex-Algo and TI-LFA are IGP features, so a BGP-only fabric relies on ECMP and fast BGP convergence instead.

docs.title: Data plane and MTU
docs.text:
• Use reduced encapsulation (H.Encaps.Red), which leaves the first SID out of the SRH because it already sits in the destination address.
  • Budget 40 bytes for the outer IPv6 header, plus 8 + 16 × n bytes when an SRH is needed. With uSID most paths need no SRH.
  • Raise the core MTU so that customer packets at 1500 bytes (or 9000 in data centers) never fragment. Fragmentation of encapsulated traffic is the most common avoidable SRv6 incident.
  • Check each platform's limits on how many SIDs it can push at line rate and how deep it can parse the SRH. The support matrix lists uSID support per implementation.

docs.title: Services
docs.text: Each VRF gets an End.DT46 (or uDT46) SID from the PE's locator, which BGP advertises with the VPN routes. EVPN uses End.DT2U and End.DT2M. Because the service SID is routable inside the SR domain, any PE reaches any other PE with no tunnels to configure. See VPN services and EVPN multihoming.

docs.title: 4. Security
docs.text:
SRv6 turns IPv6 addresses into instructions, so the security model is about keeping those instructions inside a trusted domain (RFC 8754 section 5).

  1. Filter the SID block at every external interface. Drop packets from outside the domain whose destination falls in the SID block, and drop packets with an SRH arriving from outside. With 5f00::/16 this is one filter line.
  2. Never advertise locators to the Internet. Summarize the SID block internally and keep it out of eBGP exports.
  3. Use the SRH HMAC only where SRH packets must cross a less trusted segment. Most designs rely on edge filtering instead.
  4. Rate-limit SRv6 OAM and ICMPv6 generated by endpoints, as for any IPv6 control traffic.
  5. Encrypt where the transport is not trusted. SRv6 does not encrypt anything by itself. MACsec on links, or IPsec and post-quantum key exchange on top, are covered on the security page.

docs.title: 5. Operations
docs.text:
• Reachability and path tracing. Ping and traceroute work on SIDs with standard IPv6 tools, plus the SRv6 OAM extensions of RFC 9259. See OAM and troubleshooting.
  • Performance measurement. SR Performance Measurement (TWAMP-based delay and loss per link and per policy) feeds Flex-Algo latency metrics. See SRPM.
  • Flow visibility. IPFIX exports SRv6 fields (RFC 9487). Streaming telemetry covers locator and SID counters. See telemetry.
  • Packet captures. Wireshark decodes the SRH natively. The pcap library has reference captures for every common behavior.

docs.title: 6. Migration from MPLS
docs.text:
There is no flag day. Public migrations follow four patterns, detailed on the migration page:

Strategy When it fits Greenfield SRv6 New network or new region (Iliad launched a greenfield SRv6 network) Ship in the night Run SRv6 services in parallel with MPLS, move VRFs one by one SR-MPLS first, then SRv6 Hardware not yet SRv6-ready across the whole network Direct MPLS to SRv6 Hardware is SRv6-ready and an intermediate SR-MPLS step adds nothing (Rijkswaterstaat went straight from MPLS to SRv6 uSID)

Interworking gateways and binding SIDs connect SR-MPLS and SRv6 domains during the transition, so services keep working end to end while the core changes underneath.

A practical sequence:

  1. Enable IPv6 everywhere in the core and fix the MTU.
  2. Turn on SRv6 locators in the IGP. Nothing uses them yet, so the risk is low.
  3. Add TI-LFA for SRv6 and verify repair coverage.
  4. Move one low-risk VRF to SRv6 services, then the rest.
  5. Replace RSVP-TE tunnels with Flex-Algo or SR Policy.
  6. Retire LDP and RSVP-TE.

docs.title: 7. SRv6 in AI networks
docs.text:
AI training clusters with tens of thousands of GPUs need every link busy and recovery from failures faster than any routing protocol can converge. SRv6 gives the host control of the path:

  • The NIC encapsulates each packet with an SRv6 path chosen from many parallel planes, so traffic spreads evenly instead of colliding on hashed ECMP paths.
  • Switches are plain SRv6 transit nodes running a static configuration. No routing protocol is involved in choosing paths.
  • When a path fails, the NIC retires it within tens of microseconds and the job keeps running.

OpenAI's MRC design, built with Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom and NVIDIA for clusters of more than 100,000 GPUs, is the best documented example. See MRC and SRv6, AI fabric design and SRv6 vs ECMP, adaptive routing and UEC.

docs.title: 8. Adoption and outlook
docs.text:
• Standards: the core is complete (architecture, SRH, network programming, IGP and BGP extensions, compression, OAM). Current IETF work focuses on operations (the srv6ops working group), multicast, and path tracing. See the State of SRv6 2026.
  • Silicon and software: uSID runs at line rate on current merchant silicon and is supported by Cisco, Juniper, Nokia, Arista, Huawei, the Linux kernel, FRRouting, SONiC and several eBPF data planes.
  • Where it goes next: host-based SRv6 in Kubernetes and clouds (host SRv6), SRv6 in AI back-end and scale-across networks, and SRv6 as the single transport from the GPU to the WAN.

docs.title: 9. Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Design with uSID (F3216) from day one, even if the first phase uses few SIDs.
  2. Use 5f00::/16 or a dedicated block, and filter it at every edge before the first service goes live.
  3. Prefer Flex-Algo and TI-LFA over explicit policies. Keep SR Policy for the cases that need it.
  4. Fix the MTU first. Most SRv6 incidents in early deployments are MTU incidents.
  5. Migrate services one VRF at a time with SRv6 and MPLS running side by side.
  6. Lab it before you buy it. The free Containerlab and netlab labs on this site reproduce every design element above on a laptop.
